# Merit Order

An open-source LLM gateway that cuts LLM spend for day-to-day use, without changing how
people work.

Power grids dispatch generators in **merit order**: cheapest marginal cost first, with expensive
peaker plants switched on only when demand requires them. Merit Order does the same with tokens:

- **Routes** every session to the cheapest model and backend that meets the task's quality bar,
  counting what it would cost to rebuild the prompt cache somewhere else.
- **Runs open-weight models on your own GPUs** (via SkyPilot) when steady load makes that cheaper
  than paying per token, and turns them off when it doesn't. APIs (Bedrock, Foundry, Vertex,
  Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Mistral, ...) are always there for overflow.
- **Saves tokens**: automatic prompt caching, sticky sessions, cache-safe compression of huge tool
  outputs, and an optional response cache.
- **Shows the money**: every request is recorded with what it cost and what it would have cost
  without Merit Order, broken down by cause, per user, team, project, and day.

Point Claude Code, pi, OpenAI or Anthropic SDKs, or anything that speaks either API at it.

## Quickstart (no keys needed)

```bash
uv sync
cp .env.example .env            # set MERITORDER_DEV_KEY (and any provider keys you have)
uv run meritorder serve         # http://localhost:8080, reports UI at /ui/
```

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $MERITORDER_DEV_KEY" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]}'
```

With no provider keys, requests go to built-in mock backends. `uv run meritorder check` shows
which backends and models are live with the keys you've set. Without `MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL`,
storage is in memory; use Docker Compose for the real thing.

## Run the full stack with Docker

```bash
cp .env.example .env            # add at least one provider key
docker compose up -d            # gateway + worker + Postgres + Redis on :8080
docker compose exec gateway meritorder keys create --user you@example.com --role admin
```

Bedrock with your AWS profile (including SSO): `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.aws.yaml up -d`.
Kubernetes: `helm install mo charts/meritorder` (see [docs/07-deployment.md](docs/07-deployment.md)).

## Point your harness at it

```bash
meritorder login --gateway https://llm.example.com   # Entra sign-in; or: meritorder use-key <key>
meritorder setup pi                                    # adds a "meritorder" provider to pi
meritorder setup claude-code                           # sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL + apiKeyHelper
```

Or by hand: OpenAI-compatible clients use base URL `<gateway>/v1`; Claude Code uses
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=<gateway>`. Use `model: "auto"` to let Merit Order choose, or name a model
(`claude-sonnet`, `kimi-k3.1`, `qwen3-coder`, `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, ...) to pin it.

| Header | Effect |
|---|---|
| `X-Session-Id` | Groups requests into a session (pi sends it; otherwise inferred) |
| `X-Route-Floor: coding:4` | Minimum quality for `auto` routing |
| `X-Route-Hint: cheap` / `smart` | Nudges `auto` routing down or up |
| `X-MeritOrder-Tags: project=foo` | Cost-allocation tags for reports |
| `X-MeritOrder-Cache: on` / `off` | Use or bypass the response cache |
| `X-MeritOrder-Backend: <name>` | Admins only: pin a backend (testing, debugging) |

Responses carry `x-meritorder-model`, `x-meritorder-backend`, and (non-streaming)
`x-meritorder-cost-usd` / `x-meritorder-savings-usd`.

## What's in the box

| Area | Built |
|---|---|
| APIs | OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses (stateless), Anthropic Messages, and embeddings; streaming and not; pass-through when formats match, translation when they don't |
| Backends | Anthropic, Claude in Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, OpenRouter (incl. opt-in free tier), DeepSeek, Mistral, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, any OpenAI-compatible server |
| Models | Claude, GPT, and an open-weight catalog: DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen3-Coder, MiniMax, MiMo, Muse, Mistral/Devstral, Gemma, Nemotron, gpt-oss |
| Routing | Rule-based classifier → quality floor; marginal-cost router with cache rebuild cost, context-window checks, sticky sessions, fallback across backends |
| GPUs | Break-even controller (addressable demand, hysteresis), SkyPilot/SkyServe + vLLM provisioner, static servers, utilization from vLLM metrics, spill to API when saturated |
| Savings | Automatic prompt caching, lower reasoning effort for simple `auto` tasks (stable per session), deterministic tool-output compression, opt-in response cache |
| Identity | Virtual API keys, Entra/OIDC device-code login, roles (user, team lead, finance, admin) |
| Spend | Team and user monthly budgets, per-session spend caps (stops runaway agents), requests/tokens-per-minute limits, policy allow/deny lists for models and backends |
| Control panel | Web console at `/ui/` (Mantine, dark by default): live Dispatch view (merit-order stack from real traffic, live request feed, backend health, GPU fleet, needs-attention), Reports, GPUs (incl. what-if), Backends, Models, Teams, Keys, and Config (edit, validate, version history, restore; hot-reloads every gateway) |
| Reporting | Ledger with savings by cause, reports API, CSV, JSONL/CSV ledger export to a file or S3, `meritorder usage`, Prometheus metrics, budget/spike alerts, weekly digests |
| Deployment | Docker Compose, Helm chart, CI (tests, audits, Helm lint, Compose smoke test), signed multi-arch releases |

Not yet: billing reconciliation against provider invoices, Kubernetes-native GPU provisioning
(llm-d/KServe), a learned router, OpenTelemetry traces. See [docs/](docs/README.md) for the design.

## Development

```bash
uv sync && uv run pytest                     # gateway
cd ui && npm ci && npm run build             # reporting UI (served at /ui/)
uv run python scripts/fake_vllm.py           # a stand-in vLLM server for the GPU path
uv run python scripts/smoke_providers.py     # test every enabled provider through a running gateway
```

## License

AGPL-3.0-only. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

# Changelog

## 0.1.0 (unreleased)

First release.

**Gateway**
- OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses, Anthropic Messages, and embeddings; pass-through or
  translation between the formats, streaming included.
- Backends: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI,
  OpenRouter, direct open-model vendors (DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, Mistral), and any
  OpenAI-compatible server. Keyless on Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure with workload identity.
- Works unchanged with pi, Claude Code, and the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs (`meritorder setup`).

**Routing**
- Rule-based classifier sets a quality floor; a marginal-cost router picks the backend, counting the
  cost of rebuilding a session's prompt cache before moving it.
- GPUs priced by how busy they are (near free with headroom), so spare GPU capacity is used first.
- Failover catches errors that arrive after a `200` (Anthropic's in-stream overload, OpenRouter error
  chunks) and streams that never start. Over capacity skips just that model on that backend, for the
  provider's `Retry-After`. Outage and recovery alerts go to the webhook, and responses say what they
  failed over from.
- Refusal fallback and automatic reasoning effort for `auto`; opt-in substitution for named
  models that have nowhere to run (never to a weaker model).
- A saturated GPU spills to other routes, and queues (bounded) only when it's the last resort.

**GPUs**
- Capacity controller starts and stops SkyPilot/SkyServe + vLLM deployments when demand pays for
  them, with SkyPilot catalog prices, hysteresis, and fleet-wide caps.
- Console controls: stop (drain or now), pin replicas, stop all; activity log; where each replica
  runs, uptime, burn rate, and cost.

**Spend and savings**
- Budgets per organization, GPU fleet, team, person, and session; rate limits; per-request cost cap.
  Each person can have their own monthly limit (People page, admin API, or their static key) that
  replaces their team's per-person default.
  The shipped config reads the organization-wide caps from `.env` (`MERITORDER_ORG_BUDGET_USD` and
  friends), and `.env` comments at the end of a line are read the way Docker Compose reads them.
- Savings ledger by cause (routing, caching, self-hosting, compression, response cache) against a
  per-team baseline.
- GPT-5.6 tool calls through OpenAI work: its Chat Completions endpoint rejects function tools with
  reasoning, so the OpenAI backend sends requests to the Responses API (`api: responses`) and converts
  the replies back. Agents like Claude Code and pi can use GPT models with reasoning on.
- Claude through OpenRouter is prompt-cached (it wasn't: every turn paid full price), and the router
  prices cache writes on every route, so it no longer prefers a route only because it skipped the write.
- OpenRouter requests record what OpenRouter billed, not a catalog estimate: it picks among providers
  whose prices differ (catalog prices were up to 56% low in testing). `billed_cost` sets this per backend.
- Reports API and console, CSV/JSONL export (to S3), alerts and weekly digests to a webhook,
  Prometheus metrics with a Grafana dashboard, OpenTelemetry traces.

**Identity**
- Entra/OIDC sign-in exchanged for short-lived keys, groups mapped to teams and roles, SCIM
  provisioning; roles for users, team leads, finance, and admins.

**Operations**
- Docker Compose and a Helm chart (External Secrets, Reloader, zero-restart key rotation, workload
  identity). Configuration versions in Postgres, edited in the console, followed by every process.
- Signed multi-arch images with an SBOM and provenance.

**Known limitations**
- Exercised against OpenRouter only (smoke tests, a Claude Code session, costs matched to its bill); not
  yet against other live provider accounts, a real cloud GPU, a real Entra tenant, or a
  production Kubernetes cluster: see `docs/README.md` for what's verified and how.
- Not built: reconciliation against provider bills, the native Gemini API, Kubernetes-native GPU
  provisioning, a learned router, provider batch APIs, model-based compression, Parquet export.

# Task: an interpreter for a small Scheme-like Lisp

Write a Python module that interprets the small Lisp dialect specified below. Everything the tests check is specified
here; follow it exactly, even where it differs from a real Scheme.

## API

```python
class LispError(Exception): ...

def run(source: str) -> str: ...
```

- `run` reads every top-level form in `source`, evaluates them in order in a **fresh global environment** (nothing
  carries over between calls), and returns the printed representation (see *Printing*) of the value of the **last**
  form. A source with no forms (only whitespace/comments, or empty) returns `"#<void>"`.
- **Every** error — syntax or runtime — must surface from `run` as a `LispError` (your own class, a subclass of
  `Exception`). No other exception type (`ZeroDivisionError`, `TypeError`, `IndexError`, `KeyError`, `RecursionError`,
  ...) may escape.

## Reader

- Whitespace is space, tab, newline and carriage return. `;` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.
- `(` and `)` delimit lists; `'datum` is shorthand for `(quote datum)`. A `'` with no datum after it is an error.
- **Dotted lists**: inside a list, a `.` token must be preceded by at least one datum and followed by exactly one datum
  and then the closing `)`; any other use of `.` is a syntax error (`(1 . 2 3)`, `( . 2)`, `(1 .)`, a lone `.`).
  `(1 . (2 3))` reads as the list `(1 2 3)`.
- **Strings**: `"..."`, possibly containing raw newlines. The escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t` mean double quote,
  backslash, newline and tab; any other backslash escape, or a missing closing quote, is a syntax error.
- **Atoms**: any other maximal run of characters containing no whitespace and none of `(` `)` `'` `"` `;`. An atom made
  of an optional `+` or `-` followed by one or more ASCII digits is an integer (`42`, `-7`, `+5`). `#t` and `#f` are the
  booleans; any other atom starting with `#` is a syntax error. The atom `.` is only valid as described above.
  Everything else is a symbol (case-sensitive). There are no other number literals: `1.5`, `3/4`, `1+`, `-`, `a.b`
  and `->` are all symbols.
- A missing `)` or an extra `)` is a syntax error.

## Values

- **Numbers**: unbounded integers and exact rationals (Python's `fractions.Fraction` is fine). Rationals only arise from
  `/`. A result whose denominator is 1 is always the integer (`(/ 6 3)` is the integer `2`, and `(integer? ...)` of it
  is `#t`). The booleans are **not** numbers.
- **Booleans** `#t` and `#f`; **strings**; **symbols**; the **empty list** `()` (there is exactly one empty list
  value); **pairs** made by `cons` (a list is a chain of pairs ending in `()`); **procedures** (builtins and closures);
  and the **void** value, which is what `define`, `set!`, `(begin)`, an `if` without an else branch whose test is
  false, and a `cond` with no matching clause evaluate to.

## Printing

| value | printed as |
|---|---|
| integer | decimal, with `-` if negative: `42`, `-7`, `0` |
| rational | `numerator/denominator` in lowest terms, sign on the numerator: `3/2`, `-1/2` |
| booleans | `#t`, `#f` |
| string | in double quotes, with `\` written as `\\`, `"` as `\"`, newline as `\n`, tab as `\t`; other characters as is |
| symbol | its name |
| empty list | `()` |
| list | `(1 2 3)`: elements printed recursively, separated by single spaces |
| improper list | `(1 2 . 3)`, `(1 . 2)` |
| procedure (builtin or closure) | `#<procedure>` |
| void | `#<void>` |

Quoted data is not abbreviated when printed: `''a` prints as `(quote a)`.

## Evaluation

- Numbers, booleans and strings evaluate to themselves. A symbol evaluates to the value of the nearest enclosing
  binding of that name; an unbound symbol is an error. Evaluating the empty list `()` is an error.
- A non-empty list whose first element is one of the special-form keywords (`quote if define set! lambda begin let
  let* letrec cond and or`) is that special form. Tests never rebind these keywords.
- Any other non-empty list is a procedure call: evaluate the operator expression first, then the operand expressions
  from left to right, then apply. A call form must be a proper list. Applying a value that is not a procedure is an
  error.
- **Truthiness**: only `#f` is false. `0`, `()`, `""` are all true.
- Builtins are ordinary bindings in the global environment: a program may redefine them (`(define + -)`), which only
  affects that `run`.
- Environments are lexically scoped, mutable, and shared: a closure captures the environment in which its `lambda` was
  evaluated, and a `set!` on a captured variable is seen by every closure sharing that binding.

## Special forms

A **body** is one or more expressions, evaluated in order; its value is the value of the last one. A `define` inside a
body binds in that body's own new environment (the procedure call's, or the `let`'s), so it does not leak outside.

- `(quote datum)` → `datum`, unevaluated. Exactly one operand.
- `(if test then)` / `(if test then else)`: evaluate `test`; if it is not `#f` evaluate `then`, else `else` (or produce
  void when there is no else branch). Exactly 2 or 3 operands.
- `(define name expr)`: evaluate `expr` first, then bind `name` to it in the **current** environment (adding the binding,
  or replacing it if that environment already has one). `(define x x)` at top level is therefore an unbound-symbol
  error. `(define (name . params) body...)` is `(define name (lambda params body...))`, with `params` in any of the
  forms below (e.g. `(define (f a b) ...)`, `(define (f a . rest) ...)`, `(define (f . args) ...)`). Returns void.
- `(set! name expr)`: evaluate `expr` and store it in the nearest existing binding of `name`; if there is none, error.
  Returns void.
- `(lambda params body...)` → a closure. `params` is a list of symbols `(a b c)` (exactly that many arguments), a dotted
  list `(a b . rest)` (at least 2 arguments; `rest` is bound to a fresh list of the remaining ones, possibly `()`), or a
  single symbol `args` (any number of arguments, all bound as a list). Parameter names must be distinct symbols.
  Calling a closure with the wrong number of arguments is an error. The call evaluates the body in a new environment,
  holding the parameters, whose parent is the closure's captured environment.
- `(begin expr...)`: evaluate in order in the **current** environment (no new scope, so a top-level
  `(begin (define y 7))` defines a global); value of the last, or void for `(begin)`.
- `(let ((name expr) ...) body...)`: evaluate every `expr` in the current environment, then evaluate the body in a new
  environment binding the names (distinct) to those values. `(let () body...)` is allowed.
- **Named let** `(let loop ((name expr) ...) body...)`: evaluate the `expr`s in the current environment, then call a
  procedure with parameters `name ...` and the given body, where inside the body (only) `loop` is bound to that
  procedure itself. Equivalent to `((letrec ((loop (lambda (name ...) body...))) loop) expr ...)`.
- `(let* ((name expr) ...) body...)`: like nested `let`s, one per binding: each `expr` sees the bindings before it, and
  each binding is in its own new scope (so in `(let* ((x 1) (f (lambda () x)) (x 2)) (f))` the closure sees the first
  `x` and returns 1). The body runs in a new scope inside all of them.
- `(letrec ((name expr) ...) body...)`: create a new environment in which all the names are bound but **unassigned**;
  then evaluate the `expr`s from left to right in that environment, assigning each name as soon as its `expr` has been
  evaluated; then evaluate the body there. Reading a name that is still unassigned is an error
  (`(letrec ((a b) (b 1)) a)` fails, `(letrec ((a 1) (b (+ a 1))) b)` is 2).
- `(cond clause...)`: each clause is `(test expr...)` or `(else expr...)` (`else` only as the last clause). Evaluate the
  tests in order; for the first test that is not `#f`, evaluate that clause's expressions as a body and return the last
  value — or, if the clause has no expressions, return the test's value. An `else` clause always matches. No match →
  void.
- `(and expr...)`: evaluate left to right; return the first value that is `#f` (without evaluating the rest), otherwise
  the last value; `(and)` is `#t`. `(or expr...)`: return the first value that is not `#f` (without evaluating the
  rest), otherwise `#f`; `(or)` is `#f`.

A malformed special form is an error: the wrong number of operands where a number is fixed above, a missing body
(`(lambda (x))`, `(let ((x 1)))`), a non-symbol where a name is required (`(define 5 1)`, `(set! 1 2)`,
`(lambda (1) 1)`), duplicate parameter names, or a `let`/`let*`/`letrec` binding that is not a two-element list
`(name expr)` (`(let ((x)) x)`, `(let ((x 1 2)) x)`). Tests only contain malformed forms that are actually evaluated, so
you may detect them either when the form is evaluated or earlier.

## Proper tail calls

These are **tail positions**: both branches of `if`; the last expression of a `lambda` body, of a `begin`, and of the
bodies of `let`, named `let`, `let*` and `letrec`; the last expression of the chosen `cond` clause; the last operand of
`and` and of `or`. A procedure call in a tail position must not grow the Python call stack: a loop written as tail
calls (including mutual recursion between procedures, tail calls to variadic procedures, and tail calls to procedures
passed as arguments) must run in constant Python stack depth however many iterations it does. The tests check this
directly: they run the same loop with 10 and with 1,000 iterations while counting the Python call depth with
`sys.setprofile`/`threading.setprofile`, and require the maximum depth to be the same, give or take 50 frames
(raising the recursion limit is therefore no substitute). They also run loops of 100,000 iterations.

Calls that are not in tail position may use Python recursion. Tests contain non-tail recursion at most 1000 calls deep
(e.g. a naive recursive sum of 1..1000, or building a 1000-element list recursively); if your evaluator needs several
Python frames per Lisp call, raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` (for example to 20000).

## Builtins

`n` = number (integer or rational), `i` = integer, `x` = any value. A wrong number of arguments, or an argument of the
wrong type, is an error.

| name | arguments | result |
|---|---|---|
| `+` `*` | 0 or more `n` | sum / product (`(+)` is 0, `(*)` is 1) |
| `-` | 1 or more `n` | `(- a)` is the negation; otherwise `a` minus each of the rest in turn |
| `/` | 1 or more `n` | `(/ a)` is 1/a; otherwise `a` divided by each of the rest in turn, exactly. Dividing by 0 is an error |
| `quotient` | 2 `i` | integer division truncated toward zero: `(quotient -7 2)` is -3 |
| `remainder` | 2 `i` | `a - b*(quotient a b)`, sign of the dividend: `(remainder -7 2)` is -1, `(remainder 7 -2)` is 1 |
| `modulo` | 2 `i` | remainder with the sign of the divisor: `(modulo -7 2)` is 1, `(modulo 7 -2)` is -1 |
| `abs` | 1 `n` | absolute value |
| `=` `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | 2 or more `n` | `#t` if the comparison holds between each adjacent pair (`(< 1 2 3)`), else `#f` |
| `number?` `integer?` `boolean?` `symbol?` `string?` `procedure?` `null?` `pair?` `list?` | 1 `x` | type tests; `integer?` is `#t` only for integers; `null?` only for `()`; `pair?` for any pair; `list?` for proper lists including `()` |
| `not` | 1 `x` | `#t` if `x` is `#f`, else `#f` |
| `eq?` | 2 `x` | numbers: `#t` if numerically equal (whatever their size); booleans, symbols: same value; the empty list equals itself; strings, pairs and procedures: `#t` only if they are the very same object (e.g. the same variable's value); values of different types are never `eq?` |
| `equal?` | 2 `x` | like `eq?`, but strings are compared by content and pairs structurally (car and cdr recursively) |
| `cons` | 2 `x` | a new pair |
| `car` `cdr` | 1 pair | first / rest of a pair (`(car '())` is an error) |
| `list` | 0 or more `x` | a new list of the arguments |
| `length` | 1 proper list | number of elements |
| `append` | 0 or more proper lists | a new list of all their elements, in order (`(append)` is `()`) |
| `reverse` | 1 proper list | a new reversed list |
| `apply` | a procedure and a proper list | the procedure called with the list's elements as arguments |
| `map` | a procedure and a proper list | a new list of the procedure applied to each element, in order |
| `string-append` | 0 or more strings | concatenation |
| `string-length` | 1 string | number of characters |
| `number->string` | 1 `n` | the number's printed form as a string (`"-1/2"`) |
| `symbol->string` | 1 symbol | its name as a string |
| `string->symbol` | 1 string | the symbol with that name |

## Errors (all raise `LispError`)

Syntax errors as described under *Reader* and malformed special forms; unbound symbols; reading an unassigned `letrec`
variable; `set!` of an unbound name; evaluating `()`; calling a non-procedure; wrong argument counts for closures and
builtins; argument type errors in builtins (including booleans passed where numbers are required: `(+ 1 #t)` is an
error); division by zero in `/`, `quotient`, `remainder`, `modulo`.

## Examples

```python
run("(define (sq x) (* x x)) (sq 12)")                     # "144"
run("(/ 6 4)")                                              # "3/2"
run("(cons 1 (cons 2 3))")                                  # "(1 2 . 3)"
run("'(a \"b\" #t)")                                        # '(a "b" #t)'
run("(define x 1)")                                         # "#<void>"
run("((lambda (a . r) (list a r)) 1 2 3)")                  # "(1 (2 3))"
run("(let loop ((i 0)) (if (< i 100000) (loop (+ i 1)) i))")  # "100000"
run("(car '())")                                            # raises LispError
```

"""Gateway pipeline edge paths: bad bodies, token counting, embeddings failures, pins, budgets, compaction,
refusals in every format, and failures in side work (session, ledger, tracing) that must not fail the request."""

import json

import pytest
from conftest import ADMIN_KEY, LEAD_KEY, auth, last_row, ledger_row

from meritorder.backends.base import BackendError
from meritorder.backends.mock import MockBackend
from meritorder.config import BackendConfig, ModelConfig, Route, Safeguards
from meritorder.sessions import session_key

HI = [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]


async def chat(client, body, headers=None, path="/v1/chat/completions"):
    return await client.post(path, json=body, headers=headers or auth())


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ request validation


@pytest.mark.parametrize("path", ["/v1/chat/completions", "/v1/messages", "/v1/responses"])
async def test_bad_bodies_are_400s_in_the_clients_format(client, path):
    r = await client.post(path, content=b"{not json", headers={**auth(), "content-type": "application/json"})
    assert r.status_code == 400 and "valid JSON" in r.text
    r = await client.post(path, content=b"\xff\xfe", headers={**auth(), "content-type": "application/json"})
    assert r.status_code == 400
    r = await client.post(path, json=[1, 2], headers=auth())
    assert r.status_code == 400
    if path != "/v1/responses":
        r = await client.post(path, json={"model": "small", "messages": "hi"}, headers=auth())
        assert r.status_code == 400 and "'messages' list" in r.text
    r = await client.post(path, json={"model": "small", "messages": HI})
    assert r.status_code == 401
    shape = r.json()
    assert ("type" in shape and shape["type"] == "error") if path == "/v1/messages" else "error" in shape


async def test_rejections_are_counted_in_metrics(client, gateway):
    await client.post("/v1/chat/completions", json={"model": "small", "messages": HI})
    await client.post("/v1/chat/completions", json={"model": "nope", "messages": HI}, headers=auth())
    text = (await client.get("/metrics")).text
    assert 'meritorder_rejected_requests_total{reason="authentication_error",status="401"}' in text \
        or 'meritorder_rejected_requests_total{status="401",reason="authentication_error"}' in text


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ count_tokens


async def test_count_tokens_estimates_without_an_anthropic_api_backend(client):
    r = await client.post("/v1/messages/count_tokens", json={"model": "big", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello " * 100}]},
                          headers=auth())
    assert r.status_code == 200 and r.json()["input_tokens"] > 50
    assert (await client.post("/v1/messages/count_tokens", json={"messages": HI})).status_code == 401
    r = await client.post("/v1/messages/count_tokens", content=b"nope", headers={**auth(), "content-type": "application/json"})
    assert r.status_code == 400


async def test_count_tokens_asks_the_provider_and_falls_back_on_errors(client, gateway):
    api = MockBackend(BackendConfig(name="anthropic-api", kind="api", format="anthropic"))
    gateway.backends["anthropic-api"] = api
    gateway.cfg.model("big").routes.insert(0, Route(backend="anthropic-api", model="claude-real"))
    seen = []

    async def exact(body, headers):
        seen.append(body["model"])
        return {"input_tokens": 1234}

    api.count_tokens = exact
    r = await client.post("/v1/messages/count_tokens", json={"model": "big", "messages": HI}, headers=auth())
    assert r.json() == {"input_tokens": 1234} and seen == ["claude-real"]

    async def failing(body, headers):
        raise BackendError(500, "down", retryable=True)

    api.count_tokens = failing
    r = await client.post("/v1/messages/count_tokens", json={"model": "unknown-model", "messages": HI}, headers=auth())
    assert r.status_code == 200 and isinstance(r.json()["input_tokens"], int)  # estimate, not an error


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ embeddings


async def test_embeddings_validation(client, gateway):
    post = lambda body, headers=None: client.post("/v1/embeddings", json=body, headers=headers if headers is not None else auth())  # noqa: E731
    assert (await post({"model": "embed-small", "input": "x"}, {})).status_code == 401
    r = await client.post("/v1/embeddings", content=b"{", headers={**auth(), "content-type": "application/json"})
    assert r.status_code == 400
    assert (await post({"model": "embed-small"})).status_code == 400
    assert (await post({"model": "nope", "input": "x"})).status_code == 404
    assert (await post({"model": "small", "input": "x"})).status_code == 404  # a chat model isn't an embedding model
    gateway.cfg.team("default").allowed_models = ["small"]
    r = await post({"model": "embed-small", "input": "x"})
    assert r.status_code == 403 and "not allowed" in r.text


async def test_embeddings_failover_and_errors(client, gateway):
    backup = MockBackend(BackendConfig(name="embed-backup", kind="mock", format="openai"))
    gateway.backends["embed-backup"] = backup
    gateway.cfg.model("embed-small").routes.append(Route(backend="embed-backup", model="e2", price={"input": 0.05, "output": 0}))
    primary = gateway.backends["mock-openai"]
    original = primary.embed

    async def down(body):
        raise BackendError(503, "busy", retryable=True)

    primary.embed = down
    r = await client.post("/v1/embeddings", json={"model": "embed-small", "input": ["a", "b"]}, headers=auth())
    assert r.status_code == 200 and r.headers["x-meritorder-backend"] == "embed-backup"
    row = await last_row(gateway)
    assert row["backend"] == "embed-backup" and row["upstream_model"] == "e2" and row["client_format"] == "embeddings"

    async def bad_request(body):
        raise BackendError(400, "input too long")

    primary.embed = bad_request
    r = await client.post("/v1/embeddings", json={"model": "embed-small", "input": "x"}, headers=auth())
    assert r.status_code == 400 and "input too long" in r.text  # the request's fault: no failover

    primary.embed, backup.embed = down, down
    r = await client.post("/v1/embeddings", json={"model": "embed-small", "input": "x"}, headers=auth())
    assert r.status_code == 503 and "busy" in r.text

    primary.embed = original
    for b in (primary, backup):
        for _ in range(3):
            b.record_failure(__import__("time").time())
    r = await client.post("/v1/embeddings", json={"model": "embed-small", "input": "x"}, headers=auth())
    assert r.status_code == 503 and "no healthy backend" in r.text

async def test_team_budget_reached(client, gateway):
    team = gateway.cfg.team("default")
    team.user_budget_usd_month, team.budget_usd_month = None, 1.0
    await gateway.store.record(ledger_row(user_id="bob", team="default", actual_cost=1.5))
    r = await chat(client, {"model": "small", "messages": HI})
    assert r.status_code == 429 and "team 'default' reached its monthly budget" in r.text


async def test_admin_backend_pin(client, gateway):
    body = {"model": "small", "messages": HI}
    r = await chat(client, body, {**auth(LEAD_KEY), "x-meritorder-backend": "mock-openai"})
    assert r.status_code == 403 and "only admins" in r.text

    assert r.status_code == 200 and r.headers["x-meritorder-backend"] == "mock-anthropic"


async def test_per_request_cap_treats_gpus_as_free(client, gateway):
    gpu = MockBackend(BackendConfig(name="gpu", kind="self_hosted", format="openai", mock_latency_ms=0))
    gateway.backends["gpu"] = gpu
    gateway.cfg.models.append(ModelConfig(name="pricey", quality={"general": 4}, routes=[
        Route(backend="mock-openai", model="pricey-api", price={"input": 1000, "output": 1000}),

# ------------------------------------------------------------------ sessions


async def test_compaction_resets_warm_caches_and_allows_a_move(client, gateway):
    headers = {**auth(), "x-session-id": "compact-1"}
    convo = [{"role": "user", "content": "start a long task " * 50}]
    for i in range(3):
        r = await chat(client, {"model": "small", "messages": convo}, headers)
        assert r.status_code == 200
        convo += [{"role": "assistant", "content": f"step {i}"}, {"role": "user", "content": f"continue {i}"}]
    await gateway.drain()
    before = await gateway.state.get_session(session_key("alice", "compact-1"))
    assert before["warm_until"]
    # The harness compacts: history is replaced by a summary, so the prefix no longer matches.
    r = await chat(client, {"model": "small", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "summary of earlier work"}]}, headers)
    assert r.status_code == 200
    await gateway.drain()
    after = await gateway.state.get_session(session_key("alice", "compact-1"))
    assert after["turns"] == before["turns"] + 1


async def test_side_work_failures_never_fail_the_request(client, gateway, monkeypatch, caplog):
    import meritorder.proxy as proxy

    def broken_span(row, carrier):
        raise RuntimeError("collector down")

    async def broken_session(ctx):
        raise RuntimeError("redis hiccup")

    async def broken_record(row):
        raise RuntimeError("postgres down")

    monkeypatch.setattr(proxy, "record_span", broken_span)
    monkeypatch.setattr(gateway, "update_session", broken_session)
    monkeypatch.setattr(gateway.store, "record", broken_record)
    for stream in (False, True):
        r = await chat(client, {"model": "small", "stream": stream, "messages": HI})
        assert r.status_code == 200
    await gateway.drain()
    text = caplog.text
    assert "could not record a trace span" in text and "failed to update session" in text and "failed to write ledger row" in text

"""Background jobs: monthly ledger partitions, hourly rollups for reports, alerts, live prices and quality scores, and eval runs
queued from the console."""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging
import os
import time
from datetime import UTC, datetime

from .alerts import check_budgets, check_spikes, weekly_digest
from .config import Config
from .configstore import ConfigFollower
from .evals.jobs import worker_loop as eval_loop
from .live_prices import PriceRefresher
from .quality_data import QualityRefresher
from .state import make_state
from .store import make_store

log = logging.getLogger("meritorder.worker")


async def run_worker(once: bool = False, interval: int = 60, cfg: Config | None = None, backfill: bool = False, path: str | None = None) -> None:
    store = make_store(os.environ.get("MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL"))
    if store.kind != "postgres":
        raise SystemExit("the worker needs Postgres: set MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL")
    state = make_state(os.environ.get("MERITORDER_REDIS_URL"))
    await store.init()
    follower = ConfigFollower(store, path=path, cfg=cfg)
    prices = PriceRefresher()
    quality = QualityRefresher()
    evals = None
    if not once and os.environ.get("MERITORDER_EVAL_RUNS", "on").lower() not in ("0", "off", "false", "no"):
        # Eval runs started on the console's Evals page. They call the gateway like any client would.
        evals = asyncio.create_task(eval_loop(store, os.environ.get("MERITORDER_GATEWAY_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8080")))
    try:
        while True:
            try:
                cfg = await follower.current()
                await store.ensure_partitions()
                rows = await store.rollup(full=backfill)
                backfill = False
                log.info("rollup refreshed %d hourly rows", rows)
                await check_budgets(cfg, store, state)
                await check_spikes(store, state)
                await prices.maybe(cfg, store, state, time.monotonic())
                await quality.maybe(cfg, store, state, time.monotonic())
                now = datetime.now(UTC)
                if now.weekday() == 0 and now.hour >= 9:  # Monday morning, once per week
                    await weekly_digest(cfg, store, state, now)
            except Exception:
                log.exception("worker cycle failed")
            if once:
                return
            await asyncio.sleep(interval)
    finally:
        if evals is not None:
            evals.cancel()
        await store.close()
        await state.close()

# Task: expand calendar recurrence rules

Write a Python module that expands a recurrence rule — a subset of the iCalendar `RRULE` of RFC 5545 — into the
list of dates and times it describes. The semantics are fully defined below and follow RFC 5545 closely, with a few
deliberate differences that are called out; where they differ from what you know of RFC 5545 or of
`dateutil.rrule`, these rules win.

## Interface

```python
from datetime import datetime

def expand(rule: str, dtstart: datetime, *, limit: int | None = None,
           between: tuple[datetime, datetime] | None = None) -> list[datetime]:
    ...
```

`dtstart`, the bounds in `between`, and every returned value are naive `datetime`s (no time zones anywhere). Every
error described below raises `ValueError`.

## 1. Rule syntax

- The rule may start with the prefix `RRULE:`. After it come one or more **parts** separated by `;`. Each part is
  `NAME=VALUE`: the name is everything before the part's first `=`, the value everything after it. A part without `=`
  or with an empty value is an error. Names and values are case-sensitive and use the uppercase spellings shown here;
  there is no whitespace anywhere. Parts may come in any order; a name given twice is an error.
- Supported names: `FREQ` (required), `INTERVAL`, `COUNT`, `UNTIL`, `BYMONTH`, `BYMONTHDAY`, `BYDAY`, `BYSETPOS`,
  `WKST`. Any other name — including RFC 5545 parts this task doesn't support, like `BYHOUR`, `BYWEEKNO` or
  `BYYEARDAY` — is an error.
- An *integer* is one or more ASCII digits. Only in `BYMONTHDAY`, `BYSETPOS` and `BYDAY` ordinals may it be
  preceded by one sign character, `+` or `-`. A *list* is one or more items separated by `,`, with no empty items;
  repeating a value in a list is allowed and means the same as giving it once.

| Part | Value | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `FREQ` | `DAILY`, `WEEKLY`, `MONTHLY` or `YEARLY` (anything else, e.g. `HOURLY`, is an error) | required |
| `INTERVAL` | integer ≥ 1 | 1 |
| `COUNT` | integer ≥ 1 | none |
| `UNTIL` | `YYYYMMDD` (a date) or `YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS` (a date and time); it must be a real calendar date and time, and no other form (e.g. a trailing `Z`, or dashes) is allowed | none |
| `BYMONTH` | list of integers 1..12 | see §3 |
| `BYMONTHDAY` | list of integers 1..31 or -31..-1 (-1 is the last day of the month, -2 the one before, …) | see §3 |
| `BYDAY` | list of weekday items: a code `MO` `TU` `WE` `TH` `FR` `SA` `SU`, optionally preceded by an ordinal, an integer 1..53 or -53..-1 (e.g. `MO`, `1MO`, `+2TU`, `-1FR`, `20MO`) | see §3 |
| `BYSETPOS` | list of integers 1..366 or -366..-1 | none |
| `WKST` | a weekday code | `MO` |

Further errors:

- `COUNT` and `UNTIL` in the same rule.
- `BYMONTHDAY` with `FREQ=WEEKLY`.
- A `BYDAY` item with an ordinal when `FREQ` is `DAILY` or `WEEKLY`.
- `BYSETPOS` in a rule that has none of `BYMONTH`, `BYMONTHDAY`, `BYDAY`.
- `limit` is not `None` and is less than 1.
- The rule has neither `COUNT` nor `UNTIL`, and `limit` and `between` are both `None` (the result would be infinite).

## 2. Periods

A recurrence is a sequence of **periods**. Period 0 contains `dtstart`'s date, and period *k* is *k* × `INTERVAL`
units after it:

- `DAILY`: a single day; period *k* is the day `dtstart.date()` + *k* × `INTERVAL` days.
- `WEEKLY`: seven consecutive days starting on the `WKST` weekday. Period 0 is the week (in that sense) containing
  `dtstart`'s date; period *k* starts 7 × *k* × `INTERVAL` days after period 0 starts. `WKST` has no effect on the
  other frequencies.
- `MONTHLY`: a calendar month; period 0 is `dtstart`'s month, period *k* is *k* × `INTERVAL` months later.
- `YEARLY`: a calendar year; period 0 is `dtstart`'s year, period *k* is *k* × `INTERVAL` years later.

## 3. The days a period produces

First, these **defaults** fill in parts the rule leaves out (they depend on `dtstart`):

- `WEEKLY` without `BYDAY`: `BYDAY` is `dtstart`'s weekday.
- `MONTHLY` with neither `BYDAY` nor `BYMONTHDAY`: `BYMONTHDAY` is `dtstart`'s day of the month.
- `YEARLY` with neither `BYDAY` nor `BYMONTHDAY`: `BYMONTHDAY` is `dtstart`'s day of the month and, if the rule has no
  `BYMONTH`, `BYMONTH` is `dtstart`'s month.
- No other defaults. (So `DAILY` uses only what the rule gives; `YEARLY;BYMONTHDAY=15` is the 15th of every month;
  `YEARLY;BYDAY=MO` is every Monday of the year.)

A period's **candidate days** are all its days that pass every one of these filters that is present (given or
defaulted):

- `BYMONTH`: the day's month is listed.
- `BYMONTHDAY`: the day is listed by its day of the month *d*, or by *d* - *D* - 1 where *D* is the number of days in
  its month (so -1 is the last day). A listed day that doesn't exist in a month — 31 in April, 30 or -30 in
  February — selects nothing in that month. Days are never moved or clamped to fit.
- `BYDAY`: the day matches at least one item (items are alternatives). A plain item such as `FR` matches every day
  with that weekday. An item with ordinal *n*, such as `2TU` or `-1FR`, matches a day with that weekday that is the
  *n*-th such weekday counting from the start of its **scope** (when *n* > 0) or the |*n*|-th counting back from the
  end of its scope (when *n* < 0); if the scope has no such weekday (say a 5th Monday), the item matches nothing in
  it. The scope is the day's month for `FREQ=MONTHLY`; for `FREQ=YEARLY` it is the day's month if the rule has
  `BYMONTH`, and the whole year otherwise (so `YEARLY;BYDAY=20MO` is the 20th Monday of each year).

**`BYSETPOS`**, if present, then keeps only some candidate days of each period: number the period's candidate days in
ascending order 1, 2, …, *n* and also -*n*, …, -1 (-1 being the latest); keep the days whose number is listed.
Positions beyond the set select nothing, and a day selected twice is kept once. `BYSETPOS` always sees the period's
whole candidate set, *before* the `dtstart` cut in §4 — even in period 0, whose earliest days may be before `dtstart`.
This holds for every frequency, `WEEKLY` included: period 0 is the full week containing `dtstart`.

## 4. Occurrences

The days kept in each period, taken period by period in chronological order, at `dtstart`'s time of day (hour,
minute, second and microsecond), are the **occurrences** — except that days earlier than `dtstart`'s date are
discarded (only period 0 can have any). `dtstart` itself is an occurrence only if the rule keeps its date: unlike RFC
5545, `dtstart` is *not* automatically the first occurrence.

Bounds, applied to that sequence:

- `UNTIL`: occurrences later than `UNTIL` don't exist (the recurrence ends there). With the `YYYYMMDD` form every
  occurrence on or before that date is allowed, at any time of day; with the `YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS` form, occurrences at or
  before that instant. An `UNTIL` before `dtstart` means there are no occurrences.
- `COUNT`: only the first `COUNT` occurrences exist, counted from `dtstart`.
- `between=(start, end)`: return only the occurrences with `start <= occurrence <= end`. It does not change which
  occurrences exist: `COUNT` still counts from `dtstart`, including occurrences before `start`. If `start > end` the
  result is empty.
- `limit`: return at most `limit` occurrences, the earliest of those that would otherwise be returned.

`expand` returns the occurrences that pass all the bounds as a list in ascending order, without duplicates. Dates
never go past 9999-12-31; a recurrence that reaches it simply ends there.

## Examples

```python
from datetime import datetime as dt

expand("FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=3", dt(2026, 3, 30, 9, 15))
# [dt(2026, 3, 30, 9, 15), dt(2026, 3, 31, 9, 15), dt(2026, 4, 1, 9, 15)]

expand("FREQ=MONTHLY;COUNT=4", dt(2026, 1, 31, 8))       # months without a 31st produce nothing
# [dt(2026, 1, 31, 8), dt(2026, 3, 31, 8), dt(2026, 5, 31, 8), dt(2026, 7, 31, 8)]

expand("FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2;COUNT=4;BYDAY=TU,SU;WKST=MO", dt(1997, 8, 5, 9))
# [dt(1997, 8, 5, 9), dt(1997, 8, 10, 9), dt(1997, 8, 19, 9), dt(1997, 8, 24, 9)]
expand("FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2;COUNT=4;BYDAY=TU,SU;WKST=SU", dt(1997, 8, 5, 9))
# [dt(1997, 8, 5, 9), dt(1997, 8, 17, 9), dt(1997, 8, 19, 9), dt(1997, 8, 31, 9)]

expand("FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR;COUNT=2", dt(2026, 1, 1))   # last Friday of the month
# [dt(2026, 1, 30), dt(2026, 2, 27)]

expand("FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;BYSETPOS=1;COUNT=3", dt(2026, 1, 10, 9))
# [dt(2026, 2, 2, 9), dt(2026, 3, 2, 9), dt(2026, 4, 1, 9)]   January's first weekday (Jan 1) is before dtstart

expand("FREQ=YEARLY;BYDAY=FR;BYMONTHDAY=13", dt(2026, 1, 1), limit=3)   # every Friday the 13th
# [dt(2026, 2, 13), dt(2026, 3, 13), dt(2026, 11, 13)]

expand("FREQ=DAILY;COUNT=10", dt(2026, 1, 1), between=(dt(2026, 1, 8), dt(2026, 2, 1)))
# [dt(2026, 1, 8), dt(2026, 1, 9), dt(2026, 1, 10)]

expand("FREQ=DAILY", dt(2026, 1, 1))                  # raises ValueError (unbounded)
expand("FREQ=DAILY", dt(2026, 1, 1), limit=2)         # [dt(2026, 1, 1), dt(2026, 1, 2)]
```

import os

from meritorder.config import BackendAuth, BackendConfig, Config, read_secret_file


def write(path, text, bump=0):
    path.write_text(text)
    st = os.stat(path)
    os.utime(path, ns=(st.st_atime_ns, st.st_mtime_ns + bump))  # make sure the change is visible


async def test_rotated_key_file_is_used_on_the_next_request(tmp_path):
    f = tmp_path / "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
    write(f, "sk-old\n")
    auth = ApiKeyAuth(BackendAuth(type="api_key", value_file=str(f)))
    assert auth.available()
    assert (await auth.apply("POST", "u", {}, b""))["authorization"] == "Bearer sk-old"
    write(f, "sk-new-longer", bump=1_000_000)
    assert (await auth.apply("POST", "u", {}, b""))["authorization"] == "Bearer sk-new-longer"


def test_kubernetes_style_symlink_swap(tmp_path):
    """A mounted Secret's file is a symlink into a ..data directory that Kubernetes swaps atomically."""
    v1, v2 = tmp_path / "..2026_11_01", tmp_path / "..2026_11_09"
    v1.mkdir(), v2.mkdir()
    (v1 / "KEY").write_text("first")

    os.utime(v2 / "KEY", ns=(1, 2_000_000_000_000_000_000))

    tmp = tmp_path / "..data_tmp"

# 09 — Decisions

What we decided, why, and what would make us revisit it. Newest decisions go at the bottom.

| # | Decision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Python for the core | Accepted |
| 2 | Our own backend adapters; no LiteLLM dependency | Accepted |
| 3 | No Envoy | Accepted |
| 4 | Docker Compose and Kubernetes both supported | Accepted |
| 5 | The harness owns the conversation; no content stored | Accepted |
| 6 | Route by marginal cost, including cache rebuild cost | Accepted |
| 7 | SkyPilot for GPUs, provisioning as a plugin | Accepted |
| 8 | Generic OIDC, Entra first | Accepted |
| 9 | Postgres and Redis are the only state | Accepted |
| 10 | Continuous batching only; async batch APIs out of scope | Accepted |
| 11 | AGPL-3.0-only license | Accepted |
| 12 | Reporting UI in React/TypeScript | Accepted |
| 13 | Opt-in response cache may store responses | Accepted |
| 14 | Open-weight catalog with prices from OpenRouter | Accepted |
| 15 | GPU scaling on addressable demand at API prices | Accepted |
| 16 | Deterministic, rule-based compression first | Accepted |
| 17 | Configuration versions in Postgres, YAML as the starting point | Accepted |
| 18 | Control panel in Mantine, monitoring first | Accepted |
| 19 | The IdP owns identity; Merit Order owns teams; user records decide team and role | Accepted |
| 20 | Quality scores are measured with graded tasks; judges only where nothing else works | Superseded by 28 as the default source of scores |
| 21 | Every cost is visible next to the switch that controls it | Accepted |
| 22 | GPU prices come from SkyPilot's catalog; SkyPilot runs in its own environment | Accepted |
| 23 | A named model is never silently swapped; substitution is opt-in and never to a weaker model | Accepted |
| 24 | Refusals are retried on another model only for `auto` | Accepted |
| 25 | Every process follows the stored configuration | Accepted |
| 26 | No request queue in the gateway; a full GPU queues only as a last resort | Accepted |
| 27 | Prices are live, never typed in | Accepted |
| 28 | Quality scores come from published benchmarks, anchored to the best model | Accepted |

**Still open:** reconciling computed costs with provider and cloud bills; Kubernetes-native GPU
provisioning (llm-d / KServe); a learned router; model-based compression; Parquet export;
provider batch APIs (decision 10).

## 1. Python for the core

**Why:** The team prefers it, the ML and inference ecosystem (SkyPilot, vLLM, classifiers,
compression) is Python, and gateway overhead is a few milliseconds against model latency measured
in seconds. We scale by running more gateway copies.

**Revisit if:** a real deployment hits gateway CPU limits that more replicas can't fix.

## 2. Our own backend adapters; no LiteLLM dependency

**Why:**
- LiteLLM converts everything to the OpenAI format internally. That's lossy for `cache_control`,
  thinking signatures, and other provider fields, and prompt caching is our biggest savings lever.
- It has had supply-chain incidents, a large dependency tree, and SSO in a commercially licensed
  directory.
- The rest of what it offers (keys, budgets, spend tracking, routing, UI) we'd replace anyway,
  because our ledger, router, and reporting work differently.
- Almost every backend speaks the Anthropic or OpenAI format, so pass-through plus one pair of
  translators covers them in a few thousand lines we fully control.

**What we still take:** LiteLLM's MIT-licensed price list, fetched as data by the worker (never
imported as code) for direct provider APIs (see #27), and its code as a reference for provider quirks. Anyone needing a niche provider can run LiteLLM themselves
as an OpenAI-compatible backend.

**Revisit if:** keeping our adapters current with provider API changes becomes a significant
ongoing burden.

## 3. No Envoy

**Why:** Envoy AI Gateway is strong as a proxy layer, but all of our product logic (routing,
shaping, sessions, budgets, ledger) would still be Python, called by Envoy over gRPC on every
request. That adds a second system to operate and debug, assumes Kubernetes, narrows the
contributor pool, and solves a performance problem we don't have. Merit Order runs behind whatever
load balancer or ingress an organization already uses.

**Revisit if:** large deployments ask for it. The routing and shaping code could be packaged as an
Envoy external-processing service without being rewritten. Separately, an optional plugin could use
Kubernetes inference-routing tools (llm-d) inside a customer's own GPU cluster.

## 4. Docker Compose and Kubernetes both supported

**Why:** Compose gives the clone-and-run experience an open-source project needs; Kubernetes is
what enterprises at our target spend run in production. Same images, no Kubernetes-specific code in
the app. Details in [07 — Deployment](07-deployment.md).

## 5. The harness owns the conversation; no content stored

**Why:** Harnesses already resend history and compact it. Storing conversations would make the
proxy a retention, eDiscovery, and breach liability. The gateway stores routing metadata (hashes,
timestamps, backends) only. Compression stays cache-safe by being deterministic (the same tool output
always compresses the same way), not by storing conversations.

**Revisit if:** we add the OpenAI Responses API's stored mode, which would be opt-in with explicit
retention.

## 6. Route by marginal cost, including cache rebuild cost

**Why:** A running GPU's spare capacity is already paid for, so it's nearly free, even for a better
model than the task needs. Moving a session re-pays for its whole context, so the router counts that
before moving. Details in [03 — Routing](03-routing.md).

## 7. SkyPilot for GPUs, provisioning as a plugin

**Why:** SkyPilot handles multi-cloud GPUs, spot instances, and replica scaling (SkyServe), and can
target Kubernetes clusters. Our controller decides *whether* to run a model; SkyPilot handles *how*.
A Kubernetes-native option (llm-d or KServe) can be another plugin later.

## 8. Generic OIDC, Entra first

**Why:** Entra is the first customer need; Google and others are configuration on the same code
path. Harnesses get short-lived virtual keys via a device-code login.

## 9. Postgres and Redis are the only state

**Why:** Both are available as managed services everywhere and are easy to run in Compose.
ClickHouse may become an optional reporting backend for very large deployments.

## 10. Continuous batching only; async batch APIs out of scope

**Why:** The product is for day-to-day interactive use. vLLM/SGLang batch concurrent requests on
their own. Provider batch APIs (about 50% off for work that can wait hours) may come later.

## 11. AGPL-3.0-only license

**Why:** Changes that others are offered over a network come back to the project.

## 12. Reporting UI in React/TypeScript

**Why:** Interactive filters and charts are much easier to build well, and the UI only talks to the
gateway's HTTP APIs, so it stays replaceable. The rest of the project remains Python. Decision 18
grew it into the full console, which uses the reports, console and admin APIs (`/v1/reports`,
`/v1/console`, `/v1/admin`).

**Alternative considered:** server-rendered pages with htmx (all-Python, clunkier interactivity).

## 13. Opt-in response cache may store responses

**Why:** Exact-match caching saves real money for chatbots, RAG, and evals. It can't work without
keeping the response, so it's the one exception to decision 5: off by default, enabled per team or
per request, scoped to a team or user, and expired by TTL (Redis).

## 14. Open-weight catalog with prices from OpenRouter

**Why:** There are dozens of useful open-weight models (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, MiniMax, MiMo,
Mistral, Gemma, Nemotron, Muse, gpt-oss) and their prices change often. `config/models-open.yaml`
lists them with their Hugging Face IDs (needed for self-hosting); the worker keeps
their prices, context windows and output limits current from OpenRouter's public catalog (#27). A route with
no known price is never chosen by `auto`, so a missing price can't look free. OpenRouter is one
backend among many, not the system: it adds a fee, sends prompts through another company, and
doesn't count toward cloud commitments.

## 15. GPU scaling on addressable demand at API prices

**Why:** Counting only traffic already served by a model means a stopped model never looks worth
starting. The controller counts what all traffic the model *could* serve costs at API-equivalent
prices, excluding free upgrades. That number doesn't fall when GPUs take over the traffic, so it
doesn't flap. Two self-hosted models that address the same traffic are each credited with it; the
router then splits the traffic. Revisit if that over-provisions in practice.

## 16. Deterministic, rule-based compression first

**Why:** Compression must give identical output every turn or it breaks provider caching (and, on
recent Claude models, edited history can invalidate thinking). Rules (strip ANSI codes, collapse
repeated lines, keep head and tail of huge outputs) are deterministic, need no stored state, and add
no ML dependency. A model-based compressor (LLMLingua-2) can come later behind a content-hash cache.

## 17. Configuration versions in Postgres, YAML as the starting point

**Why:** Containers mount config read-only, and a fleet of gateways needs one source of truth. Saving
from the console validates the document, stores it as a new version (who, when, why), and every
gateway hot-reloads it within seconds; in-flight requests finish on the objects they started with.
Restore is one click. The YAML file is used until the first version is saved, and stays the format
for import, export, and GitOps. Secrets never enter the database: literal keys are refused and must
stay `${ENV}` references.

## 18. Control panel in Mantine, monitoring first

**Why:** Anyone running a company's LLM traffic through Merit Order will watch it far more than
they reconfigure it. The console opens on a live Dispatch view (the merit-order stack from real
traffic, a live request feed, backend health, the GPU fleet, and what needs attention), with
configuration one page among several. Mantine gives a complete admin component set with few
dependencies; charts stay hand-written SVG.

## 19. The IdP owns identity; Merit Order owns teams; user records decide team and role

**Why:** Enterprises expect Entra to be the source of truth for who exists and which groups they're
in, but budgets and model policy belong to Merit Order. People are created at first sign-in, their
team and role come from mapped groups, and admins can pin exceptions. Each request resolves team and
role from the user record (cached for a minute), not from the key, so moves and disables apply to
existing keys. SCIM provisioning (`/scim/v2`) applies Entra changes, including deprovisioning, as they happen.

## 20. Quality scores are measured with graded tasks; judges only where nothing else works

**Why:** Routing is only as good as its quality scores. Mechanical grading (exact answers, hidden
unit tests run in a sandbox, the end state of a scripted tool environment) is cheap, repeatable and
explainable, so it grades everything it can. Easy tasks can't tell the strongest models apart, so
the `frontier` suite adds hard work at levels 3–5. Open-ended work (summaries, critiques,
recommendations) can't be checked mechanically, so two judge models from different families grade
it against concrete rubric statements; both must agree, which offsets a judge's preference for its
own family. The eval suggests scores (with a finer 0–5 "ability" and a flag where evidence is thin);
an admin decides whether to apply them.

**Superseded by 28** as the default source of scores. The eval suite still runs, and applying its
suggestions writes the models' `quality` in the config, which routing uses only with
`quality.source: config` (or until live scores are first fetched).

## 21. Every cost is visible next to the switch that controls it

**Why:** A gateway that starts cloud GPUs on its own has to be easy to overrule. The console shows
where each GPU runs, for how long, and what it has cost, with stop, pin, and stop-all controls that
take effect within seconds and are logged with who and why. Organization safeguards (org and GPU
budgets, fleet caps, a per-request ceiling) are hard limits that apply to admin pins too, so no
single action can exceed them. Limits are config (versioned, reviewable); stops and pins are
runtime controls (immediate, expiring), because an emergency shouldn't wait on a config review.

## 22. GPU prices come from SkyPilot's catalog; SkyPilot runs in its own environment

**Why:** A hand-typed `gpu_cost_per_hour` is wrong as soon as SkyPilot places a replica somewhere
else: 4×H100 spot ranges from about $4/h to over $20/h across clouds and regions. The controller
uses SkyPilot's catalog (the same prices its optimizer uses) for break-even decisions, and each
running replica's own cloud, region, instance, and spot price for burn rate, cost, and chargeback.
The configured price is the fallback, and the only price for your own hardware. These are list
prices; discounts, disks, and egress aren't included until bill reconciliation exists.

SkyPilot pulls in about 150 packages and, as a dependency, would have downgraded the gateway's
uvicorn. So it lives only in the controller's `-gpu` image, in a separate Python environment, and
Merit Order reaches it through the `sky` CLI and SkyPilot's own interpreter.

## 23. A named model is never silently swapped; substitution is opt-in and never to a weaker model

**Why:** Harnesses and apps that name a model depend on its behavior, especially with tools. When
a named model has nowhere to run (for example its GPUs were stopped), the default is a 503 that
explains why for each route and suggests `auto`. Teams that would rather keep working can turn on
`substitute_unavailable`: the request goes to a model at least as good for the task (never weaker),
and the response says which model was replaced. `auto` sessions move to another model, mid-task included, when
their model's routes are stopped, saturated, or all over capacity.

## 24. Refusals are retried on another model only for `auto`

**Why:** Safety classifiers sometimes refuse benign requests, and for `auto` the client has said any
suitable model is fine, so the next model gets a chance (the refused attempt is still billed and
logged). A client that named a model gets that model's answer, refusal included. Teams can turn the
retry off.

## 25. Every process follows the stored configuration

**Why:** Budgets and safeguards edited in the console must reach everything that enforces them.
Gateways, the worker (alerts), and the capacity controller (GPU budget, fleet caps) all load the
newest stored version and reload when it changes; the YAML file only applies until the first
version is saved. A version that fails to load is skipped and the last good one stays in effect.

## 26. No request queue in the gateway; a full GPU queues only as a last resort

**Why:** LLM calls are interactive and streaming, so a queue in Redis would add latency and a
second set of workers to pull from it, for no gain: vLLM already schedules and queues on the GPU.
A saturated GPU gets no new work while another route can take it, but when it's the only route,
sending the request there to wait beats a 503. The wait is bounded (`max_waiting` per replica) so
a backlog can't grow without limit. Gateways count in-flight requests and share the counts every
2 s, because the controller's one-minute metrics sample is too slow to catch a burst.

## 27. Prices are live, never typed in

**Why:** `auto` compares prices on every request, so a stale price sends traffic to the wrong place, and
prices change without notice: OpenRouter's provider prices move overnight, and Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon
double on 1 December 2026. Prices typed into the config were right only on the day they were typed.

**How:** The worker refreshes prices every `prices_refresh_minutes` (15): OpenRouter routes from
OpenRouter's catalog (what OpenRouter charges), and direct provider APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock,
Vertex, Azure, Foundry, Mistral) from the price list LiteLLM maintains, which also carries long-prompt
tiers (Claude Haiku 5.5 above 100K tokens, GPT-6.x above 272K) that costing and routing apply. Gateways
reload only when a price or a model limit (context window, output limit) changes. Every price change is
reported; a maker's list price that disagrees with OpenRouter's for the same model raises an alert,
since one list is then wrong; a list that can't be fetched keeps its routes' last prices and raises an
alert. The Models page shows each route's source and
when prices were last checked. OpenRouter requests also record what OpenRouter actually billed.

**Not chosen:** Scraping the providers' pricing pages (fragile, and each one differs); trusting a single
list without a cross-check. A `price:` in the config remains for what no public list knows, such as a
negotiated discount, and is shown as an override. Self-hosted GPU routes have no list: their `price:` is
the API-equivalent rate that the shadow price scales (decision 6).

## 28. Quality scores come from published benchmarks, anchored to the best model

**Why:** Our own eval suite couldn't separate the strongest models: every Claude model passed the same
48 of 56 tasks, and the order of the rest was noise (a paragraph too many, one judge's verdict).
Published suites run the same way for every model, with hundreds of hard tasks, do separate them.

**How:** By default the worker takes Epoch AI's data (CC BY 4.0, no key): every model on one ability
scale and every benchmark on the same scale by difficulty, so models are comparable even when tested on
different benchmarks. A score is a model's chance of solving a task as hard as a reference benchmark
(FrontierSWE), refined for coding by its own coding results; on the `best` scale the best model is 5
and the rest in proportion. The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is the alternative source.
`quality_override` always wins. A task type the source doesn't cover scores 0 ("unmeasured"), so `auto`
doesn't pick the model for it; requests that name the model still work. Scores written in the config
apply only until live scores are first fetched, or with `source: config`.

**Not chosen:** A worst-to-best scale by default: it depends on the weakest model configured, so adding a
cheap model reshuffles everyone, and it squeezed the frontier models together (it remains as `scale:
range`). Averaging raw scores across whatever benchmarks each model happens to have: models tested
only on easier benchmarks scored too high. Whole-number scores: six models tied at 4.

## 29. Routing state per conversation, not per session id; context limits move work instead of failing it

**Why:** Claude Code sends its subagents' turns and its side requests (titles, summaries) under the main
session's id. They are separate conversations, each with its own history and cache, so sharing one
routing record meant every subagent turn overwrote the main conversation's model, prefix hash and warm
caches: the next main turn looked compacted, re-classified, and could pay to rebuild its cache
elsewhere. Separately, a session kept its model for the whole task even after the conversation outgrew
that model's context window, so the request was sent where it couldn't fit.

**How:** Routing state is kept per thread: the session id, plus the subagent id (`x-claude-code-agent-id`)
and `/aux` for side requests. Spend limits, the ledger and reports keep the session id, so a session's
cost includes its subagents. Claude Code's request class (`x-claude-code-request-class`) caps the level
of side requests (1) and compaction summaries (3), configurable. A conversation that no longer fits its
model moves to one with room at the same floor, mid-task included; a provider's "too long" sends `auto`
to a bigger window, and the error a client sees is worded as Anthropic's ("prompt is too long"), which is
what Claude Code compacts on.

**Not chosen:** Ignoring the agent id and relying on prefix hashes: every alternation between the main
conversation and a subagent looks like compaction. Sending subagents to the cheapest model outright:
Claude Code's own subagent model settings already do that when wanted, and some subagents do the hard
part of the work. Refusing a too-long request at the gateway before sending it: the token count is an
estimate, so the gateway would refuse requests that fit.

## 30. Measured scores on the same scale as published ones, from hard tasks only

**Why:** After decision 28 the published scores routing uses had one decimal on a best-is-5 scale, but
the Evals page still scored models the old way: the highest whole level passed 75% of the time, beside
a 0–5 sum of pass rates. The two couldn't be compared, and the old scores made models look measured
when they weren't. Two Gemini models that hit rate limits on 32 and 36 of their 56 tasks showed 100%
passed and top scores from the rest, and a provider account out of credit (HTTP 402) counted as 16 wrong
answers.

**How:** For each task type, a measured score is 5 × (the model's pass rate on level-4 and level-5 tasks
÷ the best measured model's), with a 90% range, worked out together for every model's latest result.
It needs at least 10 graded hard tasks; fewer shows "too few". Scores are worked out again from stored
results each time they're shown, with today's rules for what counts (so old 402s are now skipped).
Applying them writes either `quality` (used with `source: config`) or `quality_override` (wins
everywhere), and the dialog says which will change routing.

**Not chosen:** Fitting an ability scale to our own tasks the way Epoch does: with a few dozen tasks,
most passed by every strong model, the fit would be mostly noise. Counting easy tasks: every model
passes them, which squeezes all scores towards 5. Scaling each run on its own: a run that measured only
weak models would make the best of them a 5.

## 31. GPU break-even sizes each model and prices it through SkyPilot

**Why:** The first break-even view assumed one $16-an-hour replica doing 4,000 tokens a second for every
open model. A 16 GB model doesn't need four H100s and a 1.6 TB one doesn't fit on them, and spot prices
are often a third of on-demand, so the answer (whether a GPU can ever pay) was mostly the assumption.

**How:** Each model's weights (bytes at their published precision) and active parameters come from
Hugging Face. Its replica is the cheapest machine per hour whose GPUs hold the weights in 70% of their
memory, on 1, 2, 4 or 8 GPUs, priced from SkyPilot's catalog through SkyPilot itself (spot or
on-demand, every cloud it covers), refreshed when over 6 hours old or on request. Throughput is an
estimate from the GPUs' compute and the active parameters, labeled as one; a deployment's measured
capacity replaces it. Price lookups run with no cloud credentials. Where the gateway has no SkyPilot
(the Helm chart keeps it in the controller), the controller publishes the prices.

**Not chosen:** Reading SkyPilot's catalog files directly: the same data, but SkyPilot already handles
their versions, refresh schedule and per-cloud quirks. Putting SkyPilot in the production gateway image:
~150 packages on the request path's image for a report. Choosing the machine with the lowest cost per
token: it picked eight H100s on spot for a 16 GB model, which needs far more traffic to pay than one
L4 does.

## 32. Break-even weights: real file sizes, quantizing, and the machine that pays

**Why:** Sizing counted every parameter Hugging Face reports as stored in bytes at a byte each, but
gpt-oss, Kimi and DeepSeek ship packed 4-bit weights: Kimi K3.1 looked like 2.8 TB and too big for any
machine, when it's 1.56 TB and fits on eight B300s. And "what about quantizing?" had only a switch for
FP8. Once 4-bit weights fit on old A100s, taking the cheapest machine per hour that holds them showed
"never" for models that pay on a faster machine.

**How:** Weights are the safetensors files' size (one copy of each format), split by precision from
Hugging Face's parameter counts; packed 4-bit weights are the bytes left over at about half a byte a
parameter. Weights can be served as published, in FP8 (16-bit checkpoints) or in 4 bits (everything
above 4, at 4.25 bits a weight with its scales); the GPUs compute FP8 weights at FP8 where they can, and
4-bit weights at FP8 on Blackwell and at 16 bits elsewhere. Quality scores stay those of the published
weights, and the tab says so wherever a model is quantized. Each model has the machines worth
considering (cheapest per hour first, each faster than the cheaper ones); the report takes the cheapest
that pays, or if none can, the cheapest per token (or a cheaper one within 10% of it). It also names
the best level an open model can host per task type.

**Not chosen:** A quality penalty for quantized models: there's no number to use that isn't made up, and
the eval harness can measure the real one. Full FP4 throughput on Blackwell for 4-bit weights: vLLM runs
the published MXFP4 models with 8-bit activations, so FP4's rate would double their estimate. Always the
cheapest per token: eight GPUs for a model that fits on one, which is why decision 31 took the cheapest
per hour; now that's the rule unless a faster machine is the only one that pays.

## 33. Grok, Mistral's own API, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and scores for models Epoch barely covers

**Why:** Routing matters most among the frontier APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, Mistral), and
Grok wasn't configured at all. Mistral's models only went through OpenRouter although a Mistral key was
set. DeepSeek published a better release of V4.1 Flash (1017). And eleven open models had no score at
all, partly because some are named in Epoch's data by their Hugging Face repository
(Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct), which nothing matched.

**How:** Grok 4.7 through OpenRouter and xAI's own API (the `xai` backend, off until `XAI_API_KEY` is
set); its scores come from Epoch like everyone's (coding 2.5). Mistral Large 4, Small 4 and Ministral
14B route to Mistral's API as well, at the same prices. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 is its own model next
to September's, so `auto` takes whichever qualifies more cheaply. Models are also matched by their
Hugging Face name, and names are tried in a fixed order (route ids, `hf_id`, aliases), so the first
match is always the same one. A model with neither FrontierSWE/FrontierCode results nor an index gets
its coding ability from older coding benchmarks (`quality.fallback`: Terminal Bench, GSO-Bench,
MirrorCode); Qwen3 Coder gets 1.0 that way.

**Not chosen:** Replacing September's DeepSeek release with 1017: today it would make level-2 coding
cost about four times as much at the prices `auto` uses ($0.13 against $0.034 a million tokens), and
score lower (2.0 from its index alone, against 2.4 from September's FrontierCode result), although
1017 is the better model. Using the older coding benchmarks for every model without coding results,
alone or averaged with the index: checked against the 16 models that have both kinds of results, they
predict FrontierSWE and FrontierCode results less well than the index does (they miss by about 2.6
points on the ability scale, the index by 2.2), and averaging the two gains about 0.1. WeirdML: its
first version misses by about 6, and v3's file holds a different score than the one the index is
fitted on. Mistral Medium 3.5,
Mistral's closed model: it scores below Large 4 (index 142 against 155) at twice the price.
