# 11 — Evals: measuring model quality

`auto` routing sends each request to the cheapest model good enough for it. "Good enough" comes from
each model's **quality scores**: 1–5 per task type (coding, general). The classifier gives every
request a floor (coding:3 for ordinary coding, coding:4 for agent work with many tools, +1 for hard
tasks or large contexts), and only models scoring at least that are considered. Scores that are too
high send hard work to models that can't do it; scores that are too low waste money. Evals measure
them.

## Running one

**From the console:** Models → **Evals** → *Run an eval…*. Pick models and suites, see the
estimated cost, and start it. The worker runs it in the background, against the gateway like any
client. Progress, cost, and every task's result show on the page. When it finishes, *Apply
scores…* writes the measured scores into the configuration as a new version, which you can roll
back from Config → History. *Run again…* repeats a run with the same settings.

**From the command line** (on a machine with Docker, so code tasks run too):

```bash
uv run meritorder eval --models claude-sonnet,claude-opus,claude-fable          # estimates cost, asks first
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --only 'c5-*,a5-*' --repeat 3               # just the hardest coding work, 3 times each
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --apply                                      # also write the scores into the config
```

CLI runs are recorded too, so they appear on the Evals page, and cancelling one there stops it.

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `--suite` | `starter,frontier` | Built-in suites, task directories or YAML files, comma-separated |
| `--only` | all tasks | Task id patterns, e.g. `c5-*,g4-*` |
| `--repeat` | 1 | Runs per task. More runs mean less luck in the scores, at proportional cost |
| `--judges` | `claude-opus,gpt-terra` | Models that grade open-ended tasks (those with a live route) |
| `--sandbox` | `docker` | `none` skips tasks that run model-written code |
| `--threshold` | 0.75 | Pass rate a model needs at a level to earn it |

Eval traffic goes through the gateway with its usual budgets, rate limits and per-request cap, and is
tagged `eval=<suite>-<time>` in the ledger. Its spend counts like any other (for the person who ran it,
their team, the models, and the organization), and Reports → Breakdown → **Tag** → `eval` shows each
run's cost on its own line. It isn't counted as savings: a run on Haiku isn't money saved and one on
Fable isn't money lost, because you'd have run those models anyway, so its baseline is the model it
ran. Runs from the console use
a temporary key for the person who started them, revoked when the run ends.

## How each model is run

A comparison is only fair if nothing but the model differs, so a run fixes everything else and records it:

- **No output limit.** Requests set no `max_tokens`, so each model may write as much as it can
  (`max_output_tokens`: 128,000 for current Claude and GPT models), thinking included. A reply that
  fills the model's own maximum fails and is marked *cut off*. The per-request cost limit on Controls
  still applies: if it stops a reply first, the result is *not graded* (left out of the scores) and
  says how many tokens it allowed, so you can raise the limit and run it again. At $40 per million
  output tokens, Fable's full 128,000 costs $5.12.
- **The same effort.** Each task runs at the reasoning effort `auto` uses for its level
  (`routing.effort_by_floor`: low for 1–2, medium for 3, high for 4–5), not at each model's own
  default, which differs (Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 default to medium, Fable and Sonnet to high).
  A model that doesn't take that effort runs at its default. A task can set its own (`effort: max`).
- **One route per model.** Each model runs on its first live route, which in the shipped config is
  its own provider's API, rather than whichever reseller the router finds cheapest or fastest that
  minute. Judges too.
- **Each model in its own API.** Agent tasks talk to Claude over Anthropic's Messages API, the way
  Claude Code does, sending each reply back unchanged so Claude's thinking carries from one tool call
  to the next (Chat Completions has nowhere to put it, so it would be lost). Other models use Chat
  Completions; Gemini's reasoning details go back with each turn's tool results.
- **Answers are kept.** Each result keeps what the model wrote (the first 60,000 characters), an
  agent's tool calls in order, and each judge's verdict and reason on every rubric point. Click a
  result on the Evals page to read them, for instance to see which judge was right when they
  disagree.

Long replies take a while: 100,000 tokens is 15–20 minutes on the largest models. The gateway streams
from the provider meanwhile, so nothing times out.

## The suites

| Suite | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `starter` | 24 short tasks, levels 1–5: facts, arithmetic, one tool call, small code questions. Cheap; strong models max it out |
| `frontier` | 32 hard tasks at levels 3–5, built so strong models separate from the very top: 12 code tasks with 14–48 hidden tests each (an interpreter with tail calls, a regex engine matching Python's, unified diffs, recurrence rules, cron, a streaming JSON tokenizer…), 6 multi-step tool tasks (fixing bugs in small repositories, a purchase with traps, revenue from a messy database, an incident's root cause), and 14 general tasks (multi-hop questions over documents of 6k–45k words, logic grids, exact combinatorics, writing under constraints, and 3 judged pieces of open-ended work) |

Levels mean what the classifier means by them: 3 is ordinary coding, analysis or long context;
4 is agent work with many tools, or hard reasoning; 5 is the hardest of both.

## Seeing the tasks

Models → Evals → **Tasks** lists every task in the built-in suites: what it tests and how it's graded.
Open one to read everything about it: the full prompt and the tools the model gets, then what only the
grader sees (the checks, the hidden tests with a reference solution and a plausible wrong one, an agent
task's repository and the grader's data, a judged task's rubric and reference answer), and how each
model did on it in its latest run.

## Four kinds of task

| Kind | The model gets | Graded by |
|---|---|---|
| `answer` | One prompt | Mechanical checks: an exact final answer (`Final answer: …`), a number, JSON fields, a tool call, or writing constraints (word count, bullets, required phrases) |
| `code` | A precise spec for a Python module | Hidden unit tests, run against its code in a sandbox. Every test must pass |
| `agent` | A goal and tools | A scripted environment answers the tools (a small repository, a booking API, a database, logs), then checks the end state: the right fix with stricter hidden tests, the right booking made once, the exact figure |
| `judged` | Open-ended work (a summary, a critique, a recommendation) | Two judge models from different families, against a rubric of concrete statements and a reference answer. Both must agree every point is met |

**Why two judges from different families.** A model tends to rate answers like its own higher. The
judges don't know which model wrote the answer, every criterion is a checkable statement ("states
the outage lasted 47 minutes"), and an answer passes only if a Claude judge and a GPT judge both say
every criterion is met. Their reasons are kept with the result. Everything else is graded
mechanically, which is cheaper and repeatable.

**The sandbox.** Model-written code runs in a throwaway Docker container (`python:3.12-slim`):
no network, a read-only filesystem apart from a small `/tmp`, an unprivileged user, no
capabilities, and limits on memory, CPU, processes and time. Each hidden test also has its own
CPU-time limit (10 s), so one runaway loop fails that test, not the whole task. A task can forbid
imports (the regex task forbids `re`); that's checked in the code's syntax tree, which keeps honest
solutions honest but wouldn't stop code written to get around it. Without Docker, those tasks are skipped
and the results say so. The worker in the Docker Compose stack has no Docker access by default, so
console runs skip code tasks there: run those with `meritorder eval` on a machine with Docker, and
their results land on the same page. (Giving a container the Docker socket gives it control of the
host, so it isn't on by default.)

## From results to scores

For each model and task type:

- **Score** (what routing uses): the highest level L where the model passes at least 75% of tasks at
  L **and every level below**. A model that aces level 5 but fails level 3 scores 2.
- **Ability** (0–5, shown next to it): the sum of its pass rates by level. Two models with the same
  score can differ a lot here; it's the finer view. A level the suite doesn't cover counts as the
  level below it did.
- **?**: at some level, there were too few task runs to be sure which side of 75% the model is on
  (its 90% confidence interval straddles 75%). Run again with `--repeat` to firm it up.

Beside the scores, each model shows what its tasks took, because two models that pass the same tasks
can still differ a lot in time and money:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Median time** (and 90th percentile) | The model's own time to complete a task: every request it answered, without grading, judges or the environment's tools |
| **Turns / tools** | Average requests and tool calls per task. An agent that needs 20 turns where another needs 6 is slower and costs more even at the same price per token |
| **Output** | Average output tokens per task, thinking included |
| **Per solve** | Cost divided by tasks passed: what a solved task costs on this model, which is what matters when choosing one |
| **Cut off** | Replies that hit an output limit |

Runs that say nothing about quality are skipped and don't count: no sandbox, no judges, a judge that
failed to give a verdict, a provider's rate limit or outage (HTTP 429 or 5xx), or a reply the
per-request cost limit stopped. Run again to fill them in. Other errors (a reply that fills the
model's maximum output or its context window, a request the model rejects) count as fails.

## Writing your own tasks

The best suite is made from your own work: a model that's good at public puzzles may still be wrong
for your codebase. A suite is a directory of task directories (or a YAML file of `answer` tasks).

```yaml
# my-suite/c4-invoice-rounding/task.yaml
id: c4-invoice-rounding
task: coding          # or general
level: 4
kind: code            # answer | code | agent | judged
prompt_file: prompt.md
code: {tests: tests.py, timeout: 30}   # hidden tests: top-level test_* functions; forbid: [re] bans imports
reference: reference.py                                    # a correct solution, never sent to models
```

- `answer`: `prompt` and `checks` (see `src/meritorder/evals/runner.py` → `grade`). Ask for
  `Final answer: …` on the last line and check it with `final`, `final_number` or `final_one_of`.
- `agent`: `env: module:Class`, `env_args`, `max_turns`. Environments subclass
  `meritorder.evals.envs.Env`: tools, `call`, and `grade`.
- `judged`: `rubric` (concrete statements) and `reference_answer`.
- Generated prompts (long documents built from a seed): `generate: module:function` with
  `generate_args`.
- Optional on any task: `effort` (instead of the level's) and `max_tokens` (only if you want the
  task to have a limit; built-in tasks don't).

Run it with `meritorder eval --suite ./my-suite`, or alongside the built-in ones:
`--suite starter,frontier,./my-suite`. Check every task offline before trusting it: the repository's
`tests/evals/` shows how (reference solutions pass the hidden tests, deliberately wrong ones fail).

**Public tasks leak.** Anything in a public repository can end up in a model's training data, which
makes it easier than it looks. Keep a private suite for the decisions that matter, and refresh it.

## Cost

The estimate before a run counts each task's prompt and a typical reply for every model, and
judging. Reasoning models often write several times more than that, and with no output limit a hard
task can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so treat it as a rough guide.
Long-document and agent tasks dominate: a level-5 document task sends about 60k tokens, and an agent
task resends its growing conversation every turn. Organization and personal budgets and the
per-request cap (Controls) apply to eval traffic like any other.

"""Durable storage: users, API keys, the per-request ledger, and report queries.

Postgres in real deployments (ledger partitioned by month, hourly rollups);
an in-memory version for development and tests. The ledger holds metadata
only, never prompt or response content.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
import os
import re
import secrets
import uuid
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta
from typing import Any

LEDGER_FIELDS = [
    "id", "ts", "user_id", "team", "key_id", "session_id", "tags", "client_format", "requested_model", "floor",
    "served_model", "upstream_model", "backend", "backend_kind", "status", "error", "stream", "upgraded", "proxy_cache",
    "input_tokens", "cache_read_tokens", "cache_write_tokens", "output_tokens", "latency_ms", "ttft_ms",
    "actual_cost", "served_api_cost", "baseline_cost", "list_cost",
    "savings_routing", "savings_caching", "savings_self_hosting", "savings_compression", "savings_response_cache",
]
SUM_FIELDS = [
    "input_tokens", "cache_read_tokens", "cache_write_tokens", "output_tokens",
    "actual_cost", "served_api_cost", "baseline_cost", "list_cost",
    "savings_routing", "savings_caching", "savings_self_hosting", "savings_compression", "savings_response_cache",
]
SAVINGS_FIELDS = ["savings_routing", "savings_caching", "savings_self_hosting", "savings_compression", "savings_response_cache"]
GROUPS = {"user": "user_id", "team": "team", "model": "served_model", "backend": "backend", "day": "day", "hour": "hour", "month": "month", "none": None}
_TAG = re.compile(r"^tag:([A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,64})$")


def hash_key(key: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(key.encode()).hexdigest()


def new_api_key() -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Returns (key_id, secret). The secret is shown once and stored only as a hash."""
    return f"key_{secrets.token_hex(6)}", f"mo-{secrets.token_urlsafe(32)}"


def month_start(now: datetime | None = None) -> datetime:
    now = now or datetime.now(UTC)
    return now.replace(day=1, hour=0, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)


def validate_group(group_by: str) -> str:
    if group_by in GROUPS or _TAG.match(group_by):
        return group_by
    raise ValueError(f"group_by must be one of {', '.join(GROUPS)} or tag:<name>")


def _finish_row(row: dict) -> dict:
    row["savings_total"] = sum(row.get(f) or 0 for f in SAVINGS_FIELDS)
    for k, v in list(row.items()):
        if isinstance(v, float):
            row[k] = round(v, 6)
        elif isinstance(v, datetime):
            row[k] = v.isoformat()
    return row


# ====================================================================== memory


class MemoryStore:
    kind = "memory"

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.users: dict[str, dict] = {}
        self.keys: dict[str, dict] = {}
        self.ledger: list[dict] = []

    async def init(self) -> None:
        return None

    async def close(self) -> None:
        return None

    async def migrate(self) -> None:
        return None

    async def ping(self) -> bool:
        return True

    async def upsert_user(self, user_id: str, team: str, role: str, email: str | None = None, display_name: str | None = None,
                          source: str = "idp") -> None:
        """source="idp": a login refreshes team/role unless an admin pinned them; "ensure": only create if missing."""
        u = self.users.get(user_id)
        if u is None:
            self.users[user_id] = {"id": user_id, "team": team, "role": role, "email": email, "display_name": display_name,
                                   "managed": "idp", "disabled_at": None, "created_at": datetime.now(UTC)}
            return
        if source == "idp" and u.get("managed", "idp") == "idp":
            u.update(team=team, role=role)
        if email:
            u["email"] = email
        if display_name:
            u["display_name"] = display_name

    async def get_user(self, user_id: str) -> dict | None:
        u = self.users.get(user_id)
        return dict(u) if u else None

    async def update_user(self, user_id: str, team: str | None = None, role: str | None = None, disabled: bool | None = None,
                          managed: str | None = None) -> dict | None:
        u = self.users.get(user_id)
        if u is None:
            return None
        if team is not None or role is not None:
            u["managed"] = "local"
        if team is not None:
            u["team"] = team
        if role is not None:
            u["role"] = role
        if managed is not None:
            u["managed"] = managed
        if disabled is not None:
            u["disabled_at"] = datetime.now(UTC) if disabled else None
        return dict(u)

    async def find_user_by_email(self, email: str) -> dict | None:
        return next((dict(u) for u in self.users.values() if (u.get("email") or "").lower() == email.lower()), None)

    async def scim_groups(self) -> list[dict]:
        return [dict(g) for g in self.__dict__.setdefault("groups", {}).values()]

    async def scim_group(self, gid: str) -> dict | None:
        g = self.__dict__.setdefault("groups", {}).get(gid)
        return dict(g) if g else None

    async def save_scim_group(self, group: dict) -> None:
        self.__dict__.setdefault("groups", {})[group["id"]] = dict(group)

    async def delete_scim_group(self, gid: str) -> bool:
        return self.__dict__.setdefault("groups", {}).pop(gid, None) is not None

    async def list_users(self, team: str | None = None) -> list[dict]:
        out = []
        for u in self.users.values():
            if team and u["team"] != team:
                continue
            keys = [k for k in self.keys.values() if k["user_id"] == u["id"]]
            out.append({**u, "active_keys": sum(1 for k in keys if not k["revoked_at"]),
                        "last_seen": max((k.get("last_used_at") for k in keys if k.get("last_used_at")), default=None)})
        return out

    async def create_key(self, user_id: str, team: str, role: str, name: str | None = None, tags: dict | None = None,
                         expires_at: datetime | None = None) -> tuple[str, str]:
        key_id, secret = new_api_key()
        self.keys[hash_key(secret)] = {
            "id": key_id, "user_id": user_id, "team": team, "role": role, "name": name, "tags": tags or {},
            "created_at": datetime.now(UTC), "expires_at": expires_at, "revoked_at": None,
        }
        return key_id, secret

    async def find_key(self, key_hash: str) -> dict | None:
        return self.keys.get(key_hash)

    async def list_keys(self, user_id: str | None = None, team: str | None = None) -> list[dict]:
        return [dict(k) for k in self.keys.values() if (user_id is None or k["user_id"] == user_id) and (team is None or k["team"] == team)]

    async def get_key(self, key_id: str) -> dict | None:
        return next((dict(k) for k in self.keys.values() if k["id"] == key_id), None)

    async def revoke_key(self, key_id: str) -> bool:
        for k in self.keys.values():
            if k["id"] == key_id and k["revoked_at"] is None:
                k["revoked_at"] = datetime.now(UTC)
                return True
        return False

    async def record(self, row: dict) -> None:
        self.ledger.append(dict(row))

    async def spend_since(self, field: str, value: str, since: datetime) -> float:
        return sum(r["actual_cost"] for r in self.ledger if r.get(field) == value and r["ts"] >= since)

    async def spend_all_since(self, since: datetime) -> float:
        return sum(r["actual_cost"] or 0 for r in self.ledger if r["ts"] >= since)

    # GPU time (cost of running replicas, accrued by the capacity controller) and the GPU activity log.

    async def add_gpu_usage(self, backend: str, ts: datetime, seconds: float, cost: float) -> None:
        hour = ts.replace(minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
        u = self.__dict__.setdefault("_gpu_usage", {}).setdefault((hour, backend), [0.0, 0.0])
        u[0] += seconds
        u[1] += cost

    async def gpu_spend_since(self, since: datetime) -> dict[str, float]:
        out: dict[str, float] = {}
        for (hour, backend), (_, cost) in self.__dict__.get("_gpu_usage", {}).items():
            if hour >= since.replace(minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0):
                out[backend] = out.get(backend, 0.0) + cost
        return out

    async def gpu_daily(self, since: datetime) -> list[dict]:
        days: dict = {}
        for (hour, backend), (secs, cost) in self.__dict__.get("_gpu_usage", {}).items():
            if hour >= since:
                d = days.setdefault((hour.date().isoformat(), backend), [0.0, 0.0])
                d[0] += secs / 3600
                d[1] += cost
        return [{"day": k[0], "backend": k[1], "replica_hours": v[0], "cost": v[1]} for k, v in sorted(days.items())]

    async def gpu_event(self, kind: str, backend: str | None = None, actor: str | None = None, detail: dict | None = None) -> None:
        ev = self.__dict__.setdefault("_gpu_events", [])
        ev.append({"id": len(ev) + 1, "ts": datetime.now(UTC), "backend": backend, "kind": kind, "actor": actor, "detail": detail or {}})

    async def gpu_events(self, limit: int = 100, backend: str | None = None) -> list[dict]:
        ev = [e for e in self.__dict__.get("_gpu_events", []) if backend is None or e["backend"] == backend]
        return list(reversed(ev))[:limit]

    def _key(self, r: dict, group_by: str) -> Any:
        m = _TAG.match(group_by)
        if m:
            return (r.get("tags") or {}).get(m.group(1)) or "(untagged)"
        if group_by == "none":
            return "total"
        if group_by in ("day", "hour", "month"):
            ts: datetime = r["ts"]
            if group_by == "hour":
                return ts.replace(minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0).isoformat()
            if group_by == "day":
                return ts.date().isoformat()
            return ts.strftime("%Y-%m")
        return r.get(GROUPS[group_by])

    async def summary(self, start: datetime, end: datetime, group_by: str, user_id: str | None = None,
                      team: str | None = None) -> list[dict]:
        validate_group(group_by)
        groups: dict[Any, dict] = defaultdict(lambda: {"requests": 0, "errors": 0, "upgraded": 0, **{f: 0 for f in SUM_FIELDS}})
        for r in self.ledger:
            if not (start <= r["ts"] < end):
                continue
            if user_id and r.get("user_id") != user_id:
                continue
            if team and r.get("team") != team:
                continue
            g = groups[self._key(r, group_by)]
            g["requests"] += 1
            g["errors"] += 1 if (r.get("status") or 0) >= 400 else 0
            g["upgraded"] += 1 if r.get("upgraded") else 0
            for f in SUM_FIELDS:
                g[f] += r.get(f) or 0
        rows = [_finish_row({"key": k, **v}) for k, v in groups.items()]
        return sorted(rows, key=lambda x: str(x["key"]))

    async def recent(self, limit: int, user_id: str | None = None, team: str | None = None) -> list[dict]:
        rows = [r for r in self.ledger if (not user_id or r.get("user_id") == user_id) and (not team or r.get("team") == team)]
        return [_finish_row({k: (str(v) if isinstance(v, uuid.UUID) else v) for k, v in r.items()}) for r in rows[-limit:][::-1]]

    async def needed_demand(self, model: str, since: datetime) -> float:
        return sum(r["served_api_cost"] for r in self.ledger if r.get("served_model") == model and not r.get("upgraded") and r["ts"] >= since)

    async def demand_by_hour(self, since: datetime) -> list[dict]:
        groups: dict[tuple, dict] = {}
        for r in self.ledger:
            if r["ts"] < since or r.get("upgraded") or (r.get("status") or 0) >= 400:
                continue
            hour = r["ts"].replace(minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
            k = (hour, r.get("floor"), r.get("served_model"), r.get("requested_model"))
            g = groups.setdefault(k, {"hour": hour, "floor": k[1], "served_model": k[2], "requested_model": k[3], "cost": 0.0, "tokens": 0})
            g["cost"] += r.get("served_api_cost") or 0
            g["tokens"] += sum(r.get(f) or 0 for f in ("input_tokens", "cache_read_tokens", "cache_write_tokens", "output_tokens"))
        return list(groups.values())

    async def export_rows(self, start: datetime, end: datetime, team: str | None = None):
        for r in sorted(self.ledger, key=lambda x: x["ts"]):
            if start <= r["ts"] < end and (team is None or r.get("team") == team):
                yield {k: r.get(k) for k in LEDGER_FIELDS}

    async def demand_rows(self, since: datetime) -> list[dict]:
        """Spend and tokens since ``since`` grouped by (floor, served_model, requested_model), excluding free upgrades."""
        groups: dict[tuple, dict] = {}
        for r in self.ledger:
            if r["ts"] < since or r.get("upgraded") or (r.get("status") or 0) >= 400:
                continue
            k = (r.get("floor"), r.get("served_model"), r.get("requested_model"))
            g = groups.setdefault(k, {"floor": k[0], "served_model": k[1], "requested_model": k[2], "cost": 0.0, "tokens": 0})
            g["cost"] += r.get("served_api_cost") or 0  # API-equivalent: stable whether or not GPUs serve it
            g["tokens"] += sum(r.get(f) or 0 for f in ("input_tokens", "cache_read_tokens", "cache_write_tokens", "output_tokens"))
        return list(groups.values())

    async def rollup(self, full: bool = False) -> int:
        return 0

    # --- config versions (the in-memory store keeps them for the life of the process)
    async def save_config(self, body: dict, author: str, comment: str | None) -> int:
        self.__dict__.setdefault("configs", [])
        vid = len(self.configs) + 1
        self.configs.append({"id": vid, "created_at": datetime.now(UTC), "author": author, "comment": comment, "body": body})
        return vid

    async def active_config(self) -> dict | None:
        return (self.__dict__.get("configs") or [None])[-1]

    async def config_versions(self, limit: int = 50) -> list[dict]:
        return [{k: v for k, v in c.items() if k != "body"} for c in reversed(self.__dict__.get("configs") or [])][:limit]

    async def get_config(self, vid: int) -> dict | None:
        return next((c for c in self.__dict__.get("configs") or [] if c["id"] == vid), None)

    async def get_setting(self, key: str):
        return self.__dict__.setdefault("settings", {}).get(key)

    async def set_setting(self, key: str, value) -> None:
        self.__dict__.setdefault("settings", {})[key] = value

    async def ensure_partitions(self) -> None:
        return None

class PostgresStore:
    kind = "postgres"

    def __init__(self, dsn: str) -> None:
        self.dsn = dsn
        self.pool = None

    async def init(self) -> None:
        import asyncpg

        async def setup(conn):
            await conn.set_type_codec("jsonb", encoder=json.dumps, decoder=json.loads, schema="pg_catalog")

        # Reports group by day/hour/month in UTC regardless of the database server's timezone.
        # Per process. Behind many gateway processes, put PgBouncer in front so the total stays within max_connections.
        size = int(os.environ.get("MERITORDER_DB_POOL_SIZE", "10"))
        self.pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(self.dsn, min_size=1, max_size=size, init=setup, server_settings={"timezone": "UTC"})

    async def close(self) -> None:
        if self.pool:
            await self.pool.close()

    async def ping(self) -> bool:
        async with self.pool.acquire() as c:
            return await c.fetchval("SELECT 1") == 1

    async def migrate(self) -> None:
        async with self.pool.acquire() as c:
            await c.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (version int PRIMARY KEY, applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())")
            applied = {r["version"] for r in await c.fetch("SELECT version FROM schema_migrations")}
            for version, sql in MIGRATIONS:
                if version in applied:
                    continue
                async with c.transaction():
                    await c.execute(sql)
                    await c.execute("INSERT INTO schema_migrations (version) VALUES ($1)", version)
        await self.ensure_partitions()

    async def ensure_partitions(self, months_ahead: int = 2) -> None:
        start = month_start()
        async with self.pool.acquire() as c:
            for i in range(months_ahead + 1):
                lo = (start + timedelta(days=32 * i)).replace(day=1)
                hi = (lo + timedelta(days=32)).replace(day=1)
                name = f"requests_{lo:%Y_%m}"
                exists = await c.fetchval("SELECT to_regclass($1)", name)
                if exists:
                    continue
                # Rows that landed in the default partition for this range must move first.
                async with c.transaction():
                    await c.execute(f"CREATE TABLE {name} (LIKE requests INCLUDING DEFAULTS)")
                    await c.execute(
                        f"WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM requests_default WHERE ts >= $1 AND ts < $2 RETURNING *) "
                        f"INSERT INTO {name} SELECT * FROM moved", lo, hi)
                    await c.execute(f"ALTER TABLE requests ATTACH PARTITION {name} FOR VALUES FROM ('{lo.isoformat()}') TO ('{hi.isoformat()}')")

        """Recompute hourly rollups from the raw ledger.

        or when the rollup table is empty, everything is recomputed.
        """
        sums = ", ".join(f"coalesce(sum({f}),0)" for f in SUM_FIELDS)
        cols = ", ".join(SUM_FIELDS)
        updates = ", ".join(f"{f}=EXCLUDED.{f}" for f in ["requests", "errors", "upgraded", *SUM_FIELDS])
        sql = f"""
            INSERT INTO usage_hourly (hour, user_id, team, served_model, backend, requests, errors, upgraded, {cols})
            SELECT date_trunc('hour', ts), coalesce(user_id,''), coalesce(team,''), coalesce(served_model,''), coalesce(backend,''),
                   count(*), count(*) FILTER (WHERE status >= 400), count(*) FILTER (WHERE upgraded), {sums}
            FROM requests WHERE ts >= $1
            GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5
            ON CONFLICT (hour, user_id, team, served_model, backend) DO UPDATE SET {updates}"""
        async with self.pool.acquire() as c:
            if full or not await c.fetchval("SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM usage_hourly)"):
                since = datetime(1970, 1, 1, tzinfo=UTC)
            else:
                since = (datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(hours=3)).replace(minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
            res = await c.execute(sql, since)
        return int(res.split()[-1]) if res else 0


def make_store(database_url: str | None):
    return PostgresStore(database_url) if database_url else MemoryStore()

"""Token usage, cost, and savings attribution.

Savings are split by cause and computed so they add up exactly:

    baseline_cost - actual_cost = routing + caching + self_hosting

* routing       = baseline model's cost - served model's cost, both without proxy-added caching
* caching       = served model without proxy-added caching - served model as actually billed
* self_hosting  = served model's API cost - our GPU chargeback (0 for API backends)

Caching the client set up itself would have happened without Merit Order, so it
is counted in every term alike and never shows up as savings.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass

from .config import Price


@dataclass
class Usage:
    input_tokens: int = 0  # uncached input
    cache_read_tokens: int = 0
    cache_write_tokens: int = 0
    output_tokens: int = 0
    web_search_requests: int = 0  # Anthropic server-side web searches, billed per search
    billed_usd: float | None = None  # what the backend says it charged, when it says (OpenRouter)

    @property
    def prompt_tokens(self) -> int:
        return self.input_tokens + self.cache_read_tokens + self.cache_write_tokens

    @property
    def total_tokens(self) -> int:
        return self.prompt_tokens + self.output_tokens

    def merge(self, other: "Usage") -> None:
        """Take the larger of each field (stream events repeat cumulative counts)."""
        self.input_tokens = max(self.input_tokens, other.input_tokens)
        self.cache_read_tokens = max(self.cache_read_tokens, other.cache_read_tokens)
        self.cache_write_tokens = max(self.cache_write_tokens, other.cache_write_tokens)
        self.output_tokens = max(self.output_tokens, other.output_tokens)
        self.web_search_requests = max(self.web_search_requests, other.web_search_requests)
        if other.billed_usd is not None:
            self.billed_usd = max(self.billed_usd or 0.0, other.billed_usd)


def _server_tools(price: Price, u: Usage) -> float:
    return u.web_search_requests * price.web_search_per_1k / 1000


def cost(price: Price, u: Usage) -> float:
    return (
        u.input_tokens * price.input
        + u.cache_read_tokens * price.read()
        + u.cache_write_tokens * price.write()
        + u.output_tokens * price.output
    ) / 1e6 + _server_tools(price, u)


def uncached_cost(price: Price, u: Usage) -> float:
    return (u.prompt_tokens * price.input + u.output_tokens * price.output) / 1e6 + _server_tools(price, u)


@dataclass
class Costs:
    actual: float
    served_api: float
    baseline: float
    list_price: float
    savings_routing: float
    savings_caching: float
    savings_self_hosting: float
    savings_compression: float = 0.0
    savings_response_cache: float = 0.0

    @property
    def savings_total(self) -> float:
        return (self.savings_routing + self.savings_caching + self.savings_self_hosting
                + self.savings_compression + self.savings_response_cache)

    def as_dict(self) -> dict:
        d = asdict(self)
        d["savings_total"] = self.savings_total
        return d


def chargeback(gpu_cost_per_hour: float, capacity_tokens_per_second: float, u: Usage) -> float:
    """Fair share of GPU time for this request's tokens."""
    if capacity_tokens_per_second <= 0:
        return 0.0
    seconds = u.total_tokens / capacity_tokens_per_second
    return gpu_cost_per_hour * seconds / 3600.0


def attribute(
    usage: Usage,
    served_price: Price,
    baseline_price: Price | None,
    proxy_cache: bool,
    self_hosted_cost: float | None = None,
    billed: float | None = None,
) -> Costs:
    """``billed``: what the backend reported charging. It replaces the catalog price of the served model,
    and the served model's counterfactuals are scaled by the same factor, so a provider that charged more
    or less than the catalog says doesn't show up as routing or caching savings."""
    served_api = cost(served_price, usage)
    served_no_proxy_cache = uncached_cost(served_price, usage) if proxy_cache else served_api
    list_price = uncached_cost(served_price, usage)
    if billed is not None and self_hosted_cost is None:
        if served_api > 0:
            scale = billed / served_api
            served_no_proxy_cache *= scale
            list_price *= scale
        else:
            served_no_proxy_cache = list_price = billed
        served_api = billed
    if baseline_price is None:
        baseline = served_no_proxy_cache
    elif proxy_cache:
        baseline = uncached_cost(baseline_price, usage)
    else:
        baseline = cost(baseline_price, usage)
    actual = self_hosted_cost if self_hosted_cost is not None else served_api
    return Costs(
        actual=actual,
        served_api=served_api,
        baseline=baseline,
        list_price=list_price,
        savings_routing=baseline - served_no_proxy_cache,
        savings_caching=served_no_proxy_cache - served_api,

# Path glob matcher and ignore rules

Write a Python module with two functions:

```python
def match(pattern: str, path: str) -> bool: ...
def ignored(rules: list[str], path: str) -> bool: ...
```

You may not import `re`, `fnmatch`, `glob` or `pathlib`; implement the matching yourself.

## Paths

A path is a non-empty string made of one or more non-empty **segments** separated by single `/` characters, with no
leading or trailing `/`. Every path passed to your functions is valid in this sense (you don't need to check). A
segment may contain any character except `/`, including spaces, `*`, `[`, `\`, `.` and non-ASCII characters.
Characters are compared exactly (case-sensitive, by code point).

## Pattern syntax

1. The pattern is split at **every** `/` character into segment patterns. A `/` can never be escaped and never
   appears inside a bracket expression (so `[a/b]` is the two segment patterns `[a` and `b]`). The pattern is
   **invalid** if any segment pattern is empty: the empty pattern, a leading or trailing `/`, or `//`.
2. A segment pattern that is exactly `**` is a **globstar**. Any other segment pattern is a sequence of elements,
   read left to right:
   - `\` followed by any character: a literal element matching exactly that character (`\*` matches `*`, `\a`
     matches `a`, `\\` matches `\`). A `\` that is the last character of a segment pattern makes the pattern invalid.
   - `*`: matches any sequence of characters, including the empty one.
   - `?`: matches exactly one character.
   - `[`: starts a bracket expression (rule 3).
   - any other character: a literal element matching exactly that character.

   So `**` that is not a whole segment pattern (`a**`, `**.py`, `x**y`) is simply two `*` elements.
3. **Bracket expressions.** After the `[`, an optional `!` makes the expression negated (`^` has no special meaning
   anywhere). Then items are read until the closing `]`:
   - Read a character c. If c is `\`, it is replaced by the next character, taken literally (so `\]`, `\-`, `\\` are
     items); a `\` with nothing after it in the segment pattern makes the pattern invalid. An unescaped `]` closes the
     expression, **except** when it is the very first character after `[` (after `[!` if negated): there it is a
     literal item.
   - After reading c, if the next character is `-` and there is a character after that `-` which is not `]`, this is
     a range: read d the same way as c (it may be escaped) and the item is every character whose code point is from
     `ord(c)` to `ord(d)` inclusive. If `ord(c) > ord(d)` the pattern is invalid. Otherwise c alone is the item (so a
     `-` that is first, or last before the `]`, is literal: `[-a]`, `[a-]`; `[a-c-e]` is `a`..`c`, `-`, `e`; and
     a literal first `]` can start a range too: `[]-a]` is the range `]`..`a`). Any other character inside the
     brackets, including `[`, `!` (when not first), `*` and `?`, is an ordinary item.
   - If the segment pattern ends before the closing `]`, the pattern is invalid. Consequently `[]` and `[!]` are
     invalid (the `]` is a literal item and nothing closes the expression), while `[]]` matches `]` and `[!]]`
     matches any character except `]`.

   A bracket expression matches exactly one character that is in the set of items (negated: not in the set).

## Matching

`match(pattern, path)` returns True when the path's segments can be matched, in order, by the pattern's segment
patterns, where:

- a non-globstar segment pattern matches exactly one path segment: its elements must match the whole segment;
- a globstar matches **zero or more** consecutive whole path segments.

So `**` matches every path (subject to the dot rule below); `a/**` matches `a` itself and everything under `a`;
`**/b` matches `b` and `x/y/b`; `a/**/b` matches `a/b` and `a/x/y/b`; `*` never matches across a `/`.

**Dot rule.** A path segment that starts with `.` can only be matched by a segment pattern whose first element is
a literal `.` (written `.` or `\.`). In particular: `*`, `?` and bracket expressions (negated or not, even `[.]`)
never match the `.` at the start of a segment; a `*` that matches the empty string does not let a following literal
`.` match a segment's leading dot (`*.py` does not match `.py`); and a globstar never matches a segment that starts
with `.`. A `.` anywhere else in a segment is an ordinary character (`*` matches `a.b.c`).

**Validation.** The whole pattern is checked before any matching. An invalid pattern raises `ValueError`, whatever
the path is, even if the path could be rejected without looking at the invalid part (`match("a/[", "b/c")` raises).

**Speed.** Matching must never take exponential time. Patterns have at most 64 characters and paths at most 300;
every call, including adversarial ones such as `*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*b` against a long run of `a`s or many
globstars against a deep path, must return in well under one second.

## Ignore rules

`ignored(rules, path)` decides whether `path` is ignored by a list of gitignore-like rules:

1. A rule that is the empty string or starts with `#` is skipped. (Any other rule is used, so `!#x` is a negated rule
   whose pattern is `#x`. To match a name that starts with `#` or `!`, escape it: `\#x`, `\!x`.)
2. If the rule starts with `!`, it is a **negation** rule; remove that one `!`.
3. If what remains starts with `/`, remove that one `/`; the rule is **anchored**.
4. What remains is the rule's pattern, which must be valid (rules above). If the pattern contains a `/`, the rule is
   also anchored. A rule that is not anchored is **unanchored**.
5. An anchored rule matches the path if its pattern matches the path itself or any of its ancestors (for `a/b/c`:
   `a`, `a/b`, `a/b/c`). An unanchored rule matches the path if its pattern matches any single segment of the path
   (for `a/b/c`: `a`, `b` or `c`).
6. The **last** rule that matches decides: a negation rule means not ignored (False), any other rule means ignored
   (True). If no rule matches, the result is False. Unlike git, a negation rule can re-include a path even when one
   of its parent directories is ignored.

Every rule that isn't skipped is validated: if any rule's pattern is invalid (including an empty pattern, as in the
rules `!`, `/` and `!/`), raise `ValueError`, even if that rule could not change the result.

## Examples

```python
match("*.py", "main.py")              # True
match("*.py", "src/main.py")          # False (* stays inside one segment)
match("src/**/*.py", "src/main.py")   # True  (** matches zero segments)
match("**/test_*.py", "a/b/test_x.py")  # True
match("*.py", ".py")                  # False (dot rule)
match(".*", ".bashrc")                # True
match("**/x", ".git/x")               # False (a globstar never matches .git)
match("[!a-c]x", "dx")                # True
match("[]a]", "]")                    # True
match("a[", "a[")                     # raises ValueError (unclosed bracket expression)
ignored(["*.log", "!keep.log"], "logs/keep.log")   # False (last matching rule is a negation)
ignored(["/build"], "src/build")      # False (anchored: only build and build/... at the top)
ignored(["build"], "src/build/x.o")   # True  (unanchored: the segment build matches)
```

Reply with exactly one ```python code block containing the complete module. Use only the Python 3.12 standard
library; the module must not print anything or do any work at import time.

# 09 — Decisions

What we decided, why, and what would make us revisit it. Newest decisions go at the bottom.

| # | Decision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Python for the core | Accepted |
| 2 | Our own backend adapters; no LiteLLM dependency | Accepted |
| 3 | No Envoy | Accepted |
| 4 | Docker Compose and Kubernetes both supported | Accepted |
| 5 | The harness owns the conversation; no content stored | Accepted |
| 6 | Route by marginal cost, including cache rebuild cost | Accepted |
| 7 | SkyPilot for GPUs, provisioning as a plugin | Accepted |
| 8 | Generic OIDC, Entra first | Accepted |
| 9 | Postgres and Redis are the only state | Accepted |
| 10 | Continuous batching only; async batch APIs out of scope | Accepted |
| 11 | AGPL-3.0-only license | Accepted |
| 12 | Reporting UI in React/TypeScript | Accepted |
| 13 | Opt-in response cache may store responses | Accepted |
| 14 | Open-weight catalog with prices from OpenRouter | Accepted |
| 15 | GPU scaling on addressable demand at API prices | Accepted |
| 16 | Deterministic, rule-based compression first | Accepted |
| 17 | Configuration versions in Postgres, YAML as the starting point | Accepted |
| 18 | Control panel in Mantine, monitoring first | Accepted |
| 19 | The IdP owns identity; Merit Order owns teams; user records decide team and role | Accepted |
| 20 | Quality scores are measured with graded tasks, not a judge model | Accepted |
| 21 | Every cost is visible next to the switch that controls it | Accepted |
| 22 | GPU prices come from SkyPilot's catalog; SkyPilot runs in its own environment | Accepted |
| 23 | A named model is never silently swapped; substitution is opt-in and never to a weaker model | Accepted |
| 24 | Refusals are retried on another model only for `auto` | Accepted |
| 25 | Every process follows the stored configuration | Accepted |
| 26 | No request queue in the gateway; a full GPU queues only as a last resort | Accepted |

**Still open:** reconciling computed costs with provider and cloud bills; Kubernetes-native GPU
provisioning (llm-d / KServe); a learned router; model-based compression; Parquet export;
provider batch APIs (decision 10).

## 1. Python for the core

**Why:** The team prefers it, the ML and inference ecosystem (SkyPilot, vLLM, classifiers,
compression) is Python, and gateway overhead is a few milliseconds against model latency measured
in seconds. We scale by running more gateway copies.

**Revisit if:** a real deployment hits gateway CPU limits that more replicas can't fix.

## 2. Our own backend adapters; no LiteLLM dependency

**Why:**
- LiteLLM converts everything to the OpenAI format internally. That's lossy for `cache_control`,
  thinking signatures, and other provider fields, and prompt caching is our biggest savings lever.
- It has had supply-chain incidents, a large dependency tree, and SSO in a commercially licensed
  directory.
- The rest of what it offers (keys, budgets, spend tracking, routing, UI) we'd replace anyway,
  because our ledger, router, and reporting work differently.
- Almost every backend speaks the Anthropic or OpenAI format, so pass-through plus one pair of
  translators covers them in a few thousand lines we fully control.

**What we still take:** LiteLLM's MIT-licensed pricing data, copied in with attribution, and its
code as a reference for provider quirks. Anyone needing a niche provider can run LiteLLM themselves
as an OpenAI-compatible backend.

**Revisit if:** keeping our adapters current with provider API changes becomes a significant
ongoing burden.

## 3. No Envoy

**Why:** Envoy AI Gateway is strong as a proxy layer, but all of our product logic (routing,
shaping, sessions, budgets, ledger) would still be Python, called by Envoy over gRPC on every
request. That adds a second system to operate and debug, assumes Kubernetes, narrows the
contributor pool, and solves a performance problem we don't have. Merit Order runs behind whatever
load balancer or ingress an organization already uses.

**Revisit if:** large deployments ask for it. The routing and shaping code could be packaged as an
Envoy external-processing service without being rewritten. Separately, an optional plugin could use
Kubernetes inference-routing tools (llm-d) inside a customer's own GPU cluster.

## 4. Docker Compose and Kubernetes both supported

**Why:** Compose gives the clone-and-run experience an open-source project needs; Kubernetes is
what enterprises at our target spend run in production. Same images, no Kubernetes-specific code in
the app. Details in [07 — Deployment](07-deployment.md).

## 5. The harness owns the conversation; no content stored

**Why:** Harnesses already resend history and compact it. Storing conversations would make the
proxy a retention, eDiscovery, and breach liability. The gateway stores routing metadata (hashes,
timestamps, backends) only. Compression stays cache-safe through a content-hash map, not stored
conversations.

**Revisit if:** we add the OpenAI Responses API's stored mode, which would be opt-in with explicit
retention.

## 6. Route by marginal cost, including cache rebuild cost

**Why:** A running GPU's spare capacity is already paid for, so it's nearly free, even for a better
model than the task needs. Moving a session re-pays for its whole context, so the router counts that
before moving. Details in [03 — Routing](03-routing.md).

## 7. SkyPilot for GPUs, provisioning as a plugin

**Why:** SkyPilot handles multi-cloud GPUs, spot instances, and replica scaling (SkyServe), and can
target Kubernetes clusters. Our controller decides *whether* to run a model; SkyPilot handles *how*.
A Kubernetes-native option (llm-d or KServe) can be another plugin later.

## 8. Generic OIDC, Entra first

**Why:** Entra is the first customer need; Google and others are configuration on the same code
path. Harnesses get short-lived virtual keys via a device-code login.

## 9. Postgres and Redis are the only state

**Why:** Both are available as managed services everywhere and are easy to run in Compose.
ClickHouse may become an optional reporting backend for very large deployments.

## 10. Continuous batching only; async batch APIs out of scope

**Why:** The product is for day-to-day interactive use. vLLM/SGLang batch concurrent requests on
their own. Provider batch APIs (about 50% off for work that can wait hours) may come later.

## 11. AGPL-3.0-only license

**Why:** Changes that others are offered over a network come back to the project.

## 12. Reporting UI in React/TypeScript

**Why:** Interactive filters and charts are much easier to build well, and the UI only talks to the
reports API, so it stays replaceable. The rest of the project remains Python.

**Alternative considered:** server-rendered pages with htmx (all-Python, clunkier interactivity).

## 13. Opt-in response cache may store responses

**Why:** Exact-match caching saves real money for chatbots, RAG, and evals. It can't work without
keeping the response, so it's the one exception to decision 5: off by default, enabled per team or
per request, scoped to a team or user, and expired by TTL (Redis).

## 14. Open-weight catalog with prices from OpenRouter

**Why:** There are dozens of useful open-weight models (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, MiniMax, MiMo,
Mistral, Gemma, Nemotron, Muse, gpt-oss) and their prices change often. `config/models-open.yaml`
lists them with their Hugging Face IDs (needed for self-hosting); `meritorder prices refresh` pulls
current prices and context windows from OpenRouter's public catalog into `prices.json`. A route with
no known price is never chosen by `auto`, so a missing price can't look free. OpenRouter is one
backend among many, not the system: it adds a fee, sends prompts through another company, and
doesn't count toward cloud commitments.

## 15. GPU scaling on addressable demand at API prices

**Why:** Counting only traffic already served by a model means a stopped model never looks worth
starting. The controller counts what all traffic the model *could* serve costs at API-equivalent
prices, excluding free upgrades. That number doesn't fall when GPUs take over the traffic, so it
doesn't flap. Two self-hosted models that address the same traffic are each credited with it; the
router then splits the traffic. Revisit if that over-provisions in practice.

## 16. Deterministic, rule-based compression first

**Why:** Compression must give identical output every turn or it breaks provider caching (and, on
recent Claude models, edited history can invalidate thinking). Rules (strip ANSI codes, collapse
repeated lines, keep head and tail of huge outputs) are deterministic, need no stored state, and add
no ML dependency. A model-based compressor (LLMLingua-2) can come later behind a content-hash cache.

## 17. Configuration versions in Postgres, YAML as the starting point

**Why:** Containers mount config read-only, and a fleet of gateways needs one source of truth. Saving
from the console validates the document, stores it as a new version (who, when, why), and every
gateway hot-reloads it within seconds; in-flight requests finish on the objects they started with.
Restore is one click. The YAML file is used until the first version is saved, and stays the format
for import, export, and GitOps. Secrets never enter the database: literal keys are refused and must
stay `${ENV}` references.

## 18. Control panel in Mantine, monitoring first

**Why:** Anyone running a company's LLM traffic through Merit Order will watch it far more than
they reconfigure it. The console opens on a live Dispatch view (the merit-order stack from real
traffic, a live request feed, backend health, the GPU fleet, and what needs attention), with
configuration one page among several. Mantine gives a complete admin component set with few
dependencies; charts stay hand-written SVG.

## 19. The IdP owns identity; Merit Order owns teams; user records decide team and role

**Why:** Enterprises expect Entra to be the source of truth for who exists and which groups they're
in, but budgets and model policy belong to Merit Order. People are created at first sign-in, their
team and role come from mapped groups, and admins can pin exceptions. Each request resolves team and
role from the user record (cached for a minute), not from the key, so moves and disables apply to
existing keys. SCIM provisioning (`/scim/v2`) applies Entra changes, including deprovisioning, as they happen.

## 20. Quality scores are measured with graded tasks; judges only where nothing else works

**Why:** Routing is only as good as its quality scores. Mechanical grading (exact answers, hidden
unit tests run in a sandbox, the end state of a scripted tool environment) is cheap, repeatable and
explainable, so it grades everything it can. Easy tasks can't tell the strongest models apart, so
the `frontier` suite adds hard work at levels 3–5. Open-ended work (summaries, critiques,
recommendations) can't be checked mechanically, so two judge models from different families grade
it against concrete rubric statements; both must agree, which offsets a judge's preference for its
own family. The eval suggests scores (with a finer 0–5 "ability" and a flag where evidence is thin);
an admin decides whether to apply them.

## 21. Every cost is visible next to the switch that controls it

**Why:** A gateway that starts cloud GPUs on its own has to be easy to overrule. The console shows
where each GPU runs, for how long, and what it has cost, with stop, pin, and stop-all controls that
take effect within seconds and are logged with who and why. Organization safeguards (org and GPU
budgets, fleet caps, a per-request ceiling) are hard limits that apply to admin pins too, so no
single action can exceed them. Limits are config (versioned, reviewable); stops and pins are
runtime controls (immediate, expiring), because an emergency shouldn't wait on a config review.

## 22. GPU prices come from SkyPilot's catalog; SkyPilot runs in its own environment

**Why:** A hand-typed `gpu_cost_per_hour` is wrong as soon as SkyPilot places a replica somewhere
else: 4×H100 spot ranges from about $4/h to over $20/h across clouds and regions. The controller
uses SkyPilot's catalog (the same prices its optimizer uses) for break-even decisions, and each
running replica's own cloud, region, instance, and spot price for burn rate, cost, and chargeback.
The configured price is the fallback, and the only price for your own hardware. These are list
prices; discounts, disks, and egress aren't included until bill reconciliation exists.

SkyPilot pulls in about 150 packages and, as a dependency, would have downgraded the gateway's
uvicorn. So it lives only in the controller's `-gpu` image, in a separate Python environment, and
Merit Order reaches it through the `sky` CLI and SkyPilot's own interpreter.

## 23. A named model is never silently swapped; substitution is opt-in and never to a weaker model

**Why:** Harnesses and apps that name a model depend on its behavior, especially with tools. When
a named model has nowhere to run (for example its GPUs were stopped), the default is a 503 that
explains why for each route and suggests `auto`. Teams that would rather keep working can turn on
`substitute_unavailable`: the request goes to a model at least as good for the task (never weaker),
and the response says which model was replaced. `auto` sessions always move to another model.

## 24. Refusals are retried on another model only for `auto`

**Why:** Safety classifiers sometimes refuse benign requests, and for `auto` the client has said any
suitable model is fine, so the next model gets a chance (the refused attempt is still billed and
logged). A client that named a model gets that model's answer, refusal included. Teams can turn the
retry off.

## 25. Every process follows the stored configuration

**Why:** Budgets and safeguards edited in the console must reach everything that enforces them.
Gateways, the worker (alerts), and the capacity controller (GPU budget, fleet caps) all load the
newest stored version and reload when it changes; the YAML file only applies until the first
version is saved. A version that fails to load is skipped and the last good one stays in effect.

## 26. No request queue in the gateway; a full GPU queues only as a last resort

**Why:** LLM calls are interactive and streaming, so a queue in Redis would add latency and a
second set of workers to pull from it, for no gain: vLLM already schedules and queues on the GPU.
A saturated GPU gets no new work while another route can take it, but when it's the only route,
sending the request there to wait beats a 503. The wait is bounded (`max_waiting` per replica) so
a backlog can't grow without limit. Gateways count in-flight requests and share the counts every
2 s, because the controller's one-minute metrics sample is too slow to catch a burst.

# 05 — GPU autoscaling Only open-weight models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Llama, …) can be self-hosted. Every self-hostable model should also have **at least one API route serving the same weights** (OpenRouter, the vendor, Bedrock, …). APIs are the floor; GPUs are an optimization. The console warns about models without one before anyone stops their GPUs. The full decision logic, with every rule and default, is in [10 — How it decides](10-how-it-decides.md#when-gpus-start-scale-and-stop). ## Lifecycle of a self-hosted model ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> APIOnly APIOnly --> Provisioning: demand pays for a replica for 10 min,
or pinned by an admin Provisioning --> Warm: replicas answer /v1/models Provisioning --> APIOnly: failed / timed out (30 min cooldown),
or stopped Warm --> Warm: add or remove replicas Warm --> Draining: below break-even 10 min (and warm 30 min),
or stopped with drain Warm --> APIOnly: stopped now Warm --> Provisioning: lost readiness (e.g. spot preemption) Draining --> Warm: demand returns (unless stopped) Draining --> APIOnly: after 15 min, GPUs released note right of APIOnly All traffic on API routes. Controller watches demand. end note note right of Provisioning 10–20+ min for big MoE models. Traffic stays on API meanwhile. end note note right of Draining No new sessions. Warm sessions finish there. end note ``` ## Controller loop (every 60 s) ```mermaid flowchart TD L["Read the ledger
last 1 h and last 15 min"] --> A["Addressable demand for this model:
traffic whose quality floor it meets,
valued at API prices, free upgrades excluded"] A --> R["Desired replicas =
enough for throughput,
but each must pay for itself"] R --> CT["Admin controls and safeguards
stop all · stop · pin · GPU budget · fleet caps"] CT --> SM{"State machine
api_only · provisioning · warm · draining"} SM -- "up / scale / down" --> P["Provisioner
SkyPilot (sky serve) or static"] SM --> PUB["Publish state, endpoint,
vLLM utilization → Redis"] PUB --> GW["Gateways pick it up
within 5 s"] ``` A self-hosted model therefore needs a quality score: one the live quality source doesn't cover counts no `auto` demand (only requests that name it) until it gets a `quality_override`. Why *addressable* demand: if the controller only counted traffic already sent to a model, a model that isn't running would never look worth starting, because `auto` routes its traffic elsewhere. So it counts what you currently pay for all traffic this model *could* serve (its quality meets the request's floor), at API-equivalent prices. That value doesn't drop when the GPUs start serving, so the controller doesn't flap. ## The break-even test ``` demand_per_hour = addressable API-equivalent spend per hour (max of the 1 h and 4 × 15 min windows) throughput = addressable tokens per second (same windows) by_load = ceil(throughput / (capacity_tokens_per_second × target_utilization)) affordable = floor(demand_per_hour / (replica_price × (1 + margin))) replica_price = cheapest SkyPilot catalog offer in the allowed clouds/regions, else gpu_cost_per_hour desired_replicas = clamp(min(by_load ≥ 1, affordable), min_replicas, max_replicas) ``` Defaults, per deployment under `serve:`: `margin` 0.2 (demand must pay 1.2 × the replica price), `target_utilization` 0.7, `scale_up_after_minutes` 10, `hold_minutes` 30, `drain_minutes` 15, `provision_timeout_minutes` 45. State machine (`src/meritorder/gpu.py`, pure and unit-tested): | From | To | When | |---|---|---| | api_only | provisioning | `desired ≥ 1` continuously for `scale_up_after_minutes` (or `min_replicas > 0`) | | provisioning | warm | replicas answer `/v1/models` | | provisioning | api_only | failed or `provision_timeout_minutes` passed; 30-minute cooldown | | warm | warm | replica count follows `desired` | | warm | draining | `desired = 0` for `scale_up_after_minutes`, and warm for at least `hold_minutes` | | warm | provisioning | replicas stop answering (e.g. spot preemption); traffic goes to APIs until they're back | | draining | warm | demand returns | | draining | api_only | after `drain_minutes`; GPUs released | | any | api_only / draining | an admin stops it, Stop all GPUs, or the GPU budget runs out (see [Controls](#controls-and-safeguards)) | | api_only | provisioning | an admin pins replicas: at once, skipping the wait and any cooldown | Key details: - **Free upgrades don't count.** Traffic running above its floor because a GPU had headroom is excluded, so idle capacity can't keep itself alive by attracting traffic. - **Measured capacity, not benchmarks.** `capacity_tokens_per_second` should be what one replica sustains at your latency target on real agent traffic (prefill-heavy). - **Hysteresis everywhere.** Margins, minimum hold time, and the scale-up delay stop flapping. A 20-minute cold start is expensive to waste. - **Spot where it's safe.** SkyServe handles spot preemption; overflow to the API covers the gap. ## Will a GPU ever pay? (Models → GPU break-even) Before configuring a deployment, the console's **GPU break-even** tab (Models page; also `GET /v1/reports/gpu/breakeven`, team leads and up) shows how much traffic one replica needs to pay for itself by the rule above, next to your traffic. Every open-weight model gets a replica **sized to it** and **priced from SkyPilot's catalog**: - **Size.** The model's weights in bytes, at the precision they're published in, come from Hugging Face. For a mixture-of-experts model, the parameters each token uses come from its name ("A3B") or are worked out from its config's layer sizes (gpt-oss-120b: 5.1B; Qwen3 Coder Next: 2.9B). Gated models without public metadata are sized from their name where it says, at 16 bits, or not at all. - **Machine.** The cheapest machine per hour whose GPUs hold the weights in 70% of their memory (the rest is the KV cache), on 1, 2, 4 or 8 GPUs (how vLLM splits a model), among the datacenter GPUs from L4 to B300 and MI300X. A model that needs more than one machine says so. *Serve 16-bit weights in FP8* halves those weights, as vLLM's `--quantization fp8` does. - **Price.** SkyPilot's catalog, through SkyPilot itself: on-demand or **spot** prices (a switch on the tab) for every cloud it covers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Lambda, RunPod and Nebius by default, plus your deployments' clouds; the tab can narrow them), with the region and instance. Prices are fetched when a report finds them over 6 hours old; **Get latest prices** has SkyPilot download its catalogs again now. Lookups never use cloud credentials: prices don't need them. - **Throughput** is an estimate: a share of the GPUs' peak dense compute (10% by default, adjustable) at two operations per active parameter per token, with input read from the prompt cache not computed again. A deployment's `capacity_tokens_per_second` (measure it) replaces the estimate, and its own GPUs, clouds and spot setting replace the sizing (a server you run uses its configured price). What the tab shows: - **By quality level.** A replica takes traffic that `auto` would otherwise send to the cheapest API model good enough for its level, so that model's price is the one to beat. For each level: that model and its price; the open model that qualifies and serves that work cheapest per token, on its replica; the tokens per minute (and about how many requests an hour) that replica needs; and your average and busiest hour at that level. A level where no open model qualifies, or none fits on one machine, says so. - **By open-weight model.** Its size and replica, what the traffic it could serve actually cost per million tokens over the window (the controller's own measure), its own API price, what it needs, and a verdict: pays now, pays from a given traffic, or never. - **Never** means one replica can't get there at any traffic: at full load (its target utilization) the GPU costs more per token than the API, so more replicas wouldn't help either. On 11 November 2026, with spot prices, gpt-oss-20b on one A100-80GB ($0.40 an hour on Azure) was the only way to pay for level-1 work, from about 235,000 tokens a minute; at level 2 the cheapest option (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on eight H200s) cost $0.12 per million tokens against $0.06 on APIs, and above level 2 no open model scored high enough. Prices are blended for the traffic's mix of input, cached input, cache writes and output (a level or model with at least 20 requests uses its own, otherwise everyone's; with no traffic, an assumed agent-like mix). Free tiers don't count as the price to beat: they're rate-limited and can't take sustained traffic. **Where SkyPilot runs.** The gateway asks SkyPilot directly when it has it: the compose stack builds every service with SkyPilot in its own environment (`SKYPILOT_VERSION`, empty to leave it out), and for `meritorder` run on a laptop, `uv tool install "skypilot[aws,gcp,kubernetes]==0.14.2"` puts it on the path. Otherwise (the Helm chart keeps SkyPilot in the controller only) the GPU controller publishes the prices every 6 hours and when someone asks for the latest, and the tab says if no controller is running. ## Configuring a self-hosted model ```yaml backends: gpu-qwen-coder: kind: self_hosted format: openai gpu_cost_per_hour: 16.0 # one replica (here 4× H100) capacity_tokens_per_second: 4000 serve: provisioner: skypilot # or `static` for a server you already run model: qwen3-coder-next # its hf_id is what vLLM serves accelerators: "H100:4" use_spot: true clouds: [aws, gcp, lambda] image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.11.0 vllm_args: "--max-model-len 262144" max_replicas: 4 ``` The model also needs a route to the deployment with a `price:` at the API-equivalent rate: `auto` skips unpriced routes, and the router scales that price down while the GPUs have room ([Overflow](#overflow)). Keep the API route for the same weights next to it: ```yaml models: qwen3-coder-next: hf_id: Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next routes: - {backend: gpu-qwen-coder, model: Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next, price: {input: 0.12, output: 0.80, cache_read: 0.07}} - {backend: openrouter, model: qwen/qwen3-coder-next} ``` The SkyPilot provisioner writes a SkyServe service (vLLM with `--enable-prefix-caching` and `--scheduling-policy priority`, fixed replica count, readiness probe on `/v1/models`) and drives `sky serve up / update / down`. It needs the `sky` CLI and cloud credentials (`sky check`). Set `HF_TOKEN` for gated models. ## Controls and safeguards The console's **GPUs** page shows, for every deployment: where each replica runs (cloud, region, zone, instance, spot or on-demand, from SkyPilot), how long it has been up, its burn rate, what this run and this month have cost, what demand would pay for it at API prices, and why the controller is doing what it's doing. An activity log records every state change, scale, and admin action with who did it. Admins can override the controller: | Control | Effect | |---|---| | **Stop** (drain first) | No new sessions; warm ones finish for up to `drain_minutes`, then the replicas go down. Skips the usual hold time | | **Stop now** | Replicas go down at once; their sessions continue on APIs (caches rebuild there) | | **Pin N replicas** | Runs N (up to `max_replicas`) regardless of demand, skipping the scale-up wait and any failure cooldown | | **Back to automatic** | Demand decides again | | **Stop all GPUs** | Every deployment stops and none start until someone resumes the fleet | Stops and pins can expire after a set number of hours and can carry a reason, which the activity log and the alert show. Gateways stop routing to a stopped deployment within seconds, before the controller acts; the controller wakes up as soon as a control changes. For a static server, Merit Order can only stop sending it traffic. Organization safeguards apply on top, to pins as well ([06](06-auth-and-spend.md#organization-wide-safeguards)): a monthly GPU budget, a fleet burn-rate cap, and a replica cap. ### What GPUs cost Prices come from **SkyPilot's catalog**, the same list prices its optimizer uses to pick a cloud: - **Before launching**, the break-even test uses the cheapest catalog offer for the deployment's accelerators within its allowed clouds and regions (spot or on-demand, per `use_spot`). - **While running**, each replica is priced for its actual cloud, region, instance type, and spot/on-demand, so a replica that lands in a pricier region costs what it really costs. - `gpu_cost_per_hour` is only a fallback, used for static servers (your own hardware) and when SkyPilot isn't installed where the controller runs. Cost is accrued every cycle from the moment provisioning starts until the replicas are down, and stored per hour (`gpu_usage`). Self-hosted tokens are charged back at the same live price. These are **list prices**, not your bill: they don't include negotiated discounts, reservations, or credits, and they leave out disks, egress, and the SkyServe controller VM. Spot prices in the catalog are refreshed periodically, not live. Reconciling against the cloud bill is on the roadmap. SkyPilot runs in its own Python environment (the `-gpu` image, built with `--build-arg SKYPILOT=`), so its dependencies never mix with the gateway's. Merit Order calls it through the `sky` CLI and, for prices, SkyPilot's Python (`MERITORDER_SKY_PYTHON`, found from the `sky` command when unset). If the controller stops running while GPUs are up, the console flags it: nothing would scale them down. If a stop fails at the cloud, the deployment stays marked as running and the controller keeps retrying, so a GPU that may still be billing is never shown as off. ## Overflow ```mermaid flowchart LR REQ["New session for qwen3-coder"] --> H{"Self-hosted pool
has headroom?"} H -- "yes" --> SELF["Self-hosted deployment
(SkyServe picks the replica)"] H -- "no" --> API{"Another route?
e.g. Bedrock / Together"} API -- "yes" --> SPILL["Same model via API"] API -- "no" --> Q["Waits in vLLM's queue,
up to max_waiting per replica;
then 503"] SPILL -.-> SIG["Controller sees the demand:
adds replicas"] ``` Up to 60% load (`routing.shadow_knee`), a self-hosted token is priced at 2% of its route's price (`routing.shadow_floor`). Above that the shadow price rises toward the full price, so new sessions drift to APIs before the GPU is full. At 100%, nothing new goes there while any other route can take it; sessions already there move too. A saturated GPU that's a model's only route still takes requests, which wait in vLLM, until `max_waiting` (default 32) per replica are waiting. Set `max_concurrency` so gateways see saturation within seconds instead of at the controller's next sample. Details: [When a GPU is full](10-how-it-decides.md#when-a-gpu-is-full). ## Inside the GPU pool - **Continuous batching** is the engine's job (vLLM / SGLang). The gateway sends concurrently and never serializes requests per replica. - **Replica choice** is SkyServe's: its load balancer picks the replica for each request. Sending a session back to the replica that holds its KV cache is not built yet. - **Priority scheduling**: free-upgrade requests go to vLLM with `priority: 10` (lower runs first), so traffic at its own floor goes ahead of them. - **Engine knobs** go in `vllm_args` (e.g. `--max-num-seqs`, `--max-num-batched-tokens`, chunked prefill, speculative decoding). Prefix caching and priority scheduling are always on.

# 03 — Routing The router answers: **which model, on which backend, for this request?** It optimizes **marginal cost** — what this request adds to the bill *right now* — subject to a quality floor and team policy. ## Decision flow ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Request arrives"] --> B{"Harness pinned
a model?"} B -- "yes" --> FIX["Model is fixed
(only the backend can vary)"] B -- "no, model=auto" --> C{"Existing session,
mid-task, cache warm?"} C -- "yes" --> KEEP["Keep session's model"] C -- "no" --> D["Classifier → quality floor
e.g. coding:3"] D --> E["Candidates = models allowed for team
with quality ≥ floor"] FIX --> S KEEP --> S E --> S["Score every backend of every candidate
cost = rebuild + turns × per-turn"] S --> T{"Cheapest beats current
by more than hysteresis margin?"} T -- "yes" --> MOVE["Route to cheapest
(ties → higher quality)"] T -- "no" --> STAY["Stay on current backend"] MOVE --> PRI{"Running above floor
only because it's free?"} STAY --> PRI PRI -- "yes" --> LOW["Send with low priority
(paid traffic preempts it)"] PRI -- "no" --> NORM["Send with normal priority"] ``` ## The cost function For each candidate backend `b`, over the session's expected remaining turns: ``` cost(b) = rebuild(b) + expected_remaining_turns × per_turn(b) ``` **Per-turn cost by backend type** | Backend state | `per_turn(b)` | |---|---| | API | uncached tokens × input price + cached tokens × cache-read price + output × output price | | Self-hosted, plenty of headroom | ≈ 0 (shadow price near zero) | | Self-hosted, filling up | shadow price rises toward the same model's API price | | Self-hosted, at latency target | unavailable (or priced as the API version of the same model) | **Rebuild cost** | Situation | `rebuild(b)` | |---|---| | `b` already holds a warm cache for this session | 0 | | API, cold | prefix tokens × (cache-write price − cache-read price) | | Self-hosted, cold | prefix tokens × shadow price + latency penalty for the prefill | Illustrative (check real prices): a 120k-token Claude session costs ~$0.04/turn in cache reads to stay. Moving it to another Claude backend costs ~$0.45 to rewrite the cache. A move has to save more than ~$0.41 over the rest of the session to be worth it. ## Shadow price Self-hosted tokens aren't literally free — capacity is finite. The shadow price makes spare capacity attractive while protecting latency: ![Shadow price vs replica utilization](img/shadow-price.svg) ## Free upgrades (and why they're safe) If a strong open model is running with headroom and the task only needs a medium model, the user gets the strong model at ~zero cost. Three guardrails keep this from backfiring: 1. **Low priority.** Opportunistic requests use vLLM priority scheduling, so traffic that *needs* that model always goes first. 2. **Doesn't keep GPUs alive.** The controller values upgraded traffic at its *floor* model's API price, so free traffic can't make a GPU look worth keeping. (See [05](05-gpu-autoscaling.md).) 3. **Only at boundaries.** Upgrades/downgrades happen at session start or task boundaries — never mid-task — so tool-calling behavior and caches stay stable. ## Free moments to re-route Moving costs nothing when the session's cache is already gone: - Session idle longer than the cache TTL. - The harness compacted history (prefix hash no longer matches). - The replica evicted the session's KV cache (from vLLM / llm-d KV events). - A natural task boundary. ## When a model refuses Some models decline requests through safety classifiers (Claude returns HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"`; OpenAI-style APIs use `finish_reason: "content_filter"`). For `auto` requests, Merit Order retries on the next eligible model: - Streams are buffered only until the first content arrives, so a refusal before any content is retried invisibly; one that arrives after content has started streams through. - The refused attempt is recorded in the ledger (it cost tokens), and the response carries `x-meritorder-refused-by`. - A model the client named is never substituted. Teams can turn this off (`refusal_fallback: false`). ## Measuring quality scores The 1–5 quality scores in `config/` start as informed guesses. `meritorder eval` measures them: it sends a suite of mechanically graded tasks (no model-as-judge) through the gateway to each model, and suggests a score per task type: the highest level L such that the model passes at least 75% of tasks at every level up to L. ```bash uv run meritorder eval --models claude-haiku-5-5,qwen3-coder,glm-5.3-flash # estimates cost, asks first uv run meritorder eval --models ... --apply # also write scores as a new config version ``` The starter suite (`src/meritorder/evals/starter.yaml`) covers coding and general tasks at every level; use `--suite` for your own. Results show on the console's Models page next to the configured scores, flagged where they differ. Eval traffic is tagged `eval=` in the ledger, so its cost shows up in reports. ## Harness overrides | Harness sends | Behavior | |---|---| | `model: "claude-sonnet-4-5"` (explicit) | No model substitution. Router picks the cheapest *backend* for that model. | | `model: "auto"` | Classifier + router choose. | | `model: "auto"` + `X-Route-Floor: coding:3` | Harness sets the floor; router chooses above it. | | `X-Route-Hint: cheap` / `smart` | Nudges the classifier's floor down / up. | Team policy (allowed models, allowed providers, data-residency rules) is applied **before** scoring, so an override can never escape policy.
