# Changelog

## 0.1.0 (unreleased)

First release.

**Gateway**
- OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses, Anthropic Messages, and embeddings; pass-through or
  translation between the formats, streaming included.
- Backends: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI,
  OpenRouter, direct open-model vendors (DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, Mistral), and any
  OpenAI-compatible server. Keyless on Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure with workload identity.
- Works unchanged with pi, Claude Code, and the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs (`meritorder setup`).

**Routing**
- Rule-based classifier sets a quality floor; a marginal-cost router picks the backend, counting the
  cost of rebuilding a session's prompt cache before moving it.
- GPUs priced by how busy they are (near free with headroom), so spare GPU capacity is used first.
- Routes that cost about the same go to the faster one, measured from real replies (time to first
  token and tokens per second). The `balanced` and `speed` priorities pay up to 20% or 100% more for
  a faster route, set per organization, team, or request (`X-MeritOrder-Priority`).
- Failover catches errors that arrive after a `200` (Anthropic's in-stream overload, OpenRouter error
  chunks) and streams that never start. Over capacity skips just that model on that backend, for the
  provider's `Retry-After`. Outage and recovery alerts go to the webhook, and responses say what they
  failed over from.
- Evals that separate the strongest models: a `frontier` suite of hard tasks (code checked by hidden
  tests in a Docker sandbox, multi-step tool use against scripted environments, long documents,
  exact-answer reasoning, and open-ended work graded by two judges from different model families).
  Scores come with a finer 0–5 ability figure and a flag where evidence is thin. Run them from the
  console's new Models → Evals page (estimate, progress, cancel, per-task results, apply scores as a
  config version) or with `meritorder eval`; both land in the same history.
- Outage alerts name the model's other live backends ("Requests go to anthropic, openrouter meanwhile"), even when the
  failing request was pinned to one backend. A model missing on a backend (404) is retried after 5 minutes, then
  less and less often up to hourly. Bedrock and Foundry can be switched off in `.env` until their models exist.
- Evals compare like with like: no output limit (each model may write as much as it can), every
  model at the same reasoning effort for a level, each on its own provider's API, and every answer,
  agent tool call and judge's reason kept for review. A reply cut off by the model's maximum fails
  and says so; one cut off by the per-request cost limit isn't graded. Runs also report what the
  work took: each model's median and 90th-percentile time to complete a task, turns and tool calls,
  output tokens, and cost per task solved. Agent tasks reach Claude over Anthropic's Messages API, as
  Claude Code does, so its thinking carries between tool calls (Chat Completions dropped it).
  A Tasks view lists every built-in task with how it's graded; each opens to its full prompt and tools,
  its checks, hidden tests, reference solution, environment data or rubric, and each model's latest result.
  Open-ended tasks are judged by Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon, one per family at the
  same tier (GPT-6.1 Terra, a tier below Opus, was one before), at high effort; each answer by the two
  from families other than its model's.
- No arbitrary output limits: a request without `max_tokens` may write as much as its model can
  (`max_output_tokens`, from the price catalog), less what won't fit in the context window or under
  the per-request cost limit, which now trims such a reply instead of using a 16,000-token guess.
  Non-streaming requests that may run long are streamed from the provider and assembled, so they
  don't time out. `auto` sends high reasoning effort for level 4–5 work (Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5
  default to medium).
- Refusal fallback and automatic reasoning effort for `auto`; opt-in substitution for named
  models that have nowhere to run (never to a weaker model).
- A saturated GPU spills to other routes, and queues (bounded) only when it's the last resort.

**GPUs**
- Capacity controller starts and stops SkyPilot/SkyServe + vLLM deployments when demand pays for
  them, with SkyPilot catalog prices, hysteresis, and fleet-wide caps.
- Console controls: stop (drain or now), pin replicas, stop all; activity log; where each replica
  runs, uptime, burn rate, and cost.

**Models (as of November 10, 2026)**
- Claude Fable 5.2 ($8/$40), Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5; GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra and
  GPT-6 Luna (the `gpt-terra` and `gpt-luna` names now point at the current models, and `gpt-5.6-*` names
  still resolve to them). Sonnet 5.5's cache reads are priced at $0.10 per million tokens (they were $0.20).
- Gemini 4 Carbon and 4 Argon ($2/$10 until November 30, 2026, then $4/$20), Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.5
  Flash-Lite, through OpenRouter. They have no quality scores until an eval measures them, so `auto`
  doesn't pick them yet; requests that name them work. Gemini's reasoning details (which its tool calls
  need sent back) survive replies the gateway assembles from a stream.

**Spend and savings**
- Prices are live: the worker refreshes them every 15 minutes from OpenRouter's catalog and, for direct
  provider APIs, the price list LiteLLM maintains, and gateways reload when one changes. Long-prompt
  prices apply (Claude Haiku 5.5 costs 5× above 100K prompt tokens, GPT-6.x 1.5-2× above 272K), in
  costing and in routing. Changes, a list that can't be fetched, and a provider's list price that
  disagrees with OpenRouter's raise alerts; the Models page shows each price's source and when it was
  last checked. Prices typed into the config are now only overrides.
- Budgets per organization, GPU fleet, team, person, and session; rate limits; per-request cost cap.
  Each person can have their own monthly limit (People page, admin API, or their static key) that
  replaces their team's per-person default.
  The shipped config reads the organization-wide caps from `.env` (`MERITORDER_ORG_BUDGET_USD` and
  friends), and `.env` comments at the end of a line are read the way Docker Compose reads them.
- Savings ledger by cause (routing, caching, self-hosting, compression, response cache) against a
  per-team baseline.
- GPT-5.6 tool calls through OpenAI work: its Chat Completions endpoint rejects function tools with
  reasoning, so the OpenAI backend sends requests to the Responses API (`api: responses`) and converts
  the replies back. Agents like Claude Code and pi can use GPT models with reasoning on.
- Claude through OpenRouter is prompt-cached (it wasn't: every turn paid full price), and the router
  prices cache writes on every route, so it no longer prefers a route only because it skipped the write.
- OpenRouter requests record what OpenRouter billed, not a catalog estimate: it picks among providers
  whose prices differ (catalog prices were up to 56% low in testing). `billed_cost` sets this per backend.
- Every setting on the console's Config page explains itself: a "?" beside each field (hover, keyboard
  focus, or tap) says what it does and its default. The forms also cover the OpenAI endpoint, the
  first-token timeout, cost-or-speed priority, static-key monthly limits, and GPU launch rules.
- Reports API and console, CSV/JSONL export (to S3), alerts and weekly digests to a webhook,
  Prometheus metrics with a Grafana dashboard, OpenTelemetry traces.

**Identity**
- Entra/OIDC sign-in exchanged for short-lived keys, groups mapped to teams and roles, SCIM
  provisioning; roles for users, team leads, finance, and admins.

**Operations**
- Docker Compose and a Helm chart (External Secrets, Reloader, zero-restart key rotation, workload
  identity). Configuration versions in Postgres, edited in the console, followed by every process.
- Signed multi-arch images with an SBOM and provenance.

**Known limitations**
- Exercised against OpenRouter only (smoke tests, a Claude Code session, costs matched to its bill); not
  yet against other live provider accounts, a real cloud GPU, a real Entra tenant, or a
  production Kubernetes cluster: see `docs/README.md` for what's verified and how.
- Not built: reconciliation against provider bills, the native Gemini API, Kubernetes-native GPU
  provisioning, a learned router, provider batch APIs, model-based compression, Parquet export.

# 09 — Decisions

What we decided, why, and what would make us revisit it. Newest decisions go at the bottom.

| # | Decision | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Python for the core | Accepted |
| 2 | Our own backend adapters; no LiteLLM dependency | Accepted |
| 3 | No Envoy | Accepted |
| 4 | Docker Compose and Kubernetes both supported | Accepted |
| 5 | The harness owns the conversation; no content stored | Accepted |
| 6 | Route by marginal cost, including cache rebuild cost | Accepted |
| 7 | SkyPilot for GPUs, provisioning as a plugin | Accepted |
| 8 | Generic OIDC, Entra first | Accepted |
| 9 | Postgres and Redis are the only state | Accepted |
| 10 | Continuous batching only; async batch APIs out of scope | Accepted |
| 11 | AGPL-3.0-only license | Accepted |
| 12 | Reporting UI in React/TypeScript | Accepted |
| 13 | Opt-in response cache may store responses | Accepted |
| 14 | Open-weight catalog with prices from OpenRouter | Accepted |
| 15 | GPU scaling on addressable demand at API prices | Accepted |
| 16 | Deterministic, rule-based compression first | Accepted |

## 1. Python for the core

**Why:** The team prefers it, the ML and inference ecosystem (SkyPilot, vLLM, classifiers,
compression) is Python, and gateway overhead is a few milliseconds against model latency measured
in seconds. We scale by running more gateway copies.

**Revisit if:** a real deployment hits gateway CPU limits that more replicas can't fix.

## 2. Our own backend adapters; no LiteLLM dependency

**Why:**
- LiteLLM converts everything to the OpenAI format internally. That's lossy for `cache_control`,
  thinking signatures, and other provider fields, and prompt caching is our biggest savings lever.
- It has had supply-chain incidents, a large dependency tree, and SSO in a commercially licensed
  directory.
- The rest of what it offers (keys, budgets, spend tracking, routing, UI) we'd replace anyway,
  because our ledger, router, and reporting work differently.
- Almost every backend speaks the Anthropic or OpenAI format, so pass-through plus one pair of
  translators covers them in a few thousand lines we fully control.

**What we still take:** LiteLLM's MIT-licensed pricing data, copied in with attribution, and its
code as a reference for provider quirks. Anyone needing a niche provider can run LiteLLM themselves
as an OpenAI-compatible backend.

**Revisit if:** keeping our adapters current with provider API changes becomes a significant
ongoing burden.

## 3. No Envoy

**Why:** Envoy AI Gateway is strong as a proxy layer, but all of our product logic (routing,
shaping, sessions, budgets, ledger) would still be Python, called by Envoy over gRPC on every
request. That adds a second system to operate and debug, assumes Kubernetes, narrows the
contributor pool, and solves a performance problem we don't have. Merit Order runs behind whatever
load balancer or ingress an organization already uses.

**Revisit if:** large deployments ask for it. The routing and shaping code could be packaged as an
Envoy external-processing service without being rewritten. Separately, an optional plugin could use
Kubernetes inference-routing tools (llm-d) inside a customer's own GPU cluster.

## 4. Docker Compose and Kubernetes both supported

**Why:** Compose gives the clone-and-run experience an open-source project needs; Kubernetes is
what enterprises at our target spend run in production. Same images, no Kubernetes-specific code in
the app. Details in [07 — Deployment](07-deployment.md).

## 5. The harness owns the conversation; no content stored

**Why:** Harnesses already resend history and compact it. Storing conversations would make the
proxy a retention, eDiscovery, and breach liability. The gateway stores routing metadata (hashes,
timestamps, backends) only. Compression stays cache-safe through a content-hash map, not stored
conversations.

**Revisit if:** we add the OpenAI Responses API's stored mode, which would be opt-in with explicit
retention.

## 6. Route by marginal cost, including cache rebuild cost

**Why:** A running GPU's spare capacity is already paid for, so it's nearly free, even for a better
model than the task needs. Moving a session re-pays for its whole context, so the router counts that
before moving. Details in [03 — Routing](03-routing.md).

## 7. SkyPilot for GPUs, provisioning as a plugin

**Why:** SkyPilot handles multi-cloud GPUs, spot instances, and replica scaling (SkyServe), and can
target Kubernetes clusters. Our controller decides *whether* to run a model; SkyPilot handles *how*.
A Kubernetes-native option (llm-d or KServe) can be another plugin later.

## 8. Generic OIDC, Entra first

**Why:** Entra is the first customer need; Google and others are configuration on the same code
path. Harnesses get short-lived virtual keys via a device-code login.

## 9. Postgres and Redis are the only state

**Why:** Both are available as managed services everywhere and are easy to run in Compose.
ClickHouse may become an optional reporting backend for very large deployments.

## 10. Continuous batching only; async batch APIs out of scope

**Why:** The product is for day-to-day interactive use. vLLM/SGLang batch concurrent requests on
their own. Provider batch APIs (about 50% off for work that can wait hours) may come later.

## 11. AGPL-3.0-only license

**Why:** Changes that others are offered over a network come back to the project.

## 12. Reporting UI in React/TypeScript

**Why:** Interactive filters and charts are much easier to build well, and the UI only talks to the
reports API, so it stays replaceable. The rest of the project remains Python.

**Alternative considered:** server-rendered pages with htmx (all-Python, clunkier interactivity).

## 13. Opt-in response cache may store responses

**Why:** Exact-match caching saves real money for chatbots, RAG, and evals. It can't work without
keeping the response, so it's the one exception to decision 5: off by default, enabled per team or
per request, scoped to a team or user, and expired by TTL (Redis).

## 14. Open-weight catalog with prices from OpenRouter

**Why:** There are dozens of useful open-weight models (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, MiniMax, MiMo,
Mistral, Gemma, Nemotron, Muse, gpt-oss) and their prices change often. `config/models-open.yaml`
lists them with their Hugging Face IDs (needed for self-hosting); `meritorder prices refresh` pulls
current prices and context windows from OpenRouter's public catalog into `prices.json`. A route with
no known price is never chosen by `auto`, so a missing price can't look free. OpenRouter is one
backend among many, not the system: it adds a fee, sends prompts through another company, and
doesn't count toward cloud commitments.

## 15. GPU scaling on addressable demand at API prices

**Why:** Counting only traffic already served by a model means a stopped model never looks worth
starting. The controller counts what all traffic the model *could* serve costs at API-equivalent
prices, excluding free upgrades. That number doesn't fall when GPUs take over the traffic, so it
doesn't flap. Two self-hosted models that address the same traffic are each credited with it; the
router then splits the traffic. Revisit if that over-provisions in practice.

## 16. Deterministic, rule-based compression first

**Why:** Compression must give identical output every turn or it breaks provider caching (and, on
recent Claude models, edited history can invalidate thinking). Rules (strip ANSI codes, collapse
repeated lines, keep head and tail of huge outputs) are deterministic, need no stored state, and add
no ML dependency. A model-based compressor (LLMLingua-2) can come later behind a content-hash cache.

# 08 — Reporting Merit Order exists to save money, so reporting is a core feature: what was spent, what was saved, why, by whom, and when. ## Data flow ```mermaid flowchart LR gw["Gateway"] -- "one row per request (async)" --> ledger[("Ledger
Postgres, monthly partitions")] ctl["Capacity controller"] -- "GPU cost per hour,
activity log" --> gpu[("gpu_usage, gpu_events")] ledger --> roll["Worker"] roll --> agg[("Hourly rollups
by user, team,
model, backend")] roll --> alerts["Alerts and weekly digests
webhook + console"] ctl --> alerts agg --> api["Reports API"] ledger --> api gpu --> api api --> ui["Web UI"] api --> cli["meritorder usage / export"] api --> exp["CSV / JSONL exports"] bills["Provider billing exports
AWS, GCP, Azure"] -. "not built yet" .-> recon["Monthly reconciliation"] gw -. "Prometheus / OpenTelemetry" .-> mon["Grafana, Datadog, ..."] ``` Reports never contain prompt or response content. The ledger holds metadata only. ## Savings numbers have to stand up to scrutiny If finance finds one inflated number, they stop trusting the whole dashboard. So: **1. A baseline per team.** "What you'd have done without Merit Order", set in config: ```yaml baseline_model: claude-sonnet # everyone's default: API price, no proxy-added caching teams: platform: baseline_model: claude-opus # a team that would have used Opus ``` **2. Savings broken down by cause, never one blended number.** Causes are computed in a fixed order, each against the result of the previous step, so they add up exactly to the total with no double counting: | Order | Cause | How it's counted | |---|---|---| | 1 | **Routing** | Baseline model's API cost − served model's API cost, both without caching we added | | 2 | **Prompt caching** | Discount from cache breakpoints *we added*, minus cache-write premiums we paid. Caching the harness set up itself would have happened anyway and isn't counted. | | 3 | **Self-hosting** | Served model's API cost − chargeback cost on our GPUs | | 4 | **Compression** | Tokens removed × served model's price: new tokens at the input price, older history at the cache-read price | | 5 | **Response cache** | What the request cost the first time, for each one answered from the response cache | **3. List price on every row.** The console's headline is savings caused by Merit Order. Each ledger row also records `list_cost` (the served model at list price, no caching), so savings against list price can be worked out from the API or an export; the console doesn't show it yet. **4. Negotiated prices.** A `price:` on a route replaces the live list price, so costs match what the organization actually pays. For 12% off Claude Sonnet's list price: `price: {input: 1.76, output: 8.8, cache_read: 0.088, cache_write: 2.2}`. Give the cache prices too: left out, cache reads cost 10% of input and writes cost the input price. **5. Monthly reconciliation (not built yet).** Compare our computed cost with providers' billing exports (AWS Cost and Usage Reports, GCP billing export, Azure Cost Management) and report the difference. ## What's tracked | Area | Metrics | |---|---| | **Spend** | Actual cost by user, team, tag, model, backend, and hour, day, or month; every ledger row also has the key and session; month-end pace against budgets | | **Savings** | Total and by cause (above), over time | | **GPU fleet** | Where each replica runs (cloud, region, instance, spot), uptime, burn rate, cost per run and per month (SkyPilot catalog prices), replica-hours, utilization, demand at API prices vs GPU cost, every state change and admin action | | **Routing** | Model mix, free upgrades per group, and for each request the model asked for, its quality floor, and the model served | | **Caching** | Cached tokens read and written, cache hit rate by backend or model, caching savings. Sessions that switched backends and the rebuild cost they paid aren't tracked yet | | **Operations** | Latency, time to first token, tokens/s, errors, and failovers per backend | | **Budgets** | Team, org, and GPU spend against budgets with month-end pace; each person's spend against their limit; alerts at 80% and 100%; refused requests by reason | ## Views (console pages) | Page | Audience | Shows | |---|---|---| | **Dispatch** | Admins, finance, team leads | Live: the merit-order stack from real traffic, request feed, backend health, GPU fleet, what needs attention | | **Reports** | Everyone (scoped to their role) | Spend vs baseline over time, savings by cause, breakdowns by team, person, model, backend, day, or tag; recent requests (not for finance); CSV | | **GPUs** | Admins, finance, team leads | Each deployment: where it runs, uptime, burn rate, run and month cost, demand coverage; stop / pin / stop-all (admins); activity log; what-if for models you don't host yet | | **Controls** | Admins, finance | Org, GPU, and team spend against budgets with month-end pace; safeguards and budgets (editable by admins) | | **Backends** | Admins, team leads | Health, requests, errors, latency, time to first token, measured speed | | **Models** | Admins | Routes, live prices and where each came from, quality scores and their source, eval results (Evals tab) | | **Teams** | Admins, finance, team leads | Each team's limits, policy, and spend this month | | **People, Keys** | Admins, team leads | Who's in which team, their spend and limits; API keys | | **Config** | Admins | Teams, models, backends, routing, and access mappings, saved as versions | | **My usage** | Everyone | Own spend, models used, budget remaining | ## Who sees what Roles come from Entra (or OIDC) group membership, with exceptions pinned on the People page. | Role | Can see | |---|---| | User | Their own usage | | Team lead | Their team's usage, per user | | Finance | All spend and savings, no per-request detail | | Admin | Everything | ## Ways to get reports - **Web console** with the pages above. - **Reports API.** The console is built on it, so anyone can build their own views. - **CLI:** `meritorder usage` for a quick look at your own spend. - **Exports:** CSV and JSONL of the ledger, to a file or S3, for data warehouses and BI tools. - **Weekly digests** per team, to a webhook (Slack, Teams, or anything that accepts JSON). - **Alerts** to the same webhook and the console: team, personal, org, and GPU budget thresholds, **spend spikes** (a person suddenly at 5× normal usually means an agent stuck in a loop), GPU state changes, every admin GPU action, provider outages and recoveries, and changed live prices or quality scores. - **Metrics:** Prometheus `/metrics` and OpenTelemetry traces, with a ready-made Grafana dashboard (below). ## Prometheus and Grafana `/metrics` (set `MERITORDER_METRICS_TOKEN` to require a bearer token): | Metric | Type | Labels | |---|---|---| | `meritorder_requests_total` | counter | model, backend, status | | `meritorder_rejected_requests_total` | counter | status, reason (refused before any backend: auth, budget, rate limit, routing) | | `meritorder_failovers_total` | counter | backend, status (attempts that failed on a backend and moved on to the next route) | | `meritorder_tokens_total` | counter | model, backend, kind (input, cache_read, cache_write, output) | | `meritorder_cost_usd_total`, `meritorder_baseline_usd_total` | counter | model, backend | | `meritorder_savings_usd_total` | counter | cause | | `meritorder_request_duration_seconds`, `meritorder_time_to_first_token_seconds` | histogram | model, backend | | `meritorder_inflight_requests` | gauge | backend (this process) | | `meritorder_backend_available` | gauge | backend | | `meritorder_gpu_replicas`, `meritorder_gpu_usd_per_hour`, `meritorder_gpu_utilization`, `meritorder_gpu_waiting_requests` | gauge | backend | Counters are per gateway process: sum them across pods. GPU gauges come from the controller's published state, so every gateway reports the same value: use `max`. The **Grafana dashboard** (`charts/meritorder/dashboards/meritorder.json`, generated by `scripts/build_grafana_dashboard.py`) shows spend, what it would have cost, savings rate and causes, traffic, errors and refusals by reason, prompt-cache hit ratio, backend availability, latency and time to first token, and GPU replicas, burn, utilization, and queue. """Capacity controller (docs/05-gpu-autoscaling.md).

Every interval, for each self-hosted backend with a ``serve:`` section:

1. Measure addressable demand: what traffic this model could serve costs per hour
   at API prices, and its token throughput. Free upgrades are excluded, so idle
   capacity can't keep GPUs alive by attracting traffic.
2. Size replicas: enough for throughput, but each replica must pay for itself.
   Then apply admin controls (stop, pin, stop all) and safeguards (GPU budget, fleet caps).
3. Advance the state machine (gpu.decide) and act through the provisioner.
4. Publish state, endpoint, where replicas run, and vLLM utilization to Redis for the gateways.
5. Accrue GPU cost (replicas x hourly price) and log state changes to the GPU activity log.

Only one controller is active at a time (Postgres advisory lock).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging
import os
import socket
import time
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

from .alerts import notify
from .config import Config
from .configstore import ConfigFollower
from .gpu import (API_ONLY, Deployment, Demand, Status, addressable, decide, desired_replicas, fetch_load, make_provisioner,
                  plan_fleet)
from .state import make_state
from .store import make_store, month_start

log = logging.getLogger("meritorder.controller")
LOCK_ID = 0x4D45524954  # "MERIT"


def deployments(cfg: Config) -> list[Deployment]:
    out = []
    for b in cfg.backends:
        if b.kind != "self_hosted" or b.serve is None or not b.enabled:
            continue
        model = cfg.model(b.serve.model)
        if model is None:
            log.warning("backend %s serves unknown model %r; skipping", b.name, b.serve.model)
            continue
        out.append(Deployment(backend=b, model=model, provisioner=make_provisioner(b, cfg)))
    return out


async def tick(cfg: Config, store, state, deps: list[Deployment], now: float | None = None) -> list[dict]:
    now = now or time.time()
    wall = datetime.fromtimestamp(now, UTC)
    rows_1h = await store.demand_rows(wall - timedelta(hours=1))
    rows_15m = await store.demand_rows(wall - timedelta(minutes=15))
    controls = await store.get_setting("gpu_controls") or {}
    await state.set_json("gpu:controls", controls)  # gateways read it to stop routing to stopped GPUs right away
    guards = cfg.safeguards

    # Accrue what running replicas cost since the last cycle (you pay while provisioning and draining too).
    recs: dict[str, dict] = {}
    for dep in deps:
        b = dep.backend
        rec = await state.get_json(f"deploy:{b.name}") or {}
        last = rec.get("accrued_at") or now
        elapsed = min(max(now - last, 0), 86400)
        if rec.get("state", API_ONLY) != API_ONLY and rec.get("replicas") and elapsed:
            burn = rec.get("burn_usd_per_hour")
            burn = burn if burn is not None else rec["replicas"] * b.gpu_cost_per_hour
            cost = burn * elapsed / 3600
            await store.add_gpu_usage(b.name, wall, rec["replicas"] * elapsed, cost)
            rec["run_cost"] = (rec.get("run_cost") or 0) + cost
        rec["accrued_at"] = now
        recs[b.name] = rec
    gpu_spent = sum((await store.gpu_spend_since(month_start(wall))).values())

    sized = []
    for dep in deps:
        b, serve = dep.backend, dep.backend.serve
        cost_1h, tok_1h = addressable(dep.model, rows_1h, cfg)
        cost_15, tok_15 = addressable(dep.model, rows_15m, cfg)
        demand = Demand(usd_per_hour=max(cost_1h, cost_15 * 4), tokens_per_second=max(tok_1h / 3600, tok_15 / 900))
        price = await replica_price(dep)
        desired = desired_replicas(serve, price["usd_per_hour"], b.capacity_tokens_per_second, demand)
        sized.append((dep, demand, desired, price))
    plans = plan_fleet([{"name": d.backend.name, "desired": want, "price": price["usd_per_hour"],
                         "max_replicas": d.backend.serve.max_replicas, "value": dem.usd_per_hour} for d, dem, want, price in sized],
                       controls, guards, gpu_spent, now)

    published = []
    for dep, demand, desired, price in sized:
        b, serve = dep.backend, dep.backend.serve
        plan = plans[b.name]
        key = f"deploy:{b.name}"
        rec = recs[b.name]
        before = rec.get("state", API_ONLY)
        if before == API_ONLY and serve.provisioner != "static":
            status = Status()  # don't poll the cloud for something that isn't running
        else:
            status = await dep.provisioner.status()
        new, action = decide(rec, serve, plan.desired, status, now, force=plan.force, drain=plan.drain, why=plan.note)
        if action is not None:
            try:
                if action.kind == "up":
                    await dep.provisioner.up(action.replicas)
                elif action.kind == "scale":
                    await dep.provisioner.scale(action.replicas)
                elif action.kind == "down":
                    await dep.provisioner.down()
            except Exception as e:
                log.error("%s: %s failed: %s", b.name, action.kind, e)
                await store.gpu_event("error", b.name, "controller", {"action": action.kind, "error": str(e)[:500]})
                if action.kind == "down":
                    # Keep trying to stop it: never report a GPU as off when it may still be billing.
                    new = {**rec, "reason": f"stop failed, will retry: {e}"[:300]}
                else:
                    new.update(state=API_ONLY, since=now, endpoint=None, replicas=0, cooldown_until=now + 1800, reason=f"{action.kind} failed: {e}"[:300])
            else:
                if action.kind == "scale":
                    await store.gpu_event("scale", b.name, "controller", {"replicas": action.replicas, "reason": plan.note or "demand"})
                if action.kind == "up":
                    # A server that is already running (static) or comes up fast goes warm this cycle.
                    status = await dep.provisioner.status()
                    if status.ready:
                        new, _ = decide(new, serve, plan.desired, status, now, force=plan.force, drain=plan.drain, why=plan.note)
        if new.get("state") != API_ONLY and status.replicas_info:
            new["replicas_info"] = status.replicas_info
        # What it's costing right now: each replica's own catalog price when known, else the expected price.
        running = (new.get("replicas") or 0) if new.get("state", API_ONLY) != API_ONLY else 0
        priced = [r.get("usd_per_hour") for r in new.get("replicas_info") or [] if r.get("usd_per_hour") is not None]
        if running and len(priced) >= running:
            new["burn_usd_per_hour"] = round(sum(sorted(priced)[:running]), 4)
        else:
            new["burn_usd_per_hour"] = round(running * price["usd_per_hour"], 4)
        new["price"] = price
        if new.get("endpoint"):
            load = await fetch_load(new["endpoint"])
            if load is not None:
                await state.set_utilization(b.name, load["utilization"])
                new["utilization"] = round(load["utilization"], 3)
                new["waiting"] = load["waiting"]  # gateways bound the last-resort queue with this
                new["sampled_at"] = now
        new.update(
            backend=b.name,
            model=dep.model.name,
            desired=desired,
            planned=plan.desired,
            note=plan.note,
            demand_usd_per_hour=round(demand.usd_per_hour, 4),
            demand_tokens_per_second=round(demand.tokens_per_second, 1),
            gpu_usd_per_hour=price["usd_per_hour"],
            updated=wall.isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        )
        if new.get("state") != before:
            await store.gpu_event("state", b.name, "controller", {"from": before, "to": new["state"], "reason": new.get("reason", "")})
            await notify(f"GPU tier: {b.name} ({dep.model.name}) {before} -> {new['state']}: {new.get('reason', '')}. "
                         f"Demand ${demand.usd_per_hour:,.2f}/h at API prices vs ${price['usd_per_hour']:,.2f}/h per replica.",
                         state=state, title=f"GPU {b.name}: {new['state'].replace('_', ' ')}", level="info", page="gpus")
        await state.set_json(key, new)
        published.append(new)
        log.info("%s (%s): %s, demand $%.2f/h at API prices, %.0f tok/s, desired %d replica(s) at $%.2f/h each%s",
                 b.name, dep.model.name, new["state"], demand.usd_per_hour, demand.tokens_per_second, desired, price["usd_per_hour"],
                 f" ({plan.note})" if plan.note else "")
    return published


async def replica_price(dep: Deployment) -> dict:
    """Price of one replica for sizing decisions: SkyPilot's catalog when available, else the configured price."""
    b = dep.backend
    offer = None
    getter = getattr(dep.provisioner, "expected_price", None)
    if getter is not None:
        try:
            offer = await getter()
        except Exception as e:
            log.debug("%s: price lookup failed: %s", b.name, e)
    if offer:
        return {**offer, "source": "skypilot_catalog", "configured_usd_per_hour": b.gpu_cost_per_hour}
    return {"usd_per_hour": b.gpu_cost_per_hour, "source": "configured"}


async def wait_or_kick(state, interval: int, seen: str | None) -> str | None:
    """Sleep until the next cycle, waking early when an admin changes a GPU control."""
    deadline = time.monotonic() + interval
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        await asyncio.sleep(min(2, max(0.0, deadline - time.monotonic())))
        kick = await state.get_json("controller:kick")
        if kick and kick != seen:
            return kick
    return seen


async def run_controller(cfg: Config | None = None, once: bool = False, interval: int = 60, path: str | None = None) -> None:
    store = make_store(os.environ.get("MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL"))
    state = make_state(os.environ.get("MERITORDER_REDIS_URL"))
    if store.kind != "postgres":
        raise SystemExit("the controller needs Postgres: set MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL")
    await store.init()
    follower = ConfigFollower(store, path=path, cfg=cfg)
    cfg = await follower.current()
    deps = deployments(cfg)
    if not deps:
        log.warning("no self-hosted backends with a `serve:` section are enabled; nothing to control")
    lock_conn = await store.pool.acquire()
    try:
        while not await lock_conn.fetchval("SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1)", LOCK_ID):
            log.info("another controller is active; standing by")
            if once:
                return
            await asyncio.sleep(interval)
        log.info("controller is active for: %s", ", ".join(d.backend.name for d in deps) or "(none)")
        kick = await state.get_json("controller:kick")
        while True:
            try:
                latest = await follower.current()
                if latest is not cfg:
                    cfg, deps = latest, deployments(latest)
                    log.info("configuration changed; controlling: %s", ", ".join(d.backend.name for d in deps) or "(none)")
                await tick(cfg, store, state, deps)
            except Exception:
                log.exception("controller cycle failed")
            await state.set_json("controller:heartbeat", {"at": time.time(), "host": socket.gethostname(), "interval": interval,
                                                          "deployments": [d.backend.name for d in deps]})
            if once:
                return
            kick = await wait_or_kick(state, interval, kick)
    finally:
        await store.pool.release(lock_conn)
        await store.close()
        await state.close()

"""Marginal-cost router (docs/03-routing.md).

For each candidate backend b over the session's expected remaining turns:

    cost(b) = rebuild(b) + expected_remaining_turns * per_turn(b)

* per_turn uses API prices, or for self-hosted backends a shadow price that is
  near zero while the replica has headroom and rises toward the API price as it fills.
* rebuild is zero when b already holds a warm cache for this session, otherwise
  the extra cost of re-processing the whole prefix there.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

from .backends import Backend
from .classifier import Floor, classify, parse_floor
from .config import Config, ModelConfig, Price, Route, TeamConfig
from .sessions import Session


class RoutingError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status: int, message: str, kind: str = "invalid_request_error"):
        super().__init__(message)
        self.status = status
        self.message = message
        self.kind = kind


@dataclass
class Candidate:
    model: ModelConfig
    route: Route
    backend: Backend
    cost: float
    warm: bool
    quality: int
    upgraded: bool = False

    @property
    def self_hosted(self) -> bool:
        return self.backend.kind == "self_hosted"


@dataclass
class Decision:
    requested: str
    auto: bool
    floor: Floor | None
    candidates: list[Candidate] = field(default_factory=list)
    reason: str = ""


def shadow_multiplier(util: float, knee: float, floor: float) -> float | None:
    """Fraction of API price a self-hosted token "costs" at this utilization. None = full."""
    if util >= 1.0:
        return None
    if util <= knee:
        return floor
    return floor + (1.0 - floor) * ((util - knee) / (1.0 - knee)) ** 2


def _scaled(price: Price, m: float) -> Price:
    return Price(input=price.input * m, output=price.output * m, cache_read=price.read() * m, cache_write=price.write() * m)


class Router:
    def __init__(self, cfg: Config, backends: dict[str, Backend]):
        self.cfg = cfg
        self.backends = backends

    def resolve(self, requested: str) -> ModelConfig | None:
        return self.cfg.model(requested)

    def _expected_turns(self, session: Session | None) -> int:
        r = self.cfg.routing
        turns = session.turns if session else 0
        return max(r.min_expected_turns, min(r.max_expected_turns, turns or r.min_expected_turns))

    def estimate(
        self, price: Price, backend: Backend, prompt_tokens: int, session: Session | None, warm: bool, turns: int
    ) -> float:
        r = self.cfg.routing
        new = r.est_new_tokens_per_turn
        if session and session.prefix_tokens:
            new = max(prompt_tokens - session.prefix_tokens, 200)
        cached = max(prompt_tokens - new, 0)
        # Steady state: the prefix is read from cache, new tokens are written to it.
        write_price = price.write() if backend.format == "anthropic" else price.input
        per_turn = (cached * price.read() + new * write_price + r.est_output_tokens * price.output) / 1e6
        rebuild = 0.0 if warm else cached * max(write_price - price.read(), 0.0) / 1e6
        return rebuild + turns * per_turn

    def decide(
        self,
        requested: str,
        team: TeamConfig,
        body: dict,
        headers: dict[str, str],
        session: Session | None,
        prompt_tokens: int,
        boundary: bool,
        utilization: dict[str, float],
        now: float,
    ) -> Decision:
        r = self.cfg.routing
        auto = requested == r.auto_model or requested == ""
        floor: Floor | None = None

        if auto:
            if session and session.model and not boundary and team.allows_model(session.model) and self.cfg.model(session.model):
                models = [self.cfg.model(session.model)]
                floor = parse_floor(session.floor or "")
                reason = f"mid-task: keeping session model {session.model}"
            else:
                floor = classify(body, headers)
                models = [m for m in self.cfg.models
                          if m.kind == "chat" and m.q(floor.task) >= floor.level and team.allows_model(m.name)]
                reason = f"classified {floor} ({floor.reason})"
                if not models:
                    # Nothing meets the floor: fall back to the best allowed models.
                    allowed = [m for m in self.cfg.models if m.kind == "chat" and team.allows_model(m.name)]
                    best = max((m.q(floor.task) for m in allowed), default=0)
                    models = [m for m in allowed if m.q(floor.task) == best]
                    reason += f"; no model meets the floor, using best available (level {best})"
        else:
            model = self.resolve(requested)
            if model is None:
                raise RoutingError(404, f"model '{requested}' is not configured", "not_found_error")
            if model.kind != "chat":
                raise RoutingError(400, f"'{model.name}' is an embedding model; use /v1/embeddings", "invalid_request_error")
            if not team.allows_model(model.name):
                raise RoutingError(403, f"model '{model.name}' is not allowed for team '{team.name}'", "permission_error")
            models = [model]
            reason = f"harness requested {model.name}"

        turns = self._expected_turns(session)
        task = floor.task if floor else "general"
        cands: list[Candidate] = []
        too_small = [m.name for m in models if m.context_window and prompt_tokens > m.context_window * 0.95]
        if too_small and len(too_small) < len(models):
            models = [m for m in models if m.name not in too_small]
            reason += f"; skipped {', '.join(too_small)} (context window too small)"
        for m in models:
            for route in m.routes:
                backend = self.backends.get(route.backend)
                if backend is None or not backend.available or not backend.healthy(now) or not team.allows_backend(route.backend):
                    continue
                if backend.draining and not (session and session.warm(backend.name, now)):
                    continue  # draining: only finish sessions whose cache is already there
                if auto and not route.priced:
                    continue  # an unknown price must never look free
                price = route.cost_price()
                if backend.kind == "self_hosted":
                    mult = shadow_multiplier(utilization.get(backend.name, 0.0), r.shadow_knee, r.shadow_floor)
                    if mult is None:
                        continue  # saturated: new work spills to API routes
                    price = _scaled(price, mult)
                warm = bool(session and session.warm(backend.name, now))
                quality = m.q(task)
                cands.append(
                    Candidate(
                        model=m,
                        route=route,
                        backend=backend,
                        cost=self.estimate(price, backend, prompt_tokens, session, warm, turns),
                        warm=warm,
                        quality=quality,
                        upgraded=bool(auto and floor and quality > floor.level and backend.kind == "self_hosted"),
                    )
                )
        if not cands:
            if auto and session and session.model and not boundary:
                # The session's model has nowhere to run (e.g. its GPUs were stopped): pick again.
                again = self.decide(requested, team, body, headers, session, prompt_tokens, True, utilization, now)
                again.reason = f"session model {session.model} is unavailable; re-routed: {again.reason}"
                return again
            raise RoutingError(503, self._unavailable_message(models, team, now, auto), "overloaded_error")
        if auto and any(c.backend.kind != "mock" for c in cands):
            # Mocks are for trying things out; never let them win against real backends.
            cands = [c for c in cands if c.backend.kind != "mock"]

        cands.sort(key=lambda c: (c.cost, -c.quality))
        if auto and len(cands) > 1:
            # Near-ties go to the higher-quality model.
            cheapest = cands[0].cost
            near = [c for c in cands if c.cost <= cheapest * 1.02 + 1e-9]
            best = max(near, key=lambda c: c.quality)
            cands.remove(best)
            cands.insert(0, best)

        # Stickiness: only move a session off its current backend if it's clearly cheaper.
        if session and session.backend:
            current = next((c for c in cands if c.backend.name == session.backend and c.model.name == session.model), None)
            if current is not None and current is not cands[0]:
                margin = current.cost * r.switch_margin_pct / 100.0 + r.switch_margin_usd
                if cands[0].cost + margin >= current.cost:
                    cands.remove(current)
                    cands.insert(0, current)
                    reason += f"; staying on {current.backend.name} (move would not pay for cache rebuild)"

        return Decision(requested=requested, auto=auto, floor=floor, candidates=cands, reason=reason)

    def _unavailable_message(self, models: list[ModelConfig], team: TeamConfig, now: float, auto: bool) -> str:
        """Say why nothing can serve the request, route by route, so people know what to fix or switch to."""
        if auto or len(models) != 1:
            return "no healthy backend is available for this request"
        why = []
        for route in models[0].routes:
            b = self.backends.get(route.backend)
            bc = self.cfg.backend(route.backend)
            if b is None:
                why.append(f"{route.backend}: {(bc.disabled_reason if bc else None) or 'not enabled'}")
            elif not team.allows_backend(route.backend):
                why.append(f"{route.backend}: not allowed for team '{team.name}'")
            elif not b.available:
                why.append(f"{route.backend}: {getattr(b, 'unavailable_reason', None) or 'not running'}")
            elif not b.healthy(now):
                why.append(f"{route.backend}: failing, retrying shortly")
            elif b.draining:
                why.append(f"{route.backend}: draining, only finishing existing sessions")
            else:
                why.append(f"{route.backend}: saturated")
        return (f"'{models[0].name}' has nowhere to run right now ({'; '.join(why)}). "
                f"Use model '{self.cfg.routing.auto_model}' to let Merit Order pick another model, or try again later.")

"""/metrics: time-to-first-token histogram, in-flight and availability gauges, and GPU state for dashboards."""

import re

from conftest import auth

from meritorder.backends.mock import MockBackend
from meritorder.config import BackendConfig


def series(text: str, name: str) -> dict[str, float]:
    return {m.group(1): float(m.group(2)) for m in re.finditer(rf"^{name}(\{{[^}}]*\}})? ([0-9.e+-]+)$", text, re.M)}


async def test_metrics_expose_ttft_inflight_availability_and_gpu_state(gateway, client):
    r = await client.post("/v1/chat/completions", headers=auth(),
                          json={"model": "small", "stream": True, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]})
    assert r.status_code == 200
    gpu = MockBackend(BackendConfig(name="gpu", kind="self_hosted", format="openai", mock_latency_ms=0))
    gpu.deploy = {"state": "warm", "replicas": 2, "burn_usd_per_hour": 8.7, "utilization": 0.64, "waiting": 3}
    gateway.backends["gpu"] = gpu
    hold = gateway.inflight.acquire("gpu", 60)

# 00 — How it all works (start here) Merit Order sits between your tools and the model providers. Your tools keep speaking the API they already speak; Merit Order translates when the chosen model speaks another. For every request sent with the model name `auto`, it asks two questions: 1. **How hard is this?** The request gets a **level** for its kind of work: coding or general, 1 to 5. 2. **What's the cheapest model that's good enough?** Every model has a **score** for each kind of work, 1 to 5. Models scoring at least the level, with room for the conversation, qualify, and the cheapest of those wins, counting the whole rest of the conversation, not just this request. Everything else in this document is detail on those two questions: how tools connect, where the levels, scores and prices come from, what "cheapest" really means, how long conversations are handled, what happens when something fails, and when your own GPUs are worth switching on. The numbers are from the live configuration on 11 November 2026; prices and scores refresh on their own, so yours will drift. A request that **names a model** (`claude-opus`, `gpt-sol`, …) skips both questions: it always gets that model, and Merit Order only chooses where to run it (section 10). ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Your tool
(any API format)"] --> R["Request
model: auto"] R --> L["2. Level
coding:3"] L --> Q["3–4. Models scoring ≥ 3,
with room, allowed for the team"] Q --> C["5. Cheapest for the rest
of the session"] C --> E["6. Effort and output limit
for that level"] E --> S["Send, translated if needed;
on failure, the next cheapest (8)"] ``` ## 1. Your tools connect as they are Point a tool's base URL at Merit Order and give it a Merit Order key. Nothing else about the tool changes, because Merit Order speaks both common APIs: | Your tool speaks | For example | Merit Order endpoint | |---|---|---| | Anthropic Messages | Claude Code, Anthropic SDKs | `/v1/messages` (and `/v1/messages/count_tokens`) | | OpenAI Chat Completions | pi, Cursor, OpenAI SDKs, most other tools | `/v1/chat/completions` | | OpenAI Responses | Codex CLI | `/v1/responses` | | Embeddings | RAG pipelines | `/v1/embeddings` | **The model's own format is Merit Order's problem, not the tool's.** Each provider speaks one of the two formats. When the tool and the chosen provider speak the same one, the request passes through untouched, so provider features such as Claude's cache markers and thinking signatures survive. When they differ, Merit Order converts the request, the reply and the stream both ways: messages, tool calls, images, streaming, usage and stop reasons. Two things don't cross: a model's reasoning from earlier turns (each turn still works; the model just thinks again), and `temperature`/`top_p`, which current Claude models reject. The Responses API is converted to Chat Completions inside the gateway; GPT models that need the Responses API for tools with reasoning are converted on the way out. **The model name says what you want:** - `auto`: Merit Order chooses (the rest of this document). - A model's name or one of its aliases: that model. Aliases cover the names tools already send, so `claude-sonnet-5-5`, `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5` and `sonnet` all mean Claude Sonnet. - Anything else: an error saying the model isn't configured. `GET /v1/models` lists `auto` and every model your team may use, with each one's context window. **Every reply says what happened**, in headers: `X-MeritOrder-Model` (the model that answered), `X-MeritOrder-Backend` (the provider), `X-MeritOrder-Floor` (the level, for `auto`), `X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens` and its source, `X-MeritOrder-Failed-Over` when a provider failed first, and for replies that aren't streamed `X-MeritOrder-Cost-Usd`. The console's Reports → Requests tab shows the model, provider, level and cost of every request. Setting up Claude Code and pi is in section 11. ## 2. Every request gets a level The level is how demanding the request is. It's worked out from the request itself, with simple rules and no model call, so it's instant and free: | The request | Level | |---|---| | Plain text, short (under ~400 tokens), no tools | general 1 | | Plain text | general 2 | | Plain text with words like analyze, compare, plan, strategy, trade-offs, evaluate or reason, or over 20,000 tokens long | general 3 | | Any tools, or text that looks like code (code fences, `def`, `import`, stack traces, file names, "refactor", "bug", SQL, …) | coding 3 | | 5 or more tools: an agent at work | coding 4 | | Coding with "hard" wording (architecture, race condition, security, performance, migration, concurrency, …) or over 60,000 tokens of context | one level higher, at most 5 | Clients can take over: `X-Route-Floor: coding:4` sets the level exactly, and `X-Route-Hint: cheap` or `smart` moves it one level down or up. Every `auto` response says what it got (`X-MeritOrder-Floor`). What that means in practice: | Request | Level | |---|---| | "What's the capital of Portugal?" | general 1 | | "Draft a reply to this customer email" (pasted) | general 2 | | "Compare these three vendor proposals" | general 3 | | "Why does this function return None?" with a code block | coding 3 | | A coding agent's turn: 20 tools, 30,000 tokens of conversation | coding 4 | | The same agent, 90,000 tokens into the session | coding 5 | **Claude Code's side jobs get lower levels.** Claude Code labels each request (when its hint headers are on; section 11): a turn of the conversation, a subagent's turn, the summary it writes when it compacts a long conversation, or a side request such as a session title or summary. Those last two don't need the level of the work itself, so `auto` caps them: | Claude Code request | Highest level | |---|---| | Side request (titles, summaries) | 1 | | Compaction summary | 3 | | Conversation or subagent turn | not capped | An explicit `X-Route-Floor` is never capped. Auto mode's permission checks name Claude Sonnet, so they never go through `auto` at all. The caps are under Config → Routing → Claude Code request types. The level rules themselves live in code (`src/meritorder/classifier.py`); the console doesn't show or change them yet. ## 3. Every model gets a score for each kind of work A score says how good a model is at a kind of work, **compared with the best model you have**. It isn't typed in: the worker works it out once a day from published benchmarks. **What a score means.** By default (source `epoch`), each model's score is based on its chance of solving a task as hard as **FrontierSWE**, a set of real, hard software-engineering tasks. The best model scores 5 and every other model scores in proportion: one that solves 60% as many such tasks as the best scores 3. | Model | Chance on a FrontierSWE-hard task (coding) | Coding score | General score | |---|---|---|---| | Claude Fable 5.2 | 70% | 5.0 | 5.0 | | Gemini 4 Carbon | 61% | 4.4 | not measured yet | | GPT-6.1 Terra | 62% | 4.4 * | 3.8 | | Claude Opus 5.5 | 58% | 4.2 | 3.9 | | GPT-6 Astra | 59% | 4.2 | 4.1 | | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | 56% | 4.0 | 3.4 | | Gemini 4 Argon | 48% | 3.4 | 3.4 | | GPT-6.1 Sol | 46% | 3.3 | 4.0 | | Claude Haiku 5.5 | 41% | 3.0 | 2.0 | | GPT-6 Luna | 32% | 2.3 | 1.3 | | Gemini 3.8 Flash | 24% | 1.7 | 1.6 | | Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite | 4% | 1.0 * | 1.0 | \* Estimated from the model's general ability: no coding results published yet. **Where the numbers come from.** [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/benchmarks) (CC BY 4.0) places every model on one ability scale, fitted across about 40 benchmarks, and every benchmark on the same scale by difficulty. That's what makes models comparable even when they were tested on different benchmarks, and lets a model's ability be turned into a chance of solving tasks of a given difficulty. For coding, a model's own results on FrontierSWE and FrontierCode refine its general ability, so coding strength counts; results at the effort `auto` uses for hard work are preferred where published. The alternative source is the [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai) Intelligence Index (needs `ARTIFICIAL_ANALYSIS_API_KEY`). It's a single number per model, so coding and general get the same score. The third option is scores written on each model by hand (`config`), for example from your own eval runs ([11 — Evals](11-evals.md)). **Two choices shape the scores** (Config → Routing → Quality scores): - **Scale.** `best` (default): the best model is 5 and the rest in proportion; adding a weak model changes nobody else's score. `range`: the weakest model with data is 1 and the best 5, which depends on which weak models you happen to have configured. - **Reference task.** A harder reference spreads models further apart and sends more work up the ladder. Against Remote Labor Index (real paid remote work, which Fable solves 37% of the time), Opus would score 2.8 for general work, and ordinary level-3 work would go only to Fable. FrontierSWE keeps level 3 within reach of models like Sonnet. **Models the source doesn't cover** aren't picked by `auto`: a score nobody measured would compete with measured ones, and because the cheapest qualifying model wins, an optimistic guess would win. They still answer requests that name them. To put one back, give it a `quality_override` (Config → Models), which always wins over the source; that's also how to record that your own evals disagree with the benchmarks (Models → Evals → *Apply scores…* → *Write as override*). Measured scores use the same 1–5 scale, so the Evals page shows them beside the ones in use. On 11 November 2026, 11 open models weren't covered, among them Qwen3 Coder, Devstral and MiMo. Hover a score on the Models page to see how it was worked out. ## 4. Which models qualify A model qualifies for a request when: - its score for that kind of work is **at least the request's level**. A level-3 coding request can go to any model with a coding score of 3.0 or more; level 5 means "as good as the best", which today is only Fable; - the conversation **fits in its context window** (section 7); and - the team is allowed to use it (Config → Teams → allowed models and backends). ## 5. The cheapest qualifying route wins Each qualifying model has one or more **routes**: the providers that serve it (Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, OpenRouter, your own GPUs, …). Merit Order prices every route and picks the cheapest. **Prices are live.** The worker refreshes them every 15 minutes: OpenRouter routes from OpenRouter's catalog, direct provider APIs from the price list LiteLLM maintains, cross-checked against each other. Long-prompt prices apply (Claude Haiku 5.5 costs five times as much above 100,000 prompt tokens), and a price change, a list that can't be fetched, or two lists that disagree raises an alert. **"Cheapest" means the rest of the session**, because in a conversation each turn resends everything before it, and providers charge far less for the part they still have cached: ``` cost of a route = rebuild + expected turns × cost per turn rebuild = what it costs to get this conversation into the provider's cache: zero if this provider already holds it, else the context at the full input price (or the cache-write price, for Claude, where caching is explicit), less the cache-read price the first turn already counts cost per turn = the cached part at the cache-read price + the new tokens at the input price (cache-write price for Claude): what the conversation grew by since its last turn, or about 2,000 for a new session + about 600 output tokens at the output price expected turns = the turns so far, kept between 3 and 30 (a long session will probably keep going) ``` Here's what that gives for a new coding session at level 3, 30,000 tokens in: | Model (route) | Score | Rebuild | Per turn | 3 turns | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic)** | 3.0 | $0.003 | $0.0008 | **$0.006** | | GPT-6.1 Terra (Azure) | 4.4 | $0.027 | $0.006 | $0.046 | | Gemini 4 Argon (OpenRouter) | 3.4 | $0.053 | $0.013 | $0.092 | | GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI) | 3.3 | $0.053 | $0.013 | $0.092 | And for an agent at level 4, 80,000 tokens in: | Model (route) | Score | Rebuild | Per turn | 3 turns | |---|---|---|---|---| | **GPT-6.1 Terra (Azure)** | 4.4 | $0.074 | $0.009 | **$0.101** | | Gemini 4 Carbon (OpenRouter) | 4.4 | $0.148 | $0.018 | $0.202 | | Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) | 4.0 | $0.187 | $0.019 | $0.244 | | Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) | 4.2 | $0.374 | $0.038 | $0.487 | **Sessions stay put.** Once a session is on a route, the rebuild is already paid there, so moving it must save at least 10% plus $0.01 over the rest of the session. Within a task (while the tool is sending tool results back, before the next prompt from a person) the session keeps its model outright. In practice a session moves only when a new task starts and something is clearly cheaper, its cache has expired (after 5 idle minutes), the conversation was compacted, it no longer fits (section 7), or its model is busy or down on every route (section 8). That's what keeps a session from bouncing between Bedrock and Anthropic and paying to rebuild each time. **A session can hold several conversations.** Claude Code sends its subagents' turns and its side requests under the main session's id. Each keeps its own routing state (model, level, cache), so a subagent never resets the main conversation's; budgets, the per-session spend limit and reports still count the session as one. **Near-ties go to speed.** The same model often costs the same everywhere (Claude on Anthropic, Bedrock and Vertex), so price alone can't choose. Routes within a small margin of the cheapest compete on measured speed: 2% under the default `cost` priority (where a better model among them goes first), 20% under `balanced`, 100% under `speed`. A team or a single request (`X-MeritOrder-Priority`) can choose differently. Every 10th new session may try a route within that margin whose speed is unknown or out of date, so speeds stay known. **Unpriced routes never win** for `auto`: an unknown price must never look free. ## 6. Then: effort and output length **Reasoning effort** follows the level, so every model works the same way for the same work (their own defaults differ): low for levels 1–2, medium for 3, high for 4–5. A model that doesn't take that effort keeps its default. The effort is set once per session on a model, because changing it would invalidate the prompt cache. A client's own effort setting always wins; one sent in Anthropic's format (Claude Code sends one) to a GPT or other OpenAI-format model goes over at the nearest level that model takes. **Output length** isn't capped by a guess. A request without `max_tokens` may write as much as the model can (128,000 tokens for current Claude and GPT models), less what wouldn't fit in the context window, under the per-request cost limit (Controls), or within what a provider's prepaid balance covers. A client's own `max_tokens` is kept (lowered only to the model's maximum). The response says how much it got and why (`X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens`, `X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens-Source`). ## 7. Context windows: long conversations Every model has a **context window**: the most a conversation plus its reply can hold. The windows come from the live price data, refreshed with the prices: | Window | Models | |---|---| | about 1 million tokens | Claude (all), Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, MiMo, Muse Spark, Mistral Large 4, Qwen3.8 Flash, Nemotron 3.5 Super | | 922,000 | GPT-6 and GPT-6.1 (Astra, Sol, Terra, Luna) | | 524,288 | Llama 4 Maverick | | 262,144 | Qwen3 Coder (all three), Devstral 2, Mistral Small 4, Ministral 14B, Gemma 4 31B, Nemotron 3 Ultra | | 131,072 | gpt-oss-120b, gpt-oss-20b | Two parties decide what happens as a conversation grows: **the tool**, which decides when to compact (summarize the history and start over from the summary), and **Merit Order**, which decides where the conversation can still go. **What Merit Order does:** - **Models without room drop out.** For `auto`, a model whose window the conversation fills past 95% isn't a candidate (the token count is estimated at about 4 characters per token, and the reply needs room too). A 300,000-token conversation never goes to gpt-oss or Qwen3 Coder; most qualifying models have about a million tokens, so something always fits. - **A session that outgrows its model moves, even mid-task.** The next turn goes to a model with room at the same level, paying once to rebuild the cache there. - **A provider that says "too long" isn't the end.** If a provider refuses a prompt as too long anyway (the estimate can be off), an `auto` request goes to a qualifying model with a bigger window. A request that names a model can't move; its error is worded the way Anthropic's API words it ("prompt is too long: …"), whichever provider refused, because that's what makes Claude Code compact. - **The reply shrinks to fit.** When a request doesn't set `max_tokens`, the reply may use what's left of the window and no more, so the provider doesn't refuse prompt plus reply (section 6). **What the tool does.** A tool compacts when the conversation nears the window it believes it has. `/v1/models` reports each model's window, and for `auto` the largest window among the models `auto` can pick for your team (1,048,576 tokens today). That's safe because models without room drop out: a long conversation narrows the choice to the million-token models instead of failing. - **pi**: `meritorder setup pi` writes each model's window into pi's model list. - **Claude Code**: it knows the windows of Claude models by name. For a name it doesn't know, such as `auto`, it assumes 200,000 tokens unless told otherwise; `meritorder setup claude-code` tells it the gateway's window (section 11). - **Other tools**: give them the window from `/v1/models`, or leave their default; a smaller window than the real one only means compacting earlier. ## 8. When something fails Nothing reaches the client until the chosen route has started answering, so a failure moves the request on: - **Over capacity, rate-limited, missing, or down:** the next route in the cost ranking. For a named model, or a session in the middle of a task, that's another provider for the same model; for a new `auto` task, it's the next cheapest qualifying route, whatever its model. A request gets 3 tries at most (`routing.max_attempts`). An `auto` session whose model is busy or down on every route moves to another qualifying model at its next turn, even mid-task. The failing route is skipped for a while (the provider's `Retry-After`, or a growing back-off) and an alert says where its traffic went. - **Too long for the model:** for `auto`, a qualifying model with a bigger window (section 7). - **The model refuses:** for `auto`, the next qualifying model (the refusal is billed and logged); a named model's refusal is returned as it is. - **A provider can't cover the whole reply on its prepaid balance:** the same route again, asking for what it says it can pay for. - **Budgets and limits:** organization, team, person and session budgets, rate limits, and the per-request cost limit stop requests before they're sent, with a message saying which. Every rule and timing is in [10 — How it decides](10-how-it-decides.md). ## 9. Your own GPUs: when they start and stop Power grids run the cheapest generators all the time (baseload) and switch on expensive ones (peakers) only for peaks. Merit Order does the same: your own GPUs, running an open model, are the baseload when there's enough steady work to keep them busy, and the APIs are the peakers that are always there. **A GPU deployment starts only when sustained demand pays for it.** Every minute the controller asks: what does the traffic this model could serve cost me at API prices? - **Traffic it could serve** means requests whose level its score covers. A model with a coding score of 3.0 counts every coding request at levels 1–3, wherever it was actually sent. - **At API prices** means what you're paying for that traffic today. - One replica is worth starting when that spend, per hour, exceeds the replica's hourly price plus a 20% margin, **continuously for 10 minutes**. The number of replicas follows the throughput (enough to run at 70% load), as long as each one pays for itself by the same rule. For example, Qwen3 Coder Next on four H100s costs about $16 an hour per replica (SkyPilot's cheapest offer in the allowed clouds, or the configured fallback). It starts once the work it could do would cost you more than $19.20 an hour at API prices for 10 minutes straight. **While it runs, it's the first choice.** A GPU you're already paying for costs almost nothing per token while it has room, so the router prices it at 2% of the API price up to 60% load, rising to the full API price as it fills. Up to that point it wins every request it qualifies for; past it, the APIs take over, and at 100% new work spills to them. Requests that only went to the GPU because it had room (a better model than the level needed) don't count as demand, so idle capacity can't keep itself alive. **It stops when demand no longer pays for it.** When the work it could do drops below break-even for 10 minutes, and it has been running at least 30 minutes, it **drains**: no new sessions, existing ones finish, and after 15 minutes the GPUs are released. If demand comes back while draining, it simply stays. Starting takes 10–20 minutes for a big model, and traffic stays on the APIs meanwhile, so the delays and margins are there to avoid paying for start-ups that don't last. **A self-hosted model needs a score.** Demand is counted by level, so a model the quality source doesn't cover has none, and its GPUs never start for `auto` traffic. On 11 November 2026 that's the case for Qwen3 Coder Next: give it a `quality_override` (Config → Models) to have the controller consider it. Its window (262,144 tokens) also means conversations longer than about 249,000 tokens go to the APIs. **Whether a GPU can ever pay** shows on Models → **GPU break-even**. Each open-weight model gets the cheapest machine whose GPUs hold its weights (sizes from Hugging Face), priced from SkyPilot's catalog, spot or on-demand, across the clouds SkyPilot covers. For each quality level and each model it shows the traffic one replica needs (tokens per minute and about how many requests an hour), your busiest hour of that traffic, and what the replica can serve. The price a GPU has to beat at a level is the cheapest API model good enough for it, because that's where `auto` would send the work otherwise. On 11 November 2026, with spot prices, only level-1 work could pay: gpt-oss-20b on one A100-80GB ($0.40 an hour) from about 235,000 tokens a minute. At level 2 the cheapest open option cost twice the API, and above that no open model scored high enough. *Get latest prices* has SkyPilot download its catalogs again. Admins can also stop a deployment (draining first or at once), pin a number of replicas, stop all GPUs, or cap GPU spend per month, per hour, or in replicas (GPUs page and Controls). Details: [05 — GPU autoscaling](05-gpu-autoscaling.md). ## 10. Requests that name a model A request for `claude-opus` gets Claude Opus, never another model. Merit Order still picks the route: the cheapest of Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and OpenRouter for the rest of the session, with the same stickiness, speed tie-breaks and failover between them. If none of its routes can run, the request fails with the reason for each, unless the team allows substituting a model at least as good. A named model is never skipped for its window: a conversation it can't hold gets the provider's error, worded so Claude Code compacts. Claude Code sends Claude model names unless it's set to `auto`, so by default it gets exactly what it asks for; `meritorder setup claude-code` sets it to `auto` (section 11). ## 11. Setting up Claude Code and pi Log in once (`meritorder login`, or `meritorder use-key` with a key from an admin), then: ```bash meritorder setup claude-code # Claude Code meritorder setup pi # pi ``` **Claude Code** isn't tied to Anthropic or Foundry: any gateway that speaks Anthropic's API can stand in via `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, and Merit Order does. The setup command writes these into Claude Code's settings file (`$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json`, or `~/.claude/settings.json`): | Setting | Value | Why | |---|---|---| | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | the gateway | Send every request to Merit Order | | `apiKeyHelper` | reads `~/.config/meritorder/api_key` | Your Merit Order key; logging in again rotates it | | `model` | `auto` | New sessions let Merit Order choose (`--model claude-sonnet-5-5` picks one; `--model none` leaves Claude Code's choice) | | `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS` | the gateway's window for that model | Claude Code would otherwise assume 200,000 tokens for `auto` and compact early | | `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION`, `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION_NAME` | `auto`, `auto (Merit Order)` | Adds "auto (Merit Order)" to the `/model` picker | | `CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS` | `1` | Claude Code labels side requests and compaction only when asked (section 2) | With `--model` set to a Claude model name, it leaves out the window and `/model` settings (and removes earlier ones): Claude Code already knows those names. It changes every Claude Code session that uses that settings folder. To keep Merit Order in a separate profile (for example, away from work that uses another account): ```bash meritorder setup claude-code --config-dir ~/.claude-meritorder CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-meritorder claude ``` What to expect: - **Billing.** With the Merit Order key, Claude Code doesn't use your claude.ai login for these requests: subscription limits don't apply, and the cost is per token on the providers' accounts behind the gateway. - **Non-Claude models.** `auto` can send Claude Code's turns to GPT, Gemini or open models, translated. It works, but Anthropic doesn't support running Claude Code on non-Claude models, so expect rough edges. - **Cost display.** Claude Code's own cost figure guesses prices for a name it doesn't know (a test request it showed as $0.038 cost $0.0096). The gateway's numbers (My usage page, `meritorder usage`) are the real ones. - **Reply length.** For a model name it doesn't know, Claude Code asks for up to 32,000 output tokens per reply. `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` raises it (to 128,000 at most); Merit Order lowers a request to the chosen model's own maximum when that's smaller. - **Effort.** Claude Code sends its own reasoning effort (its `/effort` setting), and a client's setting always wins, so the per-level effort (section 6) doesn't apply to its turns. - **A startup line** `[claude-code:unrecognized_model] {"model":"auto"}` is informational. - **Subagents** each get their own routing thread within the session (section 5), and their own level. **pi** gets a "Merit Order" provider listing `auto` and every model with its context window, sends its session id so sessions stay on the backend that holds their cache, and adds cache markers that survive translation. **Codex CLI** and other OpenAI-compatible tools need only the base URL (`/v1`) and the key. ## 12. Where everything is set | What | Where in the console | In the config file | |---|---|---| | Quality source, scale, reference, refresh | Config → Routing → Quality scores | `quality:` | | A model's score override, its name in benchmark data | Config → Models | `quality_override`, `benchmark_name` | | The name that means "choose for me" | Config → Routing → Automatic routing | `routing.auto_model` | | How much cheaper a move must be | Config → Routing → Automatic routing | `routing.switch_margin_pct`, `switch_margin_usd` | | Expected turns and tokens per turn | Config → Routing → Automatic routing | `routing.min_expected_turns`, `est_output_tokens`, … | | Cost or speed | Config → Routing → Cost or speed; Config → Teams | `routing.priority`, team `priority` | | Effort by level | Config → Routing → Reasoning effort by task difficulty | `routing.effort_by_floor` | | Levels for Claude Code's side and compaction requests | Config → Routing → Claude Code request types | `routing.request_class_levels` | | GPU price curve | Config → Routing → Self-hosted pricing curve | `routing.shadow_knee`, `shadow_floor` | | Which models and providers a team may use | Config → Teams | `allowed_models`, `allowed_backends` | | Budgets, per-request cost limit | Controls; Config → Teams | `safeguards`, team budgets | | Routes, prices you've negotiated | Config → Models | `routes[].price` (an override) | | Context windows, output limits | live price data (Models page) | `context_window`, `max_output_tokens` (overrides) | | GPU deployments | Config → Backends; GPUs page | `backends.*.serve` | | How requests get a level | not yet in the console | `classifier.py` | | Pointing Claude Code or pi at the gateway | — | `meritorder setup claude-code` / `setup pi` | The Models page shows every model's live scores, prices and windows, with where each came from; Backends shows each route's measured speed and anything being skipped. ## 13. What `auto` does today The cheapest qualifying model for a typical request at each level, on 11 November 2026: | Level | Coding | General | |---|---|---| | 1 | GLM-5.3 Flash, gpt-oss-20b | GLM-5.3 Flash, gpt-oss-20b | | 2 | DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | | 3 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Terra | | 4 | GPT-6.1 Terra | GPT-6.1 Sol | | 5 | Claude Fable 5.2 only | Claude Fable 5.2 only | A Claude Code session on `auto` is coding level 4 (it always sends many tools): GPT-6.1 Terra, until the conversation passes 60,000 tokens and it becomes level 5 (Fable) at the next prompt. Its titles and summaries go to level-1 models, and compaction summaries to level-3 models. ## 14. Known gaps - **The level rules aren't in the console,** and they're keyword-based. A coding agent sending `auto` with more than 60,000 tokens of context lands on level 5, which today only Fable meets, at $8/$40 per million tokens. Clients that name a model aren't affected. - **Some scores are estimates.** A model without published coding results gets a coding score from its general ability (marked * on the Models page), and published results come from runs at different efforts. - **A threshold, not cost per solved task.** A cheaper model that solves a little less can still cost less per solved task than a dearer one. Merit Order now has each model's chance of solving hard work, so it could pick on expected cost per success; today it picks the cheapest model above the level, which is simpler to predict. - **Token counts for routing are estimates** (about 4 characters per token), so the window check can be off near the limit; a provider's "too long" is the backstop (section 7).
