# Merit Order

An open-source LLM gateway that cuts LLM spend for day-to-day use, without changing how
people work.

Power grids dispatch generators in **merit order**: cheapest marginal cost first, with expensive
peaker plants switched on only when demand requires them. Merit Order does the same with tokens:

- **Routes** every session to the cheapest model and backend that meets the task's quality bar,
  counting what it would cost to rebuild the prompt cache somewhere else.
- **Runs open-weight models on your own GPUs** (via SkyPilot) when steady load makes that cheaper
  than paying per token, and turns them off when it doesn't. APIs (Bedrock, Foundry, Vertex,
  Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Mistral, ...) are always there for overflow.
- **Saves tokens**: automatic prompt caching, sticky sessions, cache-safe compression of huge tool
  outputs, and an optional response cache.
- **Shows the money**: every request is recorded with what it cost and what it would have cost
  without Merit Order, broken down by cause, per user, team, project, and day.

Point Claude Code, pi, OpenAI or Anthropic SDKs, or anything that speaks either API at it.

## Quickstart (no keys needed)

```bash
uv sync
cp .env.example .env            # set MERITORDER_DEV_KEY (and any provider keys you have)
uv run meritorder serve         # http://localhost:8080, reports UI at /ui/
```

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $MERITORDER_DEV_KEY" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]}'
```

With no provider keys, requests go to built-in mock backends. `uv run meritorder check` shows
which backends and models are live with the keys you've set. Without `MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL`,
storage is in memory; use Docker Compose for the real thing.

## Run the full stack with Docker

```bash
cp .env.example .env            # add at least one provider key
docker compose up -d            # gateway + worker + Postgres + Redis on :8080
docker compose exec gateway meritorder keys create --user you@example.com --role admin
```

Bedrock with your AWS profile (including SSO): `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.aws.yaml up -d`.
Kubernetes: `helm install mo charts/meritorder` (see [docs/07-deployment.md](docs/07-deployment.md)).

## Point your harness at it

```bash
meritorder login --gateway https://llm.example.com   # Entra sign-in; or: meritorder use-key <key>
meritorder setup pi                                    # adds a "meritorder" provider to pi
meritorder setup claude-code                           # sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL + apiKeyHelper
```

Or by hand: OpenAI-compatible clients use base URL `<gateway>/v1`; Claude Code uses
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=<gateway>`. Use `model: "auto"` to let Merit Order choose, or name a model
(`claude-sonnet`, `kimi-k3.1`, `qwen3-coder`, `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, ...) to pin it.

| Header | Effect |
|---|---|
| `X-Session-Id` | Groups requests into a session (pi sends it; otherwise inferred) |
| `X-Route-Floor: coding:4` | Minimum quality for `auto` routing |
| `X-Route-Hint: cheap` / `smart` | Nudges `auto` routing down or up |
| `X-MeritOrder-Tags: project=foo` | Cost-allocation tags for reports |
| `X-MeritOrder-Cache: on` / `off` | Use or bypass the response cache |
| `X-MeritOrder-Backend: <name>` | Admins only: pin a backend (testing, debugging) |

Responses carry `x-meritorder-model`, `x-meritorder-backend`, and (non-streaming)
`x-meritorder-cost-usd` / `x-meritorder-savings-usd`.

## What's in the box

| Area | Built |
|---|---|
| APIs | OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses (stateless), Anthropic Messages, and embeddings; streaming and not; pass-through when formats match, translation when they don't |
| Backends | Anthropic, Claude in Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, OpenRouter (incl. opt-in free tier), DeepSeek, Mistral, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, any OpenAI-compatible server |
| Models | Claude, GPT, and an open-weight catalog: DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen3-Coder, MiniMax, MiMo, Muse, Mistral/Devstral, Gemma, Nemotron, gpt-oss |
| Routing | Rule-based classifier → quality floor; marginal-cost router with cache rebuild cost, context-window checks, sticky sessions, fallback across backends |
| GPUs | Break-even controller (addressable demand, hysteresis), SkyPilot/SkyServe + vLLM provisioner, static servers, utilization from vLLM metrics, spill to API when saturated |
| Savings | Automatic prompt caching, lower reasoning effort for simple `auto` tasks (stable per session), deterministic tool-output compression, opt-in response cache |
| Identity | Virtual API keys, Entra/OIDC device-code login with group → team/role mapping, roles (user, team lead, finance, admin), People page to move, pin, or disable anyone (applies to existing keys within a minute) |
| Spend | Team and user monthly budgets, per-session spend caps (stops runaway agents), requests/tokens-per-minute limits, policy allow/deny lists for models and backends |
| Control panel | Web console at `/ui/` (Mantine, dark by default): live Dispatch view (merit-order stack from real traffic, live request feed, backend health, GPU fleet, needs-attention), Reports, GPUs (incl. what-if), Backends, Models, Teams, People, Keys, and Config (forms for teams, models, backends, routing, and access plus raw YAML; validate, version history, restore; hot-reloads every gateway) |
| Reporting | Ledger with savings by cause, reports API, CSV, JSONL/CSV ledger export to a file or S3, `meritorder usage`, Prometheus metrics, budget/spike alerts, weekly digests |
| Deployment | Docker Compose, Helm chart, CI (tests, audits, Helm lint, Compose smoke test), signed multi-arch releases |

Not yet: billing reconciliation against provider invoices, Kubernetes-native GPU provisioning
(llm-d/KServe), a learned router, OpenTelemetry traces. See [docs/](docs/README.md) for the design.

## Development

```bash
uv sync && uv run pytest                     # gateway
cd ui && npm ci && npm run build             # reporting UI (served at /ui/)
uv run python scripts/fake_vllm.py           # a stand-in vLLM server for the GPU path
uv run python scripts/smoke_providers.py     # test every enabled provider through a running gateway
```

## License

AGPL-3.0-only. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

# 11 — Evals: measuring model quality

`auto` routing sends each request to the cheapest model good enough for it. "Good enough" comes from
each model's **quality scores**: 1–5 per task type (coding, general). The classifier gives every
request a floor (coding:3 for ordinary coding, coding:4 for agent work with many tools, +1 for hard
tasks or large contexts), and only models scoring at least that are considered. Scores that are too
high send hard work to models that can't do it; scores that are too low waste money. Evals measure
them.

## Running one

**From the console:** Models → **Evals** → *Run an eval…*. Pick models and suites, see the
estimated cost, and start it. The worker runs it in the background, against the gateway like any
client. Progress, cost, and every task's result show on the page. When it finishes, *Apply
scores…* writes the measured scores into the configuration as a new version, which you can roll
back from Config → History. *Run again…* repeats a run with the same settings.

**From the command line** (on a machine with Docker, so code tasks run too):

```bash
uv run meritorder eval --models claude-sonnet,claude-opus,claude-fable          # estimates cost, asks first
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --only 'c5-*,a5-*' --repeat 3               # just the hardest coding work, 3 times each
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --apply                                      # also write the scores into the config
```

CLI runs are recorded too, so they appear on the Evals page, and cancelling one there stops it.

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `--suite` | `starter,frontier` | Built-in suites, task directories or YAML files, comma-separated |
| `--only` | all tasks | Task id patterns, e.g. `c5-*,g4-*` |
| `--repeat` | 1 | Runs per task. More runs mean less luck in the scores, at proportional cost |
| `--judges` | `claude-opus,gpt-terra` | Models that grade open-ended tasks (those with a live route) |
| `--sandbox` | `docker` | `none` skips tasks that run model-written code |
| `--threshold` | 0.75 | Pass rate a model needs at a level to earn it |

Eval traffic goes through the gateway with its usual budgets, rate limits and per-request cap, and is
tagged `eval=<suite>-<time>` in the ledger. Its spend counts like any other (for the person who ran it,
their team, the models, and the organization), and Reports → Breakdown → **Tag** → `eval` shows each
run's cost on its own line. It isn't counted as savings: a run on Haiku isn't money saved and one on
Fable isn't money lost, because you'd have run those models anyway, so its baseline is the model it
ran. Runs from the console use
a temporary key for the person who started them, revoked when the run ends.

## How each model is run

A comparison is only fair if nothing but the model differs, so a run fixes everything else and records it:

- **No output limit.** Requests set no `max_tokens`, so each model may write as much as it can
  (`max_output_tokens`: 128,000 for current Claude and GPT models), thinking included. A reply that
  fills the model's own maximum fails and is marked *cut off*. The per-request cost limit on Controls
  still applies: if it stops a reply first, the result is *not graded* (left out of the scores) and
  says how many tokens it allowed, so you can raise the limit and run it again. At $40 per million
  output tokens, Fable's full 128,000 costs $5.12.
- **The same effort.** Each task runs at the reasoning effort `auto` uses for its level
  (`routing.effort_by_floor`: low for 1–2, medium for 3, high for 4–5), not at each model's own
  default, which differs (Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 default to medium, Fable and Sonnet to high).
  A model that doesn't take that effort runs at its default. A task can set its own (`effort: max`).
- **One route per model.** Each model runs on its first live route, which in the shipped config is
  its own provider's API, rather than whichever reseller the router finds cheapest or fastest that
  minute. Judges too.
- **Answers are kept.** Each result keeps what the model wrote (the first 60,000 characters), an
  agent's tool calls in order, and each judge's verdict and reason on every rubric point. Click a
  result on the Evals page to read them, for instance to see which judge was right when they
  disagree.

Long replies take a while: 100,000 tokens is 15–20 minutes on the largest models. The gateway streams
from the provider meanwhile, so nothing times out.

## The suites

| Suite | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `starter` | 24 short tasks, levels 1–5: facts, arithmetic, one tool call, small code questions. Cheap; strong models max it out |
| `frontier` | 32 hard tasks at levels 3–5, built so strong models separate from the very top: 12 code tasks with 14–48 hidden tests each (an interpreter with tail calls, a regex engine matching Python's, unified diffs, recurrence rules, cron, a streaming JSON tokenizer…), 6 multi-step tool tasks (fixing bugs in small repositories, a purchase with traps, revenue from a messy database, an incident's root cause), and 14 general tasks (multi-hop questions over documents of 6k–45k words, logic grids, exact combinatorics, writing under constraints, and 3 judged pieces of open-ended work) |

Levels mean what the classifier means by them: 3 is ordinary coding, analysis or long context;
4 is agent work with many tools, or hard reasoning; 5 is the hardest of both.

## Four kinds of task

| Kind | The model gets | Graded by |
|---|---|---|
| `answer` | One prompt | Mechanical checks: an exact final answer (`Final answer: …`), a number, JSON fields, a tool call, or writing constraints (word count, bullets, required phrases) |
| `code` | A precise spec for a Python module | Hidden unit tests, run against its code in a sandbox. Every test must pass |
| `agent` | A goal and tools | A scripted environment answers the tools (a small repository, a booking API, a database, logs), then checks the end state: the right fix with stricter hidden tests, the right booking made once, the exact figure |
| `judged` | Open-ended work (a summary, a critique, a recommendation) | Two judge models from different families, against a rubric of concrete statements and a reference answer. Both must agree every point is met |

**Why two judges from different families.** A model tends to rate answers like its own higher. The
judges don't know which model wrote the answer, every criterion is a checkable statement ("states
the outage lasted 47 minutes"), and an answer passes only if a Claude judge and a GPT judge both say
every criterion is met. Their reasons are kept with the result. Everything else is graded
mechanically, which is cheaper and repeatable.

**The sandbox.** Model-written code runs in a throwaway Docker container (`python:3.12-slim`):
no network, a read-only filesystem apart from a small `/tmp`, an unprivileged user, no
capabilities, and limits on memory, CPU, processes and time. Each hidden test also has its own
CPU-time limit (10 s), so one runaway loop fails that test, not the whole task. A task can forbid
imports (the regex task forbids `re`); that's checked in the code's syntax tree, which keeps honest
solutions honest but wouldn't stop code written to get around it. Without Docker, those tasks are skipped
and the results say so. The worker in the Docker Compose stack has no Docker access by default, so
console runs skip code tasks there: run those with `meritorder eval` on a machine with Docker, and
their results land on the same page. (Giving a container the Docker socket gives it control of the
host, so it isn't on by default.)

## From results to scores

For each model and task type:

- **Score** (what routing uses): the highest level L where the model passes at least 75% of tasks at
  L **and every level below**. A model that aces level 5 but fails level 3 scores 2.
- **Ability** (0–5, shown next to it): the sum of its pass rates by level. Two models with the same
  score can differ a lot here; it's the finer view. A level the suite doesn't cover counts as the
  level below it did.
- **?**: at some level, there were too few task runs to be sure which side of 75% the model is on
  (its 90% confidence interval straddles 75%). Run again with `--repeat` to firm it up.

Beside the scores, each model shows what its tasks took, because two models that pass the same tasks
can still differ a lot in time and money:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Median time** (and 90th percentile) | The model's own time to complete a task: every request it answered, without grading, judges or the environment's tools |
| **Turns / tools** | Average requests and tool calls per task. An agent that needs 20 turns where another needs 6 is slower and costs more even at the same price per token |
| **Output** | Average output tokens per task, thinking included |
| **Per solve** | Cost divided by tasks passed: what a solved task costs on this model, which is what matters when choosing one |
| **Cut off** | Replies that hit an output limit |

Runs that say nothing about quality are skipped and don't count: no sandbox, no judges, a judge that
failed to give a verdict, a provider's rate limit or outage (HTTP 429 or 5xx), or a reply the
per-request cost limit stopped. Run again to fill them in. Other errors (a reply that fills the
model's maximum output or its context window, a request the model rejects) count as fails.

## Writing your own tasks

The best suite is made from your own work: a model that's good at public puzzles may still be wrong
for your codebase. A suite is a directory of task directories (or a YAML file of `answer` tasks).

```yaml
# my-suite/c4-invoice-rounding/task.yaml
id: c4-invoice-rounding
task: coding          # or general
level: 4
kind: code            # answer | code | agent | judged
prompt_file: prompt.md
code: {tests: tests.py, timeout: 30}   # hidden tests: top-level test_* functions; forbid: [re] bans imports
reference: reference.py                                    # a correct solution, never sent to models
```

- `answer`: `prompt` and `checks` (see `src/meritorder/evals/runner.py` → `grade`). Ask for
  `Final answer: …` on the last line and check it with `final`, `final_number` or `final_one_of`.
- `agent`: `env: module:Class`, `env_args`, `max_turns`. Environments subclass
  `meritorder.evals.envs.Env`: tools, `call`, and `grade`.
- `judged`: `rubric` (concrete statements) and `reference_answer`.
- Generated prompts (long documents built from a seed): `generate: module:function` with
  `generate_args`.
- Optional on any task: `effort` (instead of the level's) and `max_tokens` (only if you want the
  task to have a limit; built-in tasks don't).

Run it with `meritorder eval --suite ./my-suite`, or alongside the built-in ones:
`--suite starter,frontier,./my-suite`. Check every task offline before trusting it: the repository's
`tests/evals/` shows how (reference solutions pass the hidden tests, deliberately wrong ones fail).

**Public tasks leak.** Anything in a public repository can end up in a model's training data, which
makes it easier than it looks. Keep a private suite for the decisions that matter, and refresh it.

## Cost

The estimate before a run counts each task's prompt and a typical reply for every model, and
judging. Reasoning models often write several times more than that, and with no output limit a hard
task can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so treat it as a rough guide.
Long-document and agent tasks dominate: a level-5 document task sends about 60k tokens, and an agent
task resends its growing conversation every turn. Organization and personal budgets and the
per-request cap (Controls) apply to eval traffic like any other.

"""Free time in a working day."""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Iterable

from .intervals import Interval, clip, merge

DAY_START = 9 * 60
DAY_END = 17 * 60


def free_slots(busy: Iterable[Interval], day_start: int = DAY_START, day_end: int = DAY_END,
               min_length: int = 30) -> list[Interval]:
    """The free time between day_start and day_end, given busy intervals.

    Busy intervals may overlap, touch, or reach outside the working day. Returns the gaps between busy time as sorted
    Intervals inside [day_start, day_end); gaps shorter than min_length minutes are left out.
    """
    free = []
    cursor = day_start
    for block in merge(clip(busy, day_start, day_end)):
        if block.start > cursor:
            free.append(Interval(cursor, block.start))
        cursor = block.end
    if cursor < day_end:
        free.append(Interval(cursor, day_end))
    return [slot for slot in free if slot.length >= min_length]


def first_free(busy: Iterable[Interval], length: int, day_start: int = DAY_START, day_end: int = DAY_END) -> Interval | None:
    """The earliest free slot of exactly ``length`` minutes, or None if there's no room."""
    for slot in free_slots(busy, day_start, day_end, min_length=length):
        return Interval(slot.start, slot.start + length)
    return None

"""Alerts and weekly digests sent to a Slack/Teams/Discord-style incoming webhook.

* Budget thresholds: 80% and 100% of a team or user monthly budget (once per month each).
* Spend spikes: a user's last hour is 5x their usual hourly spend (usually an agent in a loop).
* Weekly digest per team: spend, baseline, and savings by cause (once per ISO week).
GPU state changes are sent by the capacity controller.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import os
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

import httpx

from .config import Config
from .store import month_start

log = logging.getLogger("meritorder.alerts")

THRESHOLDS = (0.8, 1.0)
SPIKE_FACTOR = 5.0
SPIKE_MIN_USD = 5.0


async def notify(text: str, url: str | None = None, state=None, title: str | None = None, level: str = "warning",
                 page: str | None = None, team: str | None = None) -> bool:
    """Log, show in the console's "needs attention" list, and send to the webhook if one is set."""
    url = url or os.environ.get("MERITORDER_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL")
    log.warning("ALERT: %s", text)
    if state is not None:
        await state.push_alert({"ts": datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(), "level": level, "title": title or text[:80],
                                "text": text, "page": page, "team": team})
    if not url:
        return False
    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as c:
            r = await c.post(url, json={"text": text, "content": text})  # Slack/Teams use text, Discord content
        return r.status_code < 300
    except httpx.HTTPError as e:
        log.error("webhook failed: %s", e)
        return False


async def _once(state, key: str, ttl: int) -> bool:
    """True the first time a key is seen (dedupes alerts)."""
    if await state.get_json(key):
        return False
    await state.set_json(key, True, ttl)
    return True


async def check_budgets(cfg: Config, store, state, now: datetime | None = None) -> list[str]:
    now = now or datetime.now(UTC)
    start = month_start(now)
    month = now.strftime("%Y-%m")
    sent: list[str] = []
    by_team = {r["key"]: r["actual_cost"] for r in await store.summary(start, now + timedelta(days=1), "team")}
    for team in cfg.teams:
        if team.budget_usd_month:
            spent = by_team.get(team.name, 0.0)
            for t in THRESHOLDS:
                if spent >= team.budget_usd_month * t and await _once(state, f"alert:budget:{month}:team:{team.name}:{t}", 40 * 86400):
                    msg = f"Team '{team.name}' has used {spent / team.budget_usd_month:.0%} of its ${team.budget_usd_month:,.0f} monthly LLM budget (${spent:,.2f})."
                    await notify(msg, state=state, title=f"Team {team.name} at {t:.0%} of budget", page="teams", team=team.name,
                                 level="critical" if t >= 1 else "warning")
                    sent.append(msg)
        if team.user_budget_usd_month:
            for r in await store.summary(start, now + timedelta(days=1), "user", team=team.name):
                for t in THRESHOLDS:
                    if r["actual_cost"] >= team.user_budget_usd_month * t and await _once(
                            state, f"alert:budget:{month}:user:{r['key']}:{t}", 40 * 86400):
                        msg = f"{r['key']} ({team.name}) has used {r['actual_cost'] / team.user_budget_usd_month:.0%} of their ${team.user_budget_usd_month:,.0f} monthly budget."
                        await notify(msg, state=state, title=f"{r['key']} at {t:.0%} of personal budget", page="teams", team=team.name)
                        sent.append(msg)
    g = cfg.safeguards
    for label, budget, consequence in (("Organization", g.org_budget_usd_month, "requests are refused"),
                                       ("GPU", g.gpu_budget_usd_month, "GPUs drain and none start")):
        if not budget:
            continue
        spent = await store.spend_all_since(start) if label == "Organization" else sum((await store.gpu_spend_since(start)).values())
        for t in g.alert_at:
            if spent >= budget * t and await _once(state, f"alert:budget:{month}:{label}:{t}", 40 * 86400):
                msg = (f"{label} spend is at {spent / budget:.0%} of its ${budget:,.2f} monthly budget (${spent:,.2f})."
                       + (f" At 100%, {consequence}." if t < 1 else f" {consequence[0].upper()}{consequence[1:]} until the budget is raised or the month ends."))
                await notify(msg, state=state, title=f"{label} spend at {t:.0%} of budget", page="controls",
                             level="critical" if t >= 1 else "warning")
                sent.append(msg)
    return sent


async def check_spikes(store, state, now: datetime | None = None) -> list[str]:
    now = now or datetime.now(UTC)
    last_hour = {r["key"]: r["actual_cost"] for r in await store.summary(now - timedelta(hours=1), now, "user")}
    week = {r["key"]: r["actual_cost"] for r in await store.summary(now - timedelta(days=7, hours=1), now - timedelta(hours=1), "user")}
    sent: list[str] = []
    for user, spent in last_hour.items():
        usual = week.get(user, 0.0) / (7 * 24)
        if spent >= SPIKE_MIN_USD and spent >= SPIKE_FACTOR * max(usual, SPIKE_MIN_USD / SPIKE_FACTOR):
            if await _once(state, f"alert:spike:{user}:{now:%Y%m%d%H}", 2 * 3600):
                msg = (f"Spend spike: {user} spent ${spent:,.2f} in the last hour vs a usual ${usual:,.2f}/hour. "
                       f"An agent may be stuck in a loop.")
                await notify(msg, state=state, title=f"Spend spike: {user}", level="critical", page="reports")
                sent.append(msg)
    return sent


async def weekly_digest(cfg: Config, store, state, now: datetime | None = None, force: bool = False) -> list[str]:
    now = now or datetime.now(UTC)
    year, week, _ = now.isocalendar()
    if not force and not await _once(state, f"digest:{year}-W{week:02d}", 8 * 86400):
        return []
    start = now - timedelta(days=7)
    rows = {r["key"]: r for r in await store.summary(start, now, "team")}
    sent = []
    for team in sorted(rows):
        r = rows[team]
        causes = ", ".join(f"{c} ${r[f'savings_{c}']:,.2f}" for c in ("routing", "caching", "self_hosting", "compression", "response_cache") if r.get(f"savings_{c}"))
        saved = round(r["savings_total"], 2)
        if saved > 0:
            verdict = f"Saved ${saved:,.2f}" + (f" ({causes})." if causes else ".")
        elif saved < 0:
            verdict = (f"Cost ${-saved:,.2f} more than the baseline ({causes}): requested models pricier than the baseline, "
                       "or prompt-cache writes not yet read back." if causes else f"Cost ${-saved:,.2f} more than the baseline.")
        else:
            verdict = "No savings this week."
        msg = (f"Weekly LLM spend for '{team}': ${r['actual_cost']:,.2f} across {r['requests']} requests. "
               f"Without Merit Order: ${r['baseline_cost']:,.2f}. {verdict}")
        await notify(msg, state=state, title=f"Weekly digest: {team}", level="info", page="reports", team=team)
        sent.append(msg)
    return sent

# 06 — Auth & spend ## Getting a key into pi and Claude Code Harnesses can't do interactive SSO, so people log in once with the CLI and get a short-lived **virtual key** tied to their identity. The harness sends it like any API key. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor U as User participant CLI as meritorder CLI participant E as Entra ID (OIDC) participant G as Gateway participant P as Postgres U->>CLI: meritorder login CLI->>E: Device-code flow E-->>U: "Go to microsoft.com/devicelogin, enter code" U->>E: Signs in (MFA, conditional access) E-->>CLI: ID token (user, groups) CLI->>G: POST /auth/exchange G->>G: Verify JWT signature, issuer, audience G->>P: Map groups → team and role G->>P: Create virtual key (expires in 30 days) G-->>CLI: Virtual key CLI->>CLI: Save to ~/.config/meritorder/api_key (mode 600) U->>CLI: meritorder setup pi / setup claude-code ``` ```bash meritorder login --gateway https://llm.example.com # or: meritorder use-key meritorder setup pi # adds a "meritorder" provider to ~/.pi/agent/models.json meritorder setup claude-code # points Claude Code at the gateway, starting sessions on auto meritorder setup claude-code --config-dir ~/.claude-meritorder # …in a separate Claude Code profile ``` Both harness configs read the key from `~/.config/meritorder/api_key` at request time (`!cat ...` for pi, `apiKeyHelper` for Claude Code), so logging in again rotates the key without touching them. pi is configured to send its session ID as `X-Session-Id` and to add cache breakpoints, which Merit Order uses for sticky routing and caching. `setup claude-code` writes to Claude Code's settings file: `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json` when that's set, else `~/.claude/settings.json`, or the folder given with `--config-dir` (then start Claude Code with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR= claude`). It sets: | Setting | Value | |---|---| | `env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | the gateway | | `apiKeyHelper` | `cat ~/.config/meritorder/api_key` | | `model` | `auto` (`--model ` for another model `/v1/models` lists for your key; `--model none` leaves Claude Code's choice) | | `env.CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS` | the gateway's context window for that model (from `/v1/models`; for `auto`, the largest among the models `auto` can pick for your key), so Claude Code doesn't assume 200,000 for a name it doesn't know | | `env.ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION`, `…_NAME` | `auto`, "auto (Merit Order)": adds it to the `/model` picker | | `env.CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS` | `1`: Claude Code labels side requests and compaction summaries only when asked; Merit Order caps their level (`routing.request_class_levels`) | For a Claude model name (`claude-…`) the window and picker entries are left out (Claude Code knows those models) and removed if an earlier setup added them. The previous file is kept as `settings.json.bak`. With the Merit Order key, Claude Code's requests don't use a claude.ai login: subscription limits don't apply, and spend is counted here like any other key's. How the gateway knows who's calling: every request carries a key (`Authorization: Bearer` or `x-api-key`). The gateway hashes it, looks it up (cached for a minute), and gets the user, team, and role, which drive budgets, policy, and reports. Unknown, revoked, or expired keys get a 401. | Client | Auth | |---|---| | People with harnesses | `meritorder login` → virtual key (above) | | Services / apps | An Entra token directly as the bearer token, or a key from `meritorder keys create` | | Local dev / quickstart | `MERITORDER_DEV_KEY` (static admin key from the environment) | | Google (later) | Another OIDC issuer: same code path | Entra login switches on when `MERITORDER_OIDC_ISSUER` and `MERITORDER_OIDC_CLIENT_ID` are set; map Entra group IDs to teams and roles in `auth.oidc` in the config. SCIM provisioning (below) disables people when they leave. ## People and teams | What | Where it's managed | |---|---| | Who exists, and their group membership | Your identity provider (Entra). People are created in Merit Order the first time they sign in with `meritorder login`, when they're issued a key, or when Entra provisions them through SCIM. | | Teams, with budgets, limits, and model policy | Merit Order: Config → Teams. An IdP has no notion of "$5,000 a month, these models only". | | Which team and role someone gets | Entra groups mapped to teams and roles in Config → Access, re-read at each sign-in. | | Exceptions | The People page: an admin can move someone or change their role (either pins team and role, so later sign-ins and SCIM don't override them), let Entra decide again, set a monthly limit, or disable them. | The user record, not the key, decides a person's team and role. Moving or disabling someone takes effect within a minute on every gateway, including keys they already have. For the same reason, a team lead can issue keys only for themselves, for new people, or for people on their own team with the user role; keys for anyone else (another team, a lead, an admin) need an admin. | Role | Sees | Can change | |---|---|---| | user | Their own usage | Nothing (`meritorder login` gets them a new key) | | team lead | Their team: reports, requests, ledger export | Keys on their team (they issue only `user` keys) | | finance | Every team, aggregated (no per-request rows or exports) | Nothing | | admin | Everything | Everything | **SCIM provisioning** (`/scim/v2`, enabled by `MERITORDER_SCIM_TOKEN`): Entra pushes people and group changes as they happen. A person's own limit replaces the per-person default ([Budgets](#budgets)) | | `max_session_usd` | Stops one session (typically an agent stuck in a loop) once it has spent this much. A Claude Code session's subagents and side requests count toward it | | `rate_limits: {user_rpm, user_tpm, team_rpm, team_tpm}` | Requests and prompt tokens per minute; 429 with `Retry-After` | ## Organization-wide safeguards Hard limits for everyone, set under `safeguards:` or on the console's **Controls** page (which shows each one next to this month's spend and the pace it's on, and saves changes as a new config version). A blank or unset variable means no limit. These are the fastest stop there is: they act on the gateway's own ledger, request by request. Cloud budgets (AWS Budgets, Azure Cost Management) see spend hours later, and on their own only send email, so treat them as a backstop for anything that doesn't go through the gateway. | Setting | What it does | |---|---| | `org_budget_usd_month` | All spend in the ledger. At 100% every request is refused until the month ends or it's raised | | `gpu_budget_usd_month` | GPU time (replicas × hourly price). At 100% running GPUs drain and none start, pins included | | `max_gpu_usd_per_hour` | Burn-rate cap for the whole GPU fleet; deployments whose demand best covers their cost get capacity first | | `max_gpu_replicas` | Replica cap across all deployments | | `max_request_usd` | Per request. # 08 — Reporting Merit Order exists to save money, so reporting is a core feature: what was spent, what was saved, why, by whom, and when. ## Data flow ```mermaid flowchart LR gw["Gateway"] -- "one row per request (async)" --> ledger[("Ledger
Postgres, monthly partitions")] ctl["Capacity controller"] -- "GPU hours, utilization" --> roll ledger --> roll["Rollup worker"] roll --> agg[("Hourly + daily rollups
by user, team, tag,
model, backend")] roll --> alerts["Alerts
budgets, spend spikes,
break-even changes"] agg --> api["Reports API"] ledger --> api api --> ui["Web UI"] api --> cli["meritorder usage"] api --> exp["CSV / Parquet exports"] api --> dig["Scheduled digests
email, Slack, Teams"] bills["Provider billing exports
AWS, GCP, Azure"] --> recon["Monthly reconciliation"] agg --> recon gw -. "Prometheus / OpenTelemetry" .-> mon["Grafana, Datadog, ..."] ``` Reports never contain prompt or response content. The ledger holds metadata only. ## Savings numbers have to stand up to scrutiny If finance finds one inflated number, they stop trusting the whole dashboard. So: **1. A baseline per team.** "What you'd have done without Merit Order", set in config: ```yaml teams: platform: baseline_model: claude-sonnet # API at list price, no proxy-added caching pricing_overrides: bedrock: { discount_pct: 12 } # negotiated / committed-spend discount ``` **2. Savings broken down by cause, never one blended number.** Causes are computed in a fixed order, each against the result of the previous step, so they add up exactly to the total with no double counting: | Order | Cause | How it's counted | |---|---|---| | 1 | **Routing** | Baseline model's API cost − served model's API cost | | 2 | **Self-hosting** | Served model's API cost − chargeback cost on our GPUs | | 3 | **Prompt caching** | Discount from cache breakpoints *we added*, minus cache-write premiums we paid. Caching the harness set up itself would have happened anyway and isn't counted. | | 4 | **Compression** | Tokens removed × served model's input price | | 5 | **Response cache** | Full cost of each request answered from cache | **3. Two headline numbers, side by side:** savings against list price, and savings caused by Merit Order. **4. Negotiated prices.** Per-provider discounts and price overrides, so costs match what the organization actually pays. **5. Monthly reconciliation.** Compare our computed cost with providers' billing exports (AWS Cost and Usage Reports, GCP billing export, Azure Cost Management) and report the difference. ## What's tracked | Area | Metrics | |---|---| | **Spend** | Actual cost by user, team, project tag, API key, model, provider, backend, time; burn rate; month-end forecast | | **Savings** | Total and by cause (above), over time | | **GPU fleet** | GPU hours and cost, utilization, effective $/M tokens vs API equivalent, break-even status per model, cold starts, overflow rate | | **Routing** | Model mix, free-upgrade rate, quality floor distribution, harness overrides | | **Caching** | Cache hit rate per backend, sessions that switched backends, rebuild cost paid | | **Operations** | Time to first token, tokens/s, error rate per backend | | **Budgets** | Users and teams near limits, soft and hard limit events | ## Views | View | Audience | Shows | |---|---|---| | **Executive summary** | Leadership, finance | Spend vs savings over time, savings by cause, forecast | | **Team chargeback** | Finance, team leads | Monthly cost per team and project tag, exportable | | **My usage** | Every user | Own spend, models used, budget remaining | | **GPU fleet** | Platform team | Per-model break-even, utilization, cost per token | | **Routing and caching** | Platform team | Where traffic went and why, cache efficiency | ## Who sees what Roles come from Entra (or OIDC) group membership. | Role | Can see | |---|---| | User | Their own usage | | Team lead | Their team's usage, per user | | Finance | All spend and savings, no per-request detail | | Admin | Everything | ## Ways to get reports - **Web UI** with the views above. - **Reports API.** The UI is built on it, so anyone can build their own views. - **CLI:** `meritorder usage` for a quick look at your own spend. - **Exports:** CSV, and Parquet to S3 / GCS / Blob storage for data warehouses and BI tools. - **Scheduled digests** to email, Slack, or Teams (e.g. weekly per team). - **Alerts:** budget thresholds, **spend spikes** (a user suddenly at 5× normal usually means an agent stuck in a loop), and a model's GPU break-even status flipping. - **Metrics:** Prometheus and OpenTelemetry, plus a ready-made Grafana dashboard. ## Cost allocation tags Requests can carry tags, and API keys can have default tags: ``` X-MeritOrder-Tags: project=checkout-rewrite,ticket=PLAT-1234 ``` Tags flow into the ledger and every report can group by them. ## Storage and scale - The ledger is a Postgres table partitioned by month. - A rollup worker keeps hourly and daily summary tables current. Dashboards read the summaries, not the raw ledger. - Postgres comfortably handles the millions of requests per month a $100k+/month organization generates. ClickHouse can be an optional backend for very large deployments. - We don't build a general-purpose BI tool. Ad-hoc analysis goes through the exports. ## What's built and what isn't yet | Piece | Status | |---|---| | Ledger, hourly rollups (`meritorder worker`, `--backfill`) | Built | | Savings by cause, baseline per team, negotiated prices (`price:` per route) | Built | | Reports API (`/v1/reports/summary`, `summary.csv`, `me`, `requests`, `gpu`) with role scoping | Built | | Web UI at `/ui/` (React/TypeScript): Overview, Breakdown (team, user, model, backend, tag), Requests, GPUs, Keys, Models, My usage | Built | | `meritorder usage` | Built | | Prometheus `/metrics` (requests, tokens, cost, baseline, savings by cause, latency histogram) | Built | | Alerts (budget 80%/100%, spend spikes, GPU state changes) and Monday digests to a webhook | Built (`MERITORDER_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL`) | | Ledger export: `/v1/reports/export.jsonl`, `meritorder export --out file.csv` or `s3://bucket/key` | Built | | Parquet export | Not yet (JSONL/CSV load into every warehouse) | | Monthly reconciliation against provider billing exports | Not yet | | ClickHouse backend for very large deployments | Not yet | The UI is a small React/TypeScript app (no charting library; hand-written SVG) built into the Python package and served by the gateway. It signs in with a Merit Order API key and shows what that key's role may see.

# Shifts change on Sunday instead of Monday; weekly report off for Sundays; add handoff_hour

## Bug

Since the move to the new scheduler, shifts change at Sunday 00:00 UTC instead of Monday 00:00 UTC.
Example: rotation ["ana", "ben", "chen"] starting 2026-03-02 (a Monday). On Sunday 2026-03-08 at 10:00
the pager goes to ben, but ana's week runs until Monday 2026-03-09 00:00.

The weekly hours export (`report.weekly_hours`) is wrong too: hours on a Sunday are counted in the
following week.

Suggested fix from #ops: "just add `+ timedelta(days=1)` in Rotation, like report.py already does".
Nobody has checked this; please find the real cause.

## Feature: handoff_hour

Teams want handoffs during working hours. Add an optional `handoff_hour`: an `int` from 0 to 23,
default 0.

- `Rotation(members, start, length_days=7, handoff_hour=0)`: every handoff happens at `handoff_hour:00`
  UTC instead of midnight. The first shift starts at `handoff_hour:00` on the Monday of the ISO week
  that contains `start`; asking about an earlier time raises ValueError, as it does today. Any other
  value than an int from 0 to 23 raises ValueError.
- `config.load_rotation` accepts an optional `"handoff_hour"` key with the same rules; invalid values
  raise ValueError naming the field, like the other fields.
- `report.weekly_hours` keeps counting hours per calendar week (Monday 00:00 UTC), whatever the handoff
  hour.
- `pager.escalation`: the backup is still whoever has the next shift.

Keep the public API backwards compatible.

# Changelog

## 0.1.0 (unreleased)

First release.

**Gateway**
- OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses, Anthropic Messages, and embeddings; pass-through or
  translation between the formats, streaming included.
- Backends: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI,
  OpenRouter, direct open-model vendors (DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, Mistral), and any
  OpenAI-compatible server. Keyless on Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure with workload identity.
- Works unchanged with pi, Claude Code, and the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs (`meritorder setup`).

**Routing**
- Rule-based classifier sets a quality floor; a marginal-cost router picks the backend, counting the
  cost of rebuilding a session's prompt cache before moving it.
- GPUs priced by how busy they are (near free with headroom), so spare GPU capacity is used first.
- Routes that cost about the same go to the faster one, measured from real replies (time to first
  token and tokens per second). The `balanced` and `speed` priorities pay up to 20% or 100% more for
  a faster route, set per organization, team, or request (`X-MeritOrder-Priority`).
- Failover catches errors that arrive after a `200` (Anthropic's in-stream overload, OpenRouter error
  chunks) and streams that never start. Over capacity skips just that model on that backend, for the
  provider's `Retry-After`. Outage and recovery alerts go to the webhook, and responses say what they
  failed over from.
- Evals that separate the strongest models: a `frontier` suite of hard tasks (code checked by hidden
  tests in a Docker sandbox, multi-step tool use against scripted environments, long documents,
  exact-answer reasoning, and open-ended work graded by two judges from different model families).
  Scores come with a finer 0–5 ability figure and a flag where evidence is thin. Run them from the
  console's new Models → Evals page (estimate, progress, cancel, per-task results, apply scores as a
  config version) or with `meritorder eval`; both land in the same history.
- Outage alerts name the model's other live backends ("Requests go to anthropic, openrouter meanwhile"), even when the
  failing request was pinned to one backend. A model missing on a backend (404) is retried after 5 minutes, then
  less and less often up to hourly. Bedrock and Foundry can be switched off in `.env` until their models exist.
- Refusal fallback and automatic reasoning effort for `auto`; opt-in substitution for named
  models that have nowhere to run (never to a weaker model).
- A saturated GPU spills to other routes, and queues (bounded) only when it's the last resort.

**GPUs**
- Capacity controller starts and stops SkyPilot/SkyServe + vLLM deployments when demand pays for
  them, with SkyPilot catalog prices, hysteresis, and fleet-wide caps.
- Console controls: stop (drain or now), pin replicas, stop all; activity log; where each replica
  runs, uptime, burn rate, and cost.

**Models (as of November 10, 2026)**
- Claude Fable 5.2 ($8/$40), Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5; GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra and
  GPT-6 Luna (the `gpt-terra` and `gpt-luna` names now point at the current models, and `gpt-5.6-*` names
  still resolve to them). Sonnet 5.5's cache reads are priced at $0.10 per million tokens (they were $0.20).

**Spend and savings**
- Budgets per organization, GPU fleet, team, person, and session; rate limits; per-request cost cap.
  Each person can have their own monthly limit (People page, admin API, or their static key) that
  replaces their team's per-person default.
  The shipped config reads the organization-wide caps from `.env` (`MERITORDER_ORG_BUDGET_USD` and
  friends), and `.env` comments at the end of a line are read the way Docker Compose reads them.
- Savings ledger by cause (routing, caching, self-hosting, compression, response cache) against a
  per-team baseline.
- GPT-5.6 tool calls through OpenAI work: its Chat Completions endpoint rejects function tools with
  reasoning, so the OpenAI backend sends requests to the Responses API (`api: responses`) and converts
  the replies back. Agents like Claude Code and pi can use GPT models with reasoning on.
- Claude through OpenRouter is prompt-cached (it wasn't: every turn paid full price), and the router
  prices cache writes on every route, so it no longer prefers a route only because it skipped the write.
- OpenRouter requests record what OpenRouter billed, not a catalog estimate: it picks among providers
  whose prices differ (catalog prices were up to 56% low in testing). `billed_cost` sets this per backend.
- Every setting on the console's Config page explains itself: a "?" beside each field (hover, keyboard
  focus, or tap) says what it does and its default. The forms also cover the OpenAI endpoint, the
  first-token timeout, cost-or-speed priority, static-key monthly limits, and GPU launch rules.
- Reports API and console, CSV/JSONL export (to S3), alerts and weekly digests to a webhook,
  Prometheus metrics with a Grafana dashboard, OpenTelemetry traces.

**Identity**
- Entra/OIDC sign-in exchanged for short-lived keys, groups mapped to teams and roles, SCIM
  provisioning; roles for users, team leads, finance, and admins.

**Operations**
- Docker Compose and a Helm chart (External Secrets, Reloader, zero-restart key rotation, workload
  identity). Configuration versions in Postgres, edited in the console, followed by every process.
- Signed multi-arch images with an SBOM and provenance.

**Known limitations**
- Exercised against OpenRouter only (smoke tests, a Claude Code session, costs matched to its bill); not
  yet against other live provider accounts, a real cloud GPU, a real Entra tenant, or a
  production Kubernetes cluster: see `docs/README.md` for what's verified and how.
- Not built: reconciliation against provider bills, the native Gemini API, Kubernetes-native GPU
  provisioning, a learned router, provider batch APIs, model-based compression, Parquet export.

ENV_VARS = ("MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL", "MERITORDER_REDIS_URL", "MERITORDER_URL", "MERITORDER_API_KEY", "MERITORDER_WORKERS",
            "MERITORDER_CONFIG", "HF_TOKEN")


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def isolated(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    """No .env, no saved credentials, no database, no real home directory: commands see only what a test sets."""
    monkeypatch.setenv("MERITORDER_ENV_FILE", str(tmp_path / "missing.env"))
    for var in ENV_VARS:
        monkeypatch.setenv(var, "")  # recorded, so anything a command sets is undone afterwards
        monkeypatch.delenv(var)
    home = tmp_path / "cfg"
    monkeypatch.setattr(harness, "CONFIG_DIR", home)
    monkeypatch.setattr(harness, "KEY_FILE", home / "api_key")
    monkeypatch.setattr(harness, "CREDENTIALS", home / "credentials.json")

    monkeypatch.setenv("HOME", str(tmp_path / "home"))
    monkeypatch.setenv("PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR", str(tmp_path / "pi"))


def write_config(tmp_path, raw: dict | None = None):
    path = tmp_path / "meritorder.yaml"
    path.write_text(yaml.safe_dump(raw or TEST_CONFIG))
    return path


@pytest.fixture
def pg_store(monkeypatch):
    """An in-memory store standing in for Postgres (these commands refuse anything else)."""
    store = MemoryStore()
    store.kind = "postgres"

    return store


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ offline commands


def test_load_dotenv_keeps_existing_variables(tmp_path, monkeypatch):

    env.write_text("# comment\n\nMO_A=1\nMO_B=\"quoted\"\nMO_C='single'\nnot a pair\nMO_SET=from-file\nMO_EMPTY=\n")

def test_check_shows_usable_backends_and_models(tmp_path, capsys):

class LiveGateway:
    """A real gateway (in-memory storage, mock backends) served by uvicorn on a free port, in a thread."""

    def __init__(self, cfg):
        self.gw = build_gateway(cfg, store=MemoryStore(), state=MemoryState())
        self.gw.file_raw = copy.deepcopy(TEST_CONFIG)
        self.server = uvicorn.Server(uvicorn.Config(create_app(gateway=self.gw), host="127.0.0.1", port=0, log_level="warning", lifespan="off"))
        self.thread = threading.Thread(target=self.server.run, daemon=True)

    def __enter__(self):
        self.thread.start()
        deadline = time.monotonic() + 10
        while not self.server.started:
            assert time.monotonic() < deadline, "gateway did not start"
            time.sleep(0.02)
        self.url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.server.servers[0].sockets[0].getsockname()[1]}"
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        self.server.should_exit = True
        self.thread.join(10)

    def chat(self, n: int = 1, key: str = TEST_KEY, model: str = "small") -> None:
        before = len(self.gw.store.ledger)
        for _ in range(n):
            r = httpx.post(f"{self.url}/v1/chat/completions", headers={"authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
                           json={"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}, timeout=30)
            assert r.status_code == 200, r.text
        deadline = time.monotonic() + 5
        while len(self.gw.store.ledger) < before + n:  # ledger rows are written just after the response
            assert time.monotonic() < deadline
            time.sleep(0.01)

# Changelog

## 0.1.0 (unreleased)

First release.

**Gateway**
- OpenAI Chat Completions and Responses, Anthropic Messages, and embeddings; pass-through or
  translation between the formats, streaming included.
- Backends: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI,
  OpenRouter, direct open-model vendors (DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, Mistral), and any
  OpenAI-compatible server. Keyless on Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure with workload identity.
- Works unchanged with pi, Claude Code, and the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs (`meritorder setup`).

**Routing**
- Rule-based classifier sets a quality floor; a marginal-cost router picks the backend, counting the
  cost of rebuilding a session's prompt cache before moving it.
- GPUs priced by how busy they are (near free with headroom), so spare GPU capacity is used first.
- Routes that cost about the same go to the faster one, measured from real replies (time to first
  token and tokens per second). The `balanced` and `speed` priorities pay up to 20% or 100% more for
  a faster route, set per organization, team, or request (`X-MeritOrder-Priority`).
- Failover catches errors that arrive after a `200` (Anthropic's in-stream overload, OpenRouter error
  chunks) and streams that never start. Over capacity skips just that model on that backend, for the
  provider's `Retry-After`. Outage and recovery alerts go to the webhook, and responses say what they
  failed over from.
- Evals that separate the strongest models: a `frontier` suite of hard tasks (code checked by hidden
  tests in a Docker sandbox, multi-step tool use against scripted environments, long documents,
  exact-answer reasoning, and open-ended work graded by two judges from different model families).
  Scores come with a finer 0–5 ability figure and a flag where evidence is thin. Run them from the
  console's new Models → Evals page (estimate, progress, cancel, per-task results, apply scores as a
  config version) or with `meritorder eval`; both land in the same history.
- Outage alerts name the model's other live backends ("Requests go to anthropic, openrouter meanwhile"), even when the
  failing request was pinned to one backend. A model missing on a backend (404) is retried after 5 minutes, then
  less and less often up to hourly. Bedrock and Foundry can be switched off in `.env` until their models exist.
- Evals compare like with like: no output limit (each model may write as much as it can), every
  model at the same reasoning effort for a level, each on its own provider's API, and every answer,
  agent tool call and judge's reason kept for review. A reply cut off by the model's maximum fails
  and says so; one cut off by the per-request cost limit isn't graded. Runs also report what the
  work took: each model's median and 90th-percentile time to complete a task, turns and tool calls,
  output tokens, and cost per task solved. Agent tasks reach Claude over Anthropic's Messages API, as
  Claude Code does, so its thinking carries between tool calls (Chat Completions dropped it).
- No arbitrary output limits: a request without `max_tokens` may write as much as its model can
  (`max_output_tokens`, from the price catalog), less what won't fit in the context window or under
  the per-request cost limit, which now trims such a reply instead of using a 16,000-token guess.
  Non-streaming requests that may run long are streamed from the provider and assembled, so they
  don't time out. `auto` sends high reasoning effort for level 4–5 work (Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5
  default to medium).
- Refusal fallback and automatic reasoning effort for `auto`; opt-in substitution for named
  models that have nowhere to run (never to a weaker model).
- A saturated GPU spills to other routes, and queues (bounded) only when it's the last resort.

**GPUs**
- Capacity controller starts and stops SkyPilot/SkyServe + vLLM deployments when demand pays for
  them, with SkyPilot catalog prices, hysteresis, and fleet-wide caps.
- Console controls: stop (drain or now), pin replicas, stop all; activity log; where each replica
  runs, uptime, burn rate, and cost.

**Models (as of November 10, 2026)**
- Claude Fable 5.2 ($8/$40), Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5; GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra and
  GPT-6 Luna (the `gpt-terra` and `gpt-luna` names now point at the current models, and `gpt-5.6-*` names
  still resolve to them). Sonnet 5.5's cache reads are priced at $0.10 per million tokens (they were $0.20).
- Gemini 4 Carbon and 4 Argon ($2/$10 until November 30, 2026, then $4/$20), Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.5
  Flash-Lite, through OpenRouter. They have no quality scores until an eval measures them, so `auto`
  doesn't pick them yet; requests that name them work. Gemini's reasoning details (which its tool calls
  need sent back) survive replies the gateway assembles from a stream.

**Spend and savings**
- Budgets per organization, GPU fleet, team, person, and session; rate limits; per-request cost cap.
  Each person can have their own monthly limit (People page, admin API, or their static key) that
  replaces their team's per-person default.
  The shipped config reads the organization-wide caps from `.env` (`MERITORDER_ORG_BUDGET_USD` and
  friends), and `.env` comments at the end of a line are read the way Docker Compose reads them.
- Savings ledger by cause (routing, caching, self-hosting, compression, response cache) against a
  per-team baseline.
- GPT-5.6 tool calls through OpenAI work: its Chat Completions endpoint rejects function tools with
  reasoning, so the OpenAI backend sends requests to the Responses API (`api: responses`) and converts
  the replies back. Agents like Claude Code and pi can use GPT models with reasoning on.
- Claude through OpenRouter is prompt-cached (it wasn't: every turn paid full price), and the router
  prices cache writes on every route, so it no longer prefers a route only because it skipped the write.
- OpenRouter requests record what OpenRouter billed, not a catalog estimate: it picks among providers
  whose prices differ (catalog prices were up to 56% low in testing). `billed_cost` sets this per backend.
- Every setting on the console's Config page explains itself: a "?" beside each field (hover, keyboard
  focus, or tap) says what it does and its default. The forms also cover the OpenAI endpoint, the
  first-token timeout, cost-or-speed priority, static-key monthly limits, and GPU launch rules.
- Reports API and console, CSV/JSONL export (to S3), alerts and weekly digests to a webhook,
  Prometheus metrics with a Grafana dashboard, OpenTelemetry traces.

**Identity**
- Entra/OIDC sign-in exchanged for short-lived keys, groups mapped to teams and roles, SCIM
  provisioning; roles for users, team leads, finance, and admins.

**Operations**
- Docker Compose and a Helm chart (External Secrets, Reloader, zero-restart key rotation, workload
  identity). Configuration versions in Postgres, edited in the console, followed by every process.
- Signed multi-arch images with an SBOM and provenance.

**Known limitations**
- Exercised against OpenRouter only (smoke tests, a Claude Code session, costs matched to its bill); not
  yet against other live provider accounts, a real cloud GPU, a real Entra tenant, or a
  production Kubernetes cluster: see `docs/README.md` for what's verified and how.
- Not built: reconciliation against provider bills, the native Gemini API, Kubernetes-native GPU
  provisioning, a learned router, provider batch APIs, model-based compression, Parquet export.

# 04 — Caching & sessions ## Who owns what ```mermaid flowchart LR H["Harness
owns the conversation
history, compaction"] G["Gateway
owns session metadata
backend, hashes, timestamps"] B["Backend
owns the prompt / KV cache
per provider, region, replica"] H -- "full history every turn" --> G G -- "same backend + byte-stable prefix" --> B B -- "cached vs uncached token counts" --> G ``` LLM APIs are stateless: pi resends the whole conversation every turn. Caching happens **on the backend**, which recognizes a prefix it processed recently and bills it at a discount. The gateway's job is to make cache hits *likely* — not to hold the conversation. ## Caches are per backend ```mermaid flowchart TB S["Session 7f3a
120k-token prefix"] S -- "warm ✓" --> A["Bedrock us-east-1
Claude"] S -. "cold — full price to move" .-> B["Bedrock us-west-2
Claude"] S -. "cold" .-> C["Anthropic direct
Claude"] S -. "cold" .-> D["Self-hosted replica-2"] ``` Each provider, region, account, and replica has its own cache. That's why sessions are sticky and why the router prices moves (see [03](03-routing.md)). | Backend | How caching works | What the gateway does | |---|---|---| | Anthropic / Bedrock (Claude) | Explicit `cache_control` breakpoints, 5 min or 1 h TTL | Inserts breakpoints if the client didn't; picks TTL from turn cadence | | OpenAI / Azure | Automatic above ~1k tokens | Sets `prompt_cache_key` to the session ID | | Gemini / Vertex | Implicit caching + explicit context caches | Keeps prefix stable; explicit caches later | | vLLM / SGLang | Automatic prefix caching per replica | Pins session to replica; LMCache to share | ## Keeping the prefix byte-stable Any change early in the prompt invalidates everything after it. The gateway: - Appends anything it adds at the **end**, never the top. - Serializes tool definitions deterministically (stable key order). - Never injects timestamps, request IDs, or per-request text into the prompt. - Passes provider reasoning blocks (Anthropic thinking signatures, OpenAI encrypted reasoning) through untouched; strips them only if a session is forced to change model. ## The session table (Redis) Metadata only. No conversation content. | Field | Used for | |---|---| | `session_id` | From `X-Session-Id`, harness metadata, or a hash of system prompt + first user message | | `user_id`, `team_id` | Policy + spend | | `model`, `backend`, `replica` | Stickiness | | `quality_floor` | Re-routing at boundaries | | `prefix_hashes[]` | Detect compaction / divergence (hash mismatch ⇒ cache is dead ⇒ free re-route) | | `cache_written_at`, `cache_ttl` | Is the cache still warm? | | `warm_until{backend}` | Which backends would be cheap to move to | | `turns`, `cost_so_far` | Estimate remaining turns; enforce per-session caps | ## Compression without storing anything Problem: if we compress a big tool output on turn 5, the harness resends the **original** on turn 6. If we compress it differently, the prefix changes and the cache misses. Solution: compression is **deterministic**. The same tool output always compresses to the same text, so applying it to every tool result in the history, on every turn, sends the provider an identical prefix each time. No map of compressed text needs to be stored. ```mermaid flowchart LR H["History from the harness
(original tool outputs)"] --> C["Deterministic rules
strip ANSI codes, collapse repeated lines,
keep head + tail of huge outputs"] C --> S["Same compressed history
every turn"] S --> P["Provider prefix unchanged
→ cache keeps hitting"] ``` Rules: - Only **tool results** above a size threshold. User and assistant text is never touched. - Off by default; enabled per team (`compression: {enabled: true, min_chars: 4000, max_chars: 24000}`). - Changing the settings mid-session changes the history once (one cache miss). - Savings are counted per request: removed tokens in the newest tool result at the input price, removed tokens in older results at the cache-read price (that's what they would have cost). - A model-based compressor (LLMLingua-2) could be added later behind the same interface; because it isn't deterministic across versions, it would need a content-hash cache. ## Stateful APIs OpenAI's Responses API can store conversation server-side (`previous_response_id`). We support `store: false` first. A stored mode, if added, is opt-in with explicit retention — because that's the point where the proxy starts holding content. ## Response caching Exact-match response caching rarely hits for agent traffic (every turn is unique), but helps chatbots, RAG, evals, and repeated pipeline calls. - **Opt-in:** per team (`response_cache: {enabled: true, ttl_seconds: 3600}`) or per request with `X-MeritOrder-Cache: on`. `off` always bypasses it. - **Scoped:** cache keys include the team (or the user, with `scope: user`), so answers never cross that boundary. - **The one exception to "no stored content":** entries hold the response in Redis until the TTL expires. See [09 — Decisions](09-decisions.md). - Hits cost $0 and are recorded with the original cost as `savings_response_cache`. Streaming requests can be served from the cache (replayed as a stream); only non-streaming responses are written to it.

| 18 | Control panel in Mantine, monitoring first | Accepted |
| 19 | The IdP owns identity; Merit Order owns teams; user records decide team and role | Accepted |
| 20 | Quality scores are measured with graded tasks, not a judge model | Accepted |
| 21 | Every cost is visible next to the switch that controls it | Accepted |
| 22 | GPU prices come from SkyPilot's catalog; SkyPilot runs in its own environment | Accepted |
| 23 | A named model is never silently swapped; substitution is opt-in and never to a weaker model | Accepted |
| 24 | Refusals are retried on another model only for `auto` | Accepted |
| 25 | Every process follows the stored configuration | Accepted |
| 26 | No request queue in the gateway; a full GPU queues only as a last resort | Accepted |

**Still open:** reconciling computed costs with provider and cloud bills; Kubernetes-native GPU
provisioning (llm-d / KServe); a learned router; model-based compression; Parquet export and a
Grafana dashboard; provider batch APIs (decision 10).

## 1. Python for the core

**Why:** The team prefers it, the ML and inference ecosystem (SkyPilot, vLLM, classifiers,
compression) is Python, and gateway overhead is a few milliseconds against model latency measured
in seconds. We scale by running more gateway copies.

**Revisit if:** a real deployment hits gateway CPU limits that more replicas can't fix.

## 2. Our own backend adapters; no LiteLLM dependency

**Why:**
- LiteLLM converts everything to the OpenAI format internally. That's lossy for `cache_control`,
  thinking signatures, and other provider fields, and prompt caching is our biggest savings lever.
- It has had supply-chain incidents, a large dependency tree, and SSO in a commercially licensed
  directory.
- The rest of what it offers (keys, budgets, spend tracking, routing, UI) we'd replace anyway,
  because our ledger, router, and reporting work differently.
- Almost every backend speaks the Anthropic or OpenAI format, so pass-through plus one pair of
  translators covers them in a few thousand lines we fully control.

**What we still take:** LiteLLM's MIT-licensed pricing data, copied in with attribution, and its
code as a reference for provider quirks. Anyone needing a niche provider can run LiteLLM themselves
as an OpenAI-compatible backend.

**Revisit if:** keeping our adapters current with provider API changes becomes a significant
ongoing burden.

## 3. No Envoy

**Why:** Envoy AI Gateway is strong as a proxy layer, but all of our product logic (routing,
shaping, sessions, budgets, ledger) would still be Python, called by Envoy over gRPC on every
request. That adds a second system to operate and debug, assumes Kubernetes, narrows the
contributor pool, and solves a performance problem we don't have. Merit Order runs behind whatever
load balancer or ingress an organization already uses.

**Revisit if:** large deployments ask for it. The routing and shaping code could be packaged as an
Envoy external-processing service without being rewritten. Separately, an optional plugin could use
Kubernetes inference-routing tools (llm-d) inside a customer's own GPU cluster.

## 4. Docker Compose and Kubernetes both supported

**Why:** Compose gives the clone-and-run experience an open-source project needs; Kubernetes is
what enterprises at our target spend run in production. Same images, no Kubernetes-specific code in
the app. Details in [07 — Deployment](07-deployment.md).

## 5. The harness owns the conversation; no content stored

**Why:** Harnesses already resend history and compact it. Storing conversations would make the
proxy a retention, eDiscovery, and breach liability. The gateway stores routing metadata (hashes,
timestamps, backends) only. Compression stays cache-safe through a content-hash map, not stored
conversations.

**Revisit if:** we add the OpenAI Responses API's stored mode, which would be opt-in with explicit
retention.

## 6. Route by marginal cost, including cache rebuild cost

**Why:** A running GPU's spare capacity is already paid for, so it's nearly free, even for a better
model than the task needs. Moving a session re-pays for its whole context, so the router counts that
before moving. Details in [03 — Routing](03-routing.md).

## 7. SkyPilot for GPUs, provisioning as a plugin

**Why:** SkyPilot handles multi-cloud GPUs, spot instances, and replica scaling (SkyServe), and can
target Kubernetes clusters. Our controller decides *whether* to run a model; SkyPilot handles *how*.
A Kubernetes-native option (llm-d or KServe) can be another plugin later.

## 8. Generic OIDC, Entra first

**Why:** Entra is the first customer need; Google and others are configuration on the same code
path. Harnesses get short-lived virtual keys via a device-code login.

## 9. Postgres and Redis are the only state

**Why:** Both are available as managed services everywhere and are easy to run in Compose.
ClickHouse may become an optional reporting backend for very large deployments.

## 10. Continuous batching only; async batch APIs out of scope

**Why:** The product is for day-to-day interactive use. vLLM/SGLang batch concurrent requests on
their own. Provider batch APIs (about 50% off for work that can wait hours) may come later.

## 11. AGPL-3.0-only license

**Why:** Changes that others are offered over a network come back to the project.

## 12. Reporting UI in React/TypeScript

**Why:** Interactive filters and charts are much easier to build well, and the UI only talks to the
reports API, so it stays replaceable. The rest of the project remains Python.

**Alternative considered:** server-rendered pages with htmx (all-Python, clunkier interactivity).

## 13. Opt-in response cache may store responses

**Why:** Exact-match caching saves real money for chatbots, RAG, and evals. It can't work without
keeping the response, so it's the one exception to decision 5: off by default, enabled per team or
per request, scoped to a team or user, and expired by TTL (Redis).

## 14. Open-weight catalog with prices from OpenRouter

**Why:** There are dozens of useful open-weight models (DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen, MiniMax, MiMo,
Mistral, Gemma, Nemotron, Muse, gpt-oss) and their prices change often. `config/models-open.yaml`
lists them with their Hugging Face IDs (needed for self-hosting); `meritorder prices refresh` pulls
current prices and context windows from OpenRouter's public catalog into `prices.json`. A route with
no known price is never chosen by `auto`, so a missing price can't look free. OpenRouter is one
backend among many, not the system: it adds a fee, sends prompts through another company, and
doesn't count toward cloud commitments.

## 15. GPU scaling on addressable demand at API prices

**Why:** Counting only traffic already served by a model means a stopped model never looks worth
starting. The controller counts what all traffic the model *could* serve costs at API-equivalent
prices, excluding free upgrades. That number doesn't fall when GPUs take over the traffic, so it
doesn't flap. Two self-hosted models that address the same traffic are each credited with it; the
router then splits the traffic. Revisit if that over-provisions in practice.

## 16. Deterministic, rule-based compression first

**Why:** Compression must give identical output every turn or it breaks provider caching (and, on
recent Claude models, edited history can invalidate thinking). Rules (strip ANSI codes, collapse
repeated lines, keep head and tail of huge outputs) are deterministic, need no stored state, and add
no ML dependency. A model-based compressor (LLMLingua-2) can come later behind a content-hash cache.

## 17. Configuration versions in Postgres, YAML as the starting point

**Why:** Containers mount config read-only, and a fleet of gateways needs one source of truth. Saving
from the console validates the document, stores it as a new version (who, when, why), and every
gateway hot-reloads it within seconds; in-flight requests finish on the objects they started with.
Restore is one click. The YAML file is used until the first version is saved, and stays the format
for import, export, and GitOps. Secrets never enter the database: literal keys are refused and must
stay `${ENV}` references.

## 18. Control panel in Mantine, monitoring first

**Why:** Anyone running a company's LLM traffic through Merit Order will watch it far more than
they reconfigure it. The console opens on a live Dispatch view (the merit-order stack from real
traffic, a live request feed, backend health, the GPU fleet, and what needs attention), with
configuration one page among several. Mantine gives a complete admin component set with few
dependencies; charts stay hand-written SVG.

## 19. The IdP owns identity; Merit Order owns teams; user records decide team and role

**Why:** Enterprises expect Entra to be the source of truth for who exists and which groups they're
in, but budgets and model policy belong to Merit Order. People are created at first sign-in, their
team and role come from mapped groups, and admins can pin exceptions. Each request resolves team and
role from the user record (cached for a minute), not from the key, so moves and disables apply to
existing keys. SCIM provisioning (`/scim/v2`) applies Entra changes, including deprovisioning, as they happen.

## 20. Quality scores are measured with graded tasks, not a judge model

**Why:** Routing is only as good as its quality scores. A model-as-judge adds its own cost and
bias; tasks with mechanical checks (exact answers, JSON shape, tool calls, a regex that must
accept and reject given strings) are cheap, repeatable, and explainable. The eval suggests
scores; an admin decides whether to apply them.

## 21. Every cost is visible next to the switch that controls it

**Why:** A gateway that starts cloud GPUs on its own has to be easy to overrule. The console shows
where each GPU runs, for how long, and what it has cost, with stop, pin, and stop-all controls that
take effect within seconds and are logged with who and why. Organization safeguards (org and GPU
budgets, fleet caps, a per-request ceiling) are hard limits that apply to admin pins too, so no
single action can exceed them. Limits are config (versioned, reviewable); stops and pins are
runtime controls (immediate, expiring), because an emergency shouldn't wait on a config review.

## 22. GPU prices come from SkyPilot's catalog; SkyPilot runs in its own environment

**Why:** A hand-typed `gpu_cost_per_hour` is wrong as soon as SkyPilot places a replica somewhere
else: 4×H100 spot ranges from about $4/h to over $20/h across clouds and regions. The controller
uses SkyPilot's catalog (the same prices its optimizer uses) for break-even decisions, and each
running replica's own cloud, region, instance, and spot price for burn rate, cost, and chargeback.
The configured price is the fallback, and the only price for your own hardware. These are list
prices; discounts, disks, and egress aren't included until bill reconciliation exists.

SkyPilot pulls in about 150 packages and, as a dependency, would have downgraded the gateway's
uvicorn. So it lives only in the controller's `-gpu` image, in a separate Python environment, and
Merit Order reaches it through the `sky` CLI and SkyPilot's own interpreter.

## 23. A named model is never silently swapped; substitution is opt-in and never to a weaker model

**Why:** Harnesses and apps that name a model depend on its behavior, especially with tools. When
a named model has nowhere to run (for example its GPUs were stopped), the default is a 503 that
explains why for each route and suggests `auto`. Teams that would rather keep working can turn on
`substitute_unavailable`: the request goes to a model at least as good for the task (never weaker),
and the response says which model was replaced. `auto` sessions always move to another model.

## 24. Refusals are retried on another model only for `auto`

**Why:** Safety classifiers sometimes refuse benign requests, and for `auto` the client has said any
suitable model is fine, so the next model gets a chance (the refused attempt is still billed and
logged). A client that named a model gets that model's answer, refusal included. Teams can turn the
retry off.

## 25. Every process follows the stored configuration

**Why:** Budgets and safeguards edited in the console must reach everything that enforces them.
Gateways, the worker (alerts), and the capacity controller (GPU budget, fleet caps) all load the
newest stored version and reload when it changes; the YAML file only applies until the first
version is saved. A version that fails to load is skipped and the last good one stays in effect.

## 26. No request queue in the gateway; a full GPU queues only as a last resort

**Why:** LLM calls are interactive and streaming, so a queue in Redis would add latency and a
second set of workers to pull from it, for no gain: vLLM already schedules and queues on the GPU.
A saturated GPU gets no new work while another route can take it, but when it's the only route,
sending the request there to wait beats a 503. The wait is bounded (`max_waiting` per replica) so
a backlog can't grow without limit. Gateways count in-flight requests and share the counts every
2 s, because the controller's one-minute metrics sample is too slow to catch a burst.

"""Live prices: from OpenRouter's catalog and the providers' list prices (LiteLLM's list), long-prompt tiers, refreshed
by the worker, with alerts when prices change, the lists disagree, or one can't be fetched."""

import copy

import httpx
import pytest
from conftest import TEST_CONFIG

from meritorder import catalog, live_prices
from meritorder.config import BackendConfig, Price, PriceTier, build_config
from meritorder.pricing import Usage, cost, uncached_cost
from meritorder.state import MemoryState
from meritorder.store import MemoryStore

HAIKU = Price(input=0.1, output=0.5, cache_read=0.01, cache_write=0.125,
              tiers=[PriceTier(above=100_000, input=0.5, output=2.5, cache_read=0.05, cache_write=0.625)])


def test_long_prompts_use_their_tier():
    assert HAIKU.at(100_000) is HAIKU and HAIKU.at(0).input == 0.1
    long = HAIKU.at(100_001)
    assert (long.input, long.output, long.read(), long.write(), long.tiers) == (0.5, 2.5, 0.05, 0.625, [])
    stepped = Price(input=2, output=10, cache_read=0.2, tiers=[PriceTier(above=272_000, input=4, output=15), PriceTier(above=128_000, input=3, output=12)])
    assert stepped.at(200_000).input == 3 and stepped.at(300_000).input == 4
    assert stepped.at(300_000).read() == pytest.approx(0.4)  # no tier cache price: the base one, scaled with input
    assert Price(input=1, output=2, tiers=[PriceTier(above=10, input=2, output=4)]).at(11).read() == pytest.approx(0.2)

    short = Usage(input_tokens=50_000, output_tokens=1000)
    assert cost(HAIKU, short) == pytest.approx((50_000 * 0.1 + 1000 * 0.5) / 1e6)
    big = Usage(input_tokens=20_000, cache_read_tokens=130_000, output_tokens=1000)  # the cache counts toward the prompt's length
    assert cost(HAIKU, big) == pytest.approx((20_000 * 0.5 + 130_000 * 0.05 + 1000 * 2.5) / 1e6)
    assert uncached_cost(HAIKU, big) == pytest.approx((150_000 * 0.5 + 1000 * 2.5) / 1e6)

    raw["backends"] = {**raw["backends"],
                       "direct": {"kind": "api", "format": "anthropic", "base_url": "https://api.anthropic.com"},

                     "terra": {"routes": [{"backend": "azure", "model": "my-deployment", "price_key": "gpt-6.1-terra"},

                     "deal": {"routes": [{"backend": "direct", "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "price": {"input": 1.5, "output": 7.5}}]}}
