# 00 — How it all works (start here) Merit Order sits between your tools and the model providers. Your tools keep speaking the API they already speak; Merit Order translates when the chosen model speaks another. For every request sent with the model name `auto`, it asks two questions: 1. **How hard is this?** The request gets a **level** for its kind of work: coding or general, 1 to 5. 2. **What's the cheapest model that's good enough?** Every model has a **score** for each kind of work, 1 to 5. Models scoring at least the level, with room for the conversation, qualify, and the cheapest of those wins, counting the whole rest of the conversation, not just this request. Everything else in this document is detail on those two questions: how tools connect, where the levels, scores and prices come from, what "cheapest" really means, how long conversations are handled, what happens when something fails, and when your own GPUs are worth switching on. The numbers are from the live configuration on 11 November 2026; prices and scores refresh on their own, so yours will drift. A request that **names a model** (`claude-opus`, `gpt-sol`, …) skips both questions: it always gets that model, and Merit Order only chooses where to run it (section 10). ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Your tool
(any API format)"] --> R["Request
model: auto"] R --> L["2. Level
coding:3"] L --> Q["3–4. Models scoring ≥ 3,
with room, allowed for the team"] Q --> C["5. Cheapest for the rest
of the session"] C --> E["6. Effort and output limit
for that level"] E --> S["Send, translated if needed;
on failure, the next cheapest (8)"] ``` ## 1. Your tools connect as they are Point a tool's base URL at Merit Order and give it a Merit Order key. Nothing else about the tool changes, because Merit Order speaks both common APIs: | Your tool speaks | For example | Merit Order endpoint | |---|---|---| | Anthropic Messages | Claude Code, Anthropic SDKs | `/v1/messages` (and `/v1/messages/count_tokens`) | | OpenAI Chat Completions | pi, Cursor, OpenAI SDKs, most other tools | `/v1/chat/completions` | | OpenAI Responses | Codex CLI | `/v1/responses` | | Embeddings | RAG pipelines | `/v1/embeddings` | **The model's own format is Merit Order's problem, not the tool's.** Each provider speaks one of the two formats. When the tool and the chosen provider speak the same one, the request passes through untouched, so provider features such as Claude's cache markers and thinking signatures survive. When they differ, Merit Order converts the request, the reply and the stream both ways: messages, tool calls, images, streaming, usage and stop reasons. Two things don't cross: a model's reasoning from earlier turns (each turn still works; the model just thinks again), and `temperature`/`top_p`, which current Claude models reject. The Responses API is converted to Chat Completions inside the gateway; GPT models that need the Responses API for tools with reasoning are converted on the way out. **The model name says what you want:** - `auto`: Merit Order chooses (the rest of this document). - A model's name or one of its aliases: that model. Aliases cover the names tools already send, so `claude-sonnet-5-5`, `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5` and `sonnet` all mean Claude Sonnet. - Anything else: an error saying the model isn't configured. `GET /v1/models` lists `auto` and every model your team may use, with each one's context window. **Every reply says what happened**, in headers: `X-MeritOrder-Model` (the model that answered), `X-MeritOrder-Backend` (the provider), `X-MeritOrder-Floor` (the level, for `auto`), `X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens` and its source, `X-MeritOrder-Failed-Over` when a provider failed first, and for replies that aren't streamed `X-MeritOrder-Cost-Usd`. The console's Reports → Requests tab shows the model, provider, level and cost of every request. Setting up Claude Code and pi is in section 11. ## 2. Every request gets a level The level is how demanding the request is. It's worked out from the request itself, with simple rules and no model call, so it's instant and free: | The request | Level | |---|---| | Plain text, short (under ~400 tokens), no tools | general 1 | | Plain text | general 2 | | Plain text with words like analyze, compare, plan, strategy, trade-offs, evaluate or reason, or over 20,000 tokens long | general 3 | | Any tools, or text that looks like code (code fences, `def`, `import`, stack traces, file names, "refactor", "bug", SQL, …) | coding 3 | | 5 or more tools: an agent at work | coding 4 | | Coding with "hard" wording (architecture, race condition, security, performance, migration, concurrency, …) or over 60,000 tokens of context | one level higher, at most 5 | Clients can take over: `X-Route-Floor: coding:4` sets the level exactly, and `X-Route-Hint: cheap` or `smart` moves it one level down or up. Every `auto` response says what it got (`X-MeritOrder-Floor`). What that means in practice: | Request | Level | |---|---| | "What's the capital of Portugal?" | general 1 | | "Draft a reply to this customer email" (pasted) | general 2 | | "Compare these three vendor proposals" | general 3 | | "Why does this function return None?" with a code block | coding 3 | | A coding agent's turn: 20 tools, 30,000 tokens of conversation | coding 4 | | The same agent, 90,000 tokens into the session | coding 5 | **Claude Code's side jobs get lower levels.** Claude Code labels each request (when its hint headers are on; section 11): a turn of the conversation, a subagent's turn, the summary it writes when it compacts a long conversation, or a side request such as a session title or summary. Those last two don't need the level of the work itself, so `auto` caps them: | Claude Code request | Highest level | |---|---| | Side request (titles, summaries) | 1 | | Compaction summary | 3 | | Conversation or subagent turn | not capped | An explicit `X-Route-Floor` is never capped. Auto mode's permission checks name Claude Sonnet, so they never go through `auto` at all. The caps are under Config → Routing → Claude Code request types. The level rules themselves live in code (`src/meritorder/classifier.py`); the console doesn't show or change them yet. ## 3. Every model gets a score for each kind of work A score says how good a model is at a kind of work, **compared with the best model you have**. It isn't typed in: the worker works it out once a day from published benchmarks. **What a score means.** By default (source `epoch`), each model's score is based on its chance of solving a task as hard as **FrontierSWE**, a set of real, hard software-engineering tasks. The best model scores 5 and every other model scores in proportion: one that solves 60% as many such tasks as the best scores 3. | Model | Chance on a FrontierSWE-hard task (coding) | Coding score | General score | |---|---|---|---| | Claude Fable 5.2 | 70% | 5.0 | 5.0 | | Gemini 4 Carbon | 61% | 4.4 | not measured yet | | GPT-6.1 Terra | 62% | 4.4 * | 3.8 | | Claude Opus 5.5 | 58% | 4.2 | 3.9 | | GPT-6 Astra | 59% | 4.2 | 4.1 | | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | 56% | 4.0 | 3.4 | | Gemini 4 Argon | 48% | 3.4 | 3.4 | | GPT-6.1 Sol | 46% | 3.3 | 4.0 | | Claude Haiku 5.5 | 41% | 3.0 | 2.0 | | GPT-6 Luna | 32% | 2.3 | 1.3 | | Gemini 3.8 Flash | 24% | 1.7 | 1.6 | | Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite | 4% | 1.0 * | 1.0 | \* Estimated from the model's general ability: no coding results published yet. **Where the numbers come from.** [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/benchmarks) (CC BY 4.0) places every model on one ability scale, fitted across about 40 benchmarks, and every benchmark on the same scale by difficulty. That's what makes models comparable even when they were tested on different benchmarks, and lets a model's ability be turned into a chance of solving tasks of a given difficulty. For coding, a model's own results on FrontierSWE and FrontierCode refine its general ability, so coding strength counts; results at the effort `auto` uses for hard work are preferred where published. The alternative source is the [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai) Intelligence Index (needs `ARTIFICIAL_ANALYSIS_API_KEY`). It's a single number per model, so coding and general get the same score. The third option is scores written on each model by hand (`config`), for example from your own eval runs ([11 — Evals](11-evals.md)). **Two choices shape the scores** (Config → Routing → Quality scores): - **Scale.** `best` (default): the best model is 5 and the rest in proportion; adding a weak model changes nobody else's score. `range`: the weakest model with data is 1 and the best 5, which depends on which weak models you happen to have configured. - **Reference task.** A harder reference spreads models further apart and sends more work up the ladder. Against Remote Labor Index (real paid remote work, which Fable solves 37% of the time), Opus would score 2.8 for general work, and ordinary level-3 work would go only to Fable. FrontierSWE keeps level 3 within reach of models like Sonnet. **Models the source doesn't cover** aren't picked by `auto`: a score nobody measured would compete with measured ones, and because the cheapest qualifying model wins, an optimistic guess would win. They still answer requests that name them. To put one back, give it a `quality_override` (Config → Models), which always wins over the source; that's also how to record that your own evals disagree with the benchmarks (Models → Evals → *Apply scores…* → *Write as override*). Measured scores use the same 1–5 scale, so the Evals page shows them beside the ones in use. On 11 November 2026, 11 open models weren't covered, among them Qwen3 Coder, Devstral and MiMo. Hover a score on the Models page to see how it was worked out. ## 4. Which models qualify A model qualifies for a request when: - its score for that kind of work is **at least the request's level**. A level-3 coding request can go to any model with a coding score of 3.0 or more; level 5 means "as good as the best", which today is only Fable; - the conversation **fits in its context window** (section 7); and - the team is allowed to use it (Config → Teams → allowed models and backends). ## 5. The cheapest qualifying route wins Each qualifying model has one or more **routes**: the providers that serve it (Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, OpenRouter, your own GPUs, …). Merit Order prices every route and picks the cheapest. **Prices are live.** The worker refreshes them every 15 minutes: OpenRouter routes from OpenRouter's catalog, direct provider APIs from the price list LiteLLM maintains, cross-checked against each other. Long-prompt prices apply (Claude Haiku 5.5 costs five times as much above 100,000 prompt tokens), and a price change, a list that can't be fetched, or two lists that disagree raises an alert. **"Cheapest" means the rest of the session**, because in a conversation each turn resends everything before it, and providers charge far less for the part they still have cached: ``` cost of a route = rebuild + expected turns × cost per turn rebuild = what it costs to get this conversation into the provider's cache: zero if this provider already holds it, else the context at the full input price (or the cache-write price, for Claude, where caching is explicit), less the cache-read price the first turn already counts cost per turn = the cached part at the cache-read price + the new tokens at the input price (cache-write price for Claude): what the conversation grew by since its last turn, or about 2,000 for a new session + about 600 output tokens at the output price expected turns = the turns so far, kept between 3 and 30 (a long session will probably keep going) ``` Here's what that gives for a new coding session at level 3, 30,000 tokens in: | Model (route) | Score | Rebuild | Per turn | 3 turns | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic)** | 3.0 | $0.003 | $0.0008 | **$0.006** | | GPT-6.1 Terra (Azure) | 4.4 | $0.027 | $0.006 | $0.046 | | Gemini 4 Argon (OpenRouter) | 3.4 | $0.053 | $0.013 | $0.092 | | GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI) | 3.3 | $0.053 | $0.013 | $0.092 | And for an agent at level 4, 80,000 tokens in: | Model (route) | Score | Rebuild | Per turn | 3 turns | |---|---|---|---|---| | **GPT-6.1 Terra (Azure)** | 4.4 | $0.074 | $0.009 | **$0.101** | | Gemini 4 Carbon (OpenRouter) | 4.4 | $0.148 | $0.018 | $0.202 | | Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic) | 4.0 | $0.187 | $0.019 | $0.244 | | Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) | 4.2 | $0.374 | $0.038 | $0.487 | **Sessions stay put.** Once a session is on a route, the rebuild is already paid there, so moving it must save at least 10% plus $0.01 over the rest of the session. Within a task (while the tool is sending tool results back, before the next prompt from a person) the session keeps its model outright. In practice a session moves only when a new task starts and something is clearly cheaper, its cache has expired (after 5 idle minutes), the conversation was compacted, it no longer fits (section 7), or its model is busy or down on every route (section 8). That's what keeps a session from bouncing between Bedrock and Anthropic and paying to rebuild each time. **A session can hold several conversations.** Claude Code sends its subagents' turns and its side requests under the main session's id. Each keeps its own routing state (model, level, cache), so a subagent never resets the main conversation's; budgets, the per-session spend limit and reports still count the session as one. **Near-ties go to speed.** The same model often costs the same everywhere (Claude on Anthropic, Bedrock and Vertex), so price alone can't choose. Routes within a small margin of the cheapest compete on measured speed: 2% under the default `cost` priority (where a better model among them goes first), 20% under `balanced`, 100% under `speed`. A team or a single request (`X-MeritOrder-Priority`) can choose differently. Every 10th new session may try a route within that margin whose speed is unknown or out of date, so speeds stay known. **Unpriced routes never win** for `auto`: an unknown price must never look free. ## 6. Then: effort and output length **Reasoning effort** follows the level, so every model works the same way for the same work (their own defaults differ): low for levels 1–2, medium for 3, high for 4–5. A model that doesn't take that effort keeps its default. The effort is set once per session on a model, because changing it would invalidate the prompt cache. A client's own effort setting always wins; one sent in Anthropic's format (Claude Code sends one) to a GPT or other OpenAI-format model goes over at the nearest level that model takes. **Output length** isn't capped by a guess. A request without `max_tokens` may write as much as the model can (128,000 tokens for current Claude and GPT models), less what wouldn't fit in the context window, under the per-request cost limit (Controls), or within what a provider's prepaid balance covers. A client's own `max_tokens` is kept (lowered only to the model's maximum). The response says how much it got and why (`X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens`, `X-MeritOrder-Max-Tokens-Source`). ## 7. Context windows: long conversations Every model has a **context window**: the most a conversation plus its reply can hold. The windows come from the live price data, refreshed with the prices: | Window | Models | |---|---| | about 1 million tokens | Claude (all), Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, MiMo, Muse Spark, Mistral Large 4, Qwen3.8 Flash, Nemotron 3.5 Super | | 922,000 | GPT-6 and GPT-6.1 (Astra, Sol, Terra, Luna) | | 524,288 | Llama 4 Maverick | | 262,144 | Qwen3 Coder (all three), Devstral 2, Mistral Small 4, Ministral 14B, Gemma 4 31B, Nemotron 3 Ultra | | 131,072 | gpt-oss-120b, gpt-oss-20b | Two parties decide what happens as a conversation grows: **the tool**, which decides when to compact (summarize the history and start over from the summary), and **Merit Order**, which decides where the conversation can still go. **What Merit Order does:** - **Models without room drop out.** For `auto`, a model whose window the conversation fills past 95% isn't a candidate (the token count is estimated at about 4 characters per token, and the reply needs room too). A 300,000-token conversation never goes to gpt-oss or Qwen3 Coder; most qualifying models have about a million tokens, so something always fits. - **A session that outgrows its model moves, even mid-task.** The next turn goes to a model with room at the same level, paying once to rebuild the cache there. - **A provider that says "too long" isn't the end.** If a provider refuses a prompt as too long anyway (the estimate can be off), an `auto` request goes to a qualifying model with a bigger window. A request that names a model can't move; its error is worded the way Anthropic's API words it ("prompt is too long: …"), whichever provider refused, because that's what makes Claude Code compact. - **The reply shrinks to fit.** When a request doesn't set `max_tokens`, the reply may use what's left of the window and no more, so the provider doesn't refuse prompt plus reply (section 6). **What the tool does.** A tool compacts when the conversation nears the window it believes it has. `/v1/models` reports each model's window, and for `auto` the largest window among the models `auto` can pick for your team (1,048,576 tokens today). That's safe because models without room drop out: a long conversation narrows the choice to the million-token models instead of failing. - **pi**: `meritorder setup pi` writes each model's window into pi's model list. - **Claude Code**: it knows the windows of Claude models by name. For a name it doesn't know, such as `auto`, it assumes 200,000 tokens unless told otherwise; `meritorder setup claude-code` tells it the gateway's window (section 11). - **Other tools**: give them the window from `/v1/models`, or leave their default; a smaller window than the real one only means compacting earlier. ## 8. When something fails Nothing reaches the client until the chosen route has started answering, so a failure moves the request on: - **Over capacity, rate-limited, missing, or down:** the next route in the cost ranking. For a named model, or a session in the middle of a task, that's another provider for the same model; for a new `auto` task, it's the next cheapest qualifying route, whatever its model. A request gets 3 tries at most (`routing.max_attempts`). An `auto` session whose model is busy or down on every route moves to another qualifying model at its next turn, even mid-task. The failing route is skipped for a while (the provider's `Retry-After`, or a growing back-off) and an alert says where its traffic went. - **Too long for the model:** for `auto`, a qualifying model with a bigger window (section 7). - **The model refuses:** for `auto`, the next qualifying model (the refusal is billed and logged); a named model's refusal is returned as it is. - **A provider can't cover the whole reply on its prepaid balance:** the same route again, asking for what it says it can pay for. - **Budgets and limits:** organization, team, person and session budgets, rate limits, and the per-request cost limit stop requests before they're sent, with a message saying which. Every rule and timing is in [10 — How it decides](10-how-it-decides.md). ## 9. Your own GPUs: when they start and stop Power grids run the cheapest generators all the time (baseload) and switch on expensive ones (peakers) only for peaks. Merit Order does the same: your own GPUs, running an open model, are the baseload when there's enough steady work to keep them busy, and the APIs are the peakers that are always there. **A GPU deployment starts only when sustained demand pays for it.** Every minute the controller asks: what does the traffic this model could serve cost me at API prices? - **Traffic it could serve** means requests whose level its score covers. A model with a coding score of 3.0 counts every coding request at levels 1–3, wherever it was actually sent. - **At API prices** means what you're paying for that traffic today. - One replica is worth starting when that spend, per hour, exceeds the replica's hourly price plus a 20% margin, **continuously for 10 minutes**. The number of replicas follows the throughput (enough to run at 70% load), as long as each one pays for itself by the same rule. For example, Qwen3 Coder Next on four H100s costs about $16 an hour per replica (SkyPilot's cheapest offer in the allowed clouds, or the configured fallback). It starts once the work it could do would cost you more than $19.20 an hour at API prices for 10 minutes straight. **While it runs, it's the first choice.** A GPU you're already paying for costs almost nothing per token while it has room, so the router prices it at 2% of the API price up to 60% load, rising to the full API price as it fills. Up to that point it wins every request it qualifies for; past it, the APIs take over, and at 100% new work spills to them. Requests that only went to the GPU because it had room (a better model than the level needed) don't count as demand, so idle capacity can't keep itself alive. **It stops when demand no longer pays for it.** When the work it could do drops below break-even for 10 minutes, and it has been running at least 30 minutes, it **drains**: no new sessions, existing ones finish, and after 15 minutes the GPUs are released. If demand comes back while draining, it simply stays. Starting takes 10–20 minutes for a big model, and traffic stays on the APIs meanwhile, so the delays and margins are there to avoid paying for start-ups that don't last. **A self-hosted model needs a score.** Demand is counted by level, so a model the quality source doesn't cover has none, and its GPUs never start for `auto` traffic. On 11 November 2026 that's the case for Qwen3 Coder Next: give it a `quality_override` (Config → Models) to have the controller consider it. Its window (262,144 tokens) also means conversations longer than about 249,000 tokens go to the APIs. **Whether a GPU can ever pay** shows on Models → **GPU break-even**. Each open-weight model gets a machine whose GPUs hold its weights (sizes from Hugging Face), priced from SkyPilot's catalog, spot or on-demand, across the clouds SkyPilot covers: of those, the one that pays from the least traffic. The weights can be served as published, in FP8, or in 4 bits; quantizing changes what fits, not the quality scores, so measure a quantized model with an eval before trusting its level. For each quality level and each model it shows the traffic one replica needs (tokens per minute and about how many requests an hour), your busiest hour of that traffic, and what the replica can serve. The price a GPU has to beat at a level is the cheapest API model good enough for it, because that's where `auto` would send the work otherwise. On 11 November 2026, with spot prices, only level-1 work could pay: gpt-oss-20b on one L4 ($0.12 an hour) from about 72,000 tokens a minute. The best level an open model could host was 2: Kimi K3.1 (coding 2.7), published in 4 bits, fits on eight B300s. Level 3 starts at Claude Haiku's 3.0, and quantizing doesn't change that, because the strongest open models already ship in 4 bits. *Get latest prices* has SkyPilot download its catalogs again. Admins can also stop a deployment (draining first or at once), pin a number of replicas, stop all GPUs, or cap GPU spend per month, per hour, or in replicas (GPUs page and Controls). Details: [05 — GPU autoscaling](05-gpu-autoscaling.md). ## 10. Requests that name a model A request for `claude-opus` gets Claude Opus, never another model. Merit Order still picks the route: the cheapest of Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and OpenRouter for the rest of the session, with the same stickiness, speed tie-breaks and failover between them. If none of its routes can run, the request fails with the reason for each, unless the team allows substituting a model at least as good. A named model is never skipped for its window: a conversation it can't hold gets the provider's error, worded so Claude Code compacts. Claude Code sends Claude model names unless it's set to `auto`, so by default it gets exactly what it asks for; `meritorder setup claude-code` sets it to `auto` (section 11). ## 11. Setting up Claude Code and pi Log in once (`meritorder login`, or `meritorder use-key` with a key from an admin), then: ```bash meritorder setup claude-code # Claude Code meritorder setup pi # pi ``` **Claude Code** isn't tied to Anthropic or Foundry: any gateway that speaks Anthropic's API can stand in via `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, and Merit Order does. The setup command writes these into Claude Code's settings file (`$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json`, or `~/.claude/settings.json`): | Setting | Value | Why | |---|---|---| | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | the gateway | Send every request to Merit Order | | `apiKeyHelper` | reads `~/.config/meritorder/api_key` | Your Merit Order key; logging in again rotates it | | `model` | `auto` | New sessions let Merit Order choose (`--model claude-sonnet-5-5` picks one; `--model none` leaves Claude Code's choice) | | `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS` | the gateway's window for that model | Claude Code would otherwise assume 200,000 tokens for `auto` and compact early | | `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION`, `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION_NAME` | `auto`, `auto (Merit Order)` | Adds "auto (Merit Order)" to the `/model` picker | | `CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS` | `1` | Claude Code labels side requests and compaction only when asked (section 2) | With `--model` set to a Claude model name, it leaves out the window and `/model` settings (and removes earlier ones): Claude Code already knows those names. It changes every Claude Code session that uses that settings folder. To keep Merit Order in a separate profile (for example, away from work that uses another account): ```bash meritorder setup claude-code --config-dir ~/.claude-meritorder CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-meritorder claude ``` What to expect: - **Billing.** With the Merit Order key, Claude Code doesn't use your claude.ai login for these requests: subscription limits don't apply, and the cost is per token on the providers' accounts behind the gateway. - **Non-Claude models.** `auto` can send Claude Code's turns to GPT, Gemini or open models, translated. It works, but Anthropic doesn't support running Claude Code on non-Claude models, so expect rough edges. - **Cost display.** Claude Code's own cost figure guesses prices for a name it doesn't know (a test request it showed as $0.038 cost $0.0096). The gateway's numbers (My usage page, `meritorder usage`) are the real ones. - **Reply length.** For a model name it doesn't know, Claude Code asks for up to 32,000 output tokens per reply. `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` raises it (to 128,000 at most); Merit Order lowers a request to the chosen model's own maximum when that's smaller. - **Effort.** Claude Code sends its own reasoning effort (its `/effort` setting), and a client's setting always wins, so the per-level effort (section 6) doesn't apply to its turns. - **A startup line** `[claude-code:unrecognized_model] {"model":"auto"}` is informational. - **Subagents** each get their own routing thread within the session (section 5), and their own level. **pi** gets a "Merit Order" provider listing `auto` and every model with its context window, sends its session id so sessions stay on the backend that holds their cache, and adds cache markers that survive translation. **Codex CLI** and other OpenAI-compatible tools need only the base URL (`/v1`) and the key. ## 12. Where everything is set | What | Where in the console | In the config file | |---|---|---| | Quality source, scale, reference, refresh | Config → Routing → Quality scores | `quality:` | | A model's score override, its name in benchmark data | Config → Models | `quality_override`, `benchmark_name` | | The name that means "choose for me" | Config → Routing → Automatic routing | `routing.auto_model` | | How much cheaper a move must be | Config → Routing → Automatic routing | `routing.switch_margin_pct`, `switch_margin_usd` | | Expected turns and tokens per turn | Config → Routing → Automatic routing | `routing.min_expected_turns`, `est_output_tokens`, … | | Cost or speed | Config → Routing → Cost or speed; Config → Teams | `routing.priority`, team `priority` | | Effort by level | Config → Routing → Reasoning effort by task difficulty | `routing.effort_by_floor` | | Levels for Claude Code's side and compaction requests | Config → Routing → Claude Code request types | `routing.request_class_levels` | | GPU price curve | Config → Routing → Self-hosted pricing curve | `routing.shadow_knee`, `shadow_floor` | | Which models and providers a team may use | Config → Teams | `allowed_models`, `allowed_backends` | | Budgets, per-request cost limit | Controls; Config → Teams | `safeguards`, team budgets | | Routes, prices you've negotiated | Config → Models | `routes[].price` (an override) | | Context windows, output limits | live price data (Models page) | `context_window`, `max_output_tokens` (overrides) | | GPU deployments | Config → Backends; GPUs page | `backends.*.serve` | | How requests get a level | not yet in the console | `classifier.py` | | Pointing Claude Code or pi at the gateway | — | `meritorder setup claude-code` / `setup pi` | The Models page shows every model's live scores, prices and windows, with where each came from; Backends shows each route's measured speed and anything being skipped. ## 13. What `auto` does today The cheapest qualifying model for a typical request at each level, on 11 November 2026: | Level | Coding | General | |---|---|---| | 1 | GLM-5.3 Flash, gpt-oss-20b | GLM-5.3 Flash, gpt-oss-20b | | 2 | DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | | 3 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Terra | | 4 | GPT-6.1 Terra | GPT-6.1 Sol | | 5 | Claude Fable 5.2 only | Claude Fable 5.2 only | A Claude Code session on `auto` is coding level 4 (it always sends many tools): GPT-6.1 Terra, until the conversation passes 60,000 tokens and it becomes level 5 (Fable) at the next prompt. Its titles and summaries go to level-1 models, and compaction summaries to level-3 models. ## 14. Known gaps - **The level rules aren't in the console,** and they're keyword-based. A coding agent sending `auto` with more than 60,000 tokens of context lands on level 5, which today only Fable meets, at $8/$40 per million tokens. Clients that name a model aren't affected. - **Some scores are estimates.** A model without published coding results gets a coding score from its general ability (marked * on the Models page), and published results come from runs at different efforts. - **A threshold, not cost per solved task.** A cheaper model that solves a little less can still cost less per solved task than a dearer one. Merit Order now has each model's chance of solving hard work, so it could pick on expected cost per success; today it picks the cheapest model above the level, which is simpler to predict. - **Token counts for routing are estimates** (about 4 characters per token), so the window check can be off near the limit; a provider's "too long" is the backstop (section 7).

# Merit Order

An open-source LLM gateway that cuts LLM spend for day-to-day use, without changing how
people work.

Power grids dispatch generators in **merit order**: cheapest marginal cost first, with expensive
peaker plants switched on only when demand requires them. Merit Order does the same with tokens:

- **Routes** every session to the cheapest model and backend that meets the task's quality bar,
  counting what it would cost to rebuild the prompt cache somewhere else.
- **Runs open-weight models on your own GPUs** (via SkyPilot) when steady load makes that cheaper
  than paying per token, and turns them off when it doesn't. APIs (Bedrock, Foundry, Vertex,
  Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Mistral, ...) are always there for overflow.
- **Saves tokens**: automatic prompt caching, sticky sessions, cache-safe compression of huge tool
  outputs, and an optional response cache.
- **Shows the money**: every request is recorded with what it cost and what it would have cost
  without Merit Order, broken down by cause, per user, team, project, and day.

Point Claude Code, pi, OpenAI or Anthropic SDKs, or anything that speaks either API at it.

## Quickstart (no keys needed)

```bash
uv sync
cp .env.example .env            # set MERITORDER_DEV_KEY (and any provider keys you have)
uv run meritorder serve         # http://localhost:8080, reports UI at /ui/
```

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $MERITORDER_DEV_KEY" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]}'
```

With no provider keys, requests go to built-in mock backends. `uv run meritorder check` shows
which backends and models are live with the keys you've set. Without `MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL`,
storage is in memory; use Docker Compose for the real thing.

## Run the full stack with Docker

```bash
cp .env.example .env            # add at least one provider key
docker compose up -d            # gateway + worker + Postgres + Redis on :8080
docker compose exec gateway meritorder keys create --user you@example.com --role admin
```

Bedrock with your AWS profile (including SSO): `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.aws.yaml up -d`.
Kubernetes: `helm install mo charts/meritorder` (see [docs/07-deployment.md](docs/07-deployment.md)).

## Point your harness at it

```bash
meritorder login --gateway https://llm.example.com   # Entra sign-in; or: meritorder use-key <key>
meritorder setup pi                                    # adds a "meritorder" provider to pi
meritorder setup claude-code                           # sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL + apiKeyHelper
```

Or by hand: OpenAI-compatible clients use base URL `<gateway>/v1`; Claude Code uses
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=<gateway>`. Use `model: "auto"` to let Merit Order choose, or name a model
(`claude-sonnet`, `kimi-k3.1`, `qwen3-coder`, `deepseek-v4.1-flash`, ...) to pin it.

| Header | Effect |
|---|---|
| `X-Session-Id` | Groups requests into a session (pi sends it; otherwise inferred) |
| `X-Route-Floor: coding:4` | Minimum quality for `auto` routing |
| `X-Route-Hint: cheap` / `smart` | Nudges `auto` routing down or up |
| `X-MeritOrder-Tags: project=foo` | Cost-allocation tags for reports |
| `X-MeritOrder-Cache: on` / `off` | Use or bypass the response cache |
| `X-MeritOrder-Backend: <name>` | Admins only: pin a backend (testing, debugging) |

Responses carry `x-meritorder-model`, `x-meritorder-backend`, and (non-streaming)
`x-meritorder-cost-usd` / `x-meritorder-savings-usd`. A model you name is never swapped for
another unless your team opted in to substitution when it can't run; reasoning effort you set is
always passed through. Every routing and scaling rule, as diagrams:
[docs/10-how-it-decides.md](docs/10-how-it-decides.md).

## What's in the box

| Area | Built |
|---|---|
| APIs | OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses (stateless), Anthropic Messages, and embeddings; streaming and not; pass-through when formats match, translation when they don't |
| Backends | Anthropic, Claude in Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, OpenRouter (incl. opt-in free tier), DeepSeek, Mistral, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, any OpenAI-compatible server |
| Models | Claude, GPT, and an open-weight catalog: DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Qwen3-Coder, MiniMax, MiMo, Muse, Mistral/Devstral, Gemma, Nemotron, gpt-oss |
| Routing | Rule-based classifier → quality floor; marginal-cost router with cache rebuild cost, context-window checks, sticky sessions, fallback across backends and on refusals; `meritorder eval` measures each model's quality scores with graded tasks |
| GPUs | Break-even controller (addressable demand, hysteresis), SkyPilot/SkyServe + vLLM provisioner, static servers, utilization from vLLM metrics, spill to API when saturated (live in-flight counts; a GPU that's the only route queues, bounded); console shows where each replica runs, uptime, burn rate, and cost, with stop / drain / pin / stop-all controls and an activity log |
| Savings | Automatic prompt caching, lower reasoning effort for simple `auto` tasks (stable per session), deterministic tool-output compression, opt-in response cache |
| Identity | Virtual API keys, Entra/OIDC device-code login with group → team/role mapping, roles (user, team lead, finance, admin), People page to move, pin, or disable anyone (applies to existing keys within a minute) |
| Spend | Organization, team, and user monthly budgets, GPU budget and fleet caps, a per-request cost ceiling, per-session spend caps (stops runaway agents), requests/tokens-per-minute limits, policy allow/deny lists for models and backends; all editable on the console's Controls page |
| Control panel | Web console at `/ui/` (Mantine, dark by default): live Dispatch view (merit-order stack from real traffic, live request feed, backend health, GPU fleet, needs-attention), Reports, GPUs (incl. what-if and controls), Controls (budgets and safeguards against spend), Backends, Models, Teams, People, Keys, and Config (forms for teams, models, backends, routing, and access plus raw YAML; validate, version history, restore; hot-reloads every gateway) |
| Reporting | Ledger with savings by cause, reports API, CSV, JSONL/CSV ledger export to a file or S3, `meritorder usage`, Prometheus metrics, budget/spike alerts, weekly digests |
| Deployment | Docker Compose, Helm chart, CI (tests, audits, Helm lint, Compose smoke test), signed multi-arch releases |

Not yet: reconciliation against provider and cloud bills, Kubernetes-native GPU provisioning
(llm-d/KServe), a learned router, Parquet export, a Grafana dashboard. See [docs/](docs/README.md)
for the design, [how it decides](docs/10-how-it-decides.md), and [the decisions](docs/09-decisions.md).

## Development

```bash
uv sync && uv run pytest                     # gateway
cd ui && npm ci && npm run build             # reporting UI (served at /ui/)
uv run python scripts/fake_vllm.py           # a stand-in vLLM server for the GPU path
uv run python scripts/smoke_providers.py     # test every enabled provider through a running gateway
```

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import AsyncIterator, Awaitable, Callable

from ..config import BackendConfig
from ..formats.sse import SSEEvent

RETRYABLE_STATUS = {408, 409, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529}


class BackendError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status: int, message: str, body: dict | None = None, retryable: bool = False):
        super().__init__(message)
        self.status = status
        self.message = message
        self.body = body
        self.retryable = retryable


@dataclass
class UpstreamResponse:
    status: int
    headers: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    body: dict | None = None
    events: AsyncIterator[SSEEvent] | None = None
    _close: Callable[[], Awaitable[None]] | None = None

    async def aclose(self) -> None:
        if self._close is not None:
            await self._close()
            self._close = None


class Backend:
    """A place a model runs. Subclasses implement ``send``."""

    def __init__(self, cfg: BackendConfig):
        self.cfg = cfg
        self.name = cfg.name
        self.format = cfg.format
        self.kind = cfg.kind
        self._failures = 0
        self._open_until = 0.0
        # Self-hosted deployments managed by the controller: set from published state.
        self.available = not (cfg.kind == "self_hosted" and cfg.serve is not None)
        self.draining = False
        self.unavailable_reason: str | None = None  # shown when a request has nowhere else to go
        self.live_cost_per_hour: float | None = None  # per replica, from the controller (SkyPilot catalog) when known

    # Simple circuit breaker: after 3 consecutive failures, skip this backend for a while.
    def healthy(self, now: float) -> bool:
        return now >= self._open_until

    def record_failure(self, now: float) -> None:
        self._failures += 1
        if self._failures >= 3:
            self._open_until = now + min(60.0, 5.0 * 2 ** (self._failures - 3))

    def record_success(self) -> None:
        self._failures = 0
        self._open_until = 0.0

    async def send(self, body: dict, stream: bool, headers: dict[str, str]) -> UpstreamResponse:
        raise NotImplementedError

    async def count_tokens(self, body: dict, headers: dict[str, str]) -> dict | None:
        return None

    async def close(self) -> None:
        return None

    assert _loads('{"city":"Paris"}') == {"city": "Paris"}

def a_ev(d):

def test_anthropic_stream_parallel_tools_and_error():

        out += s.feed(o_ev(d))
    out += s.feed(SSEEvent(data="[DONE]"))

    opened = set()
    for x in p:
        if x["type"] == "content_block_start":
            assert not opened
            opened.add(x["index"])
        elif x["type"] == "content_block_stop":

def _then(close, release):
    """A stream's close callback that also releases its in-flight slot, exactly once."""
    async def wrapped() -> None:
        try:
            if close is not None:
                await close()
        finally:
            release()

    return wrapped


NEXT_BACKEND_ON = {401, 402, 403, 404}  # the backend's fault, not the request's: try the next one
# How providers say a prompt doesn't fit the model's context window (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, vLLM).
_TOO_LONG = re.compile(r"prompt is too long|input is too long|context.length|context.window|maximum context|"
                       r"too many (input )?tokens|exceeds the (maximum|max)", re.IGNORECASE)


def too_long(e: "BackendError") -> bool:
    """The prompt doesn't fit the model: a model with a bigger window can take it; the same one can't."""
    return e.status in (400, 413) and bool(_TOO_LONG.search(e.message or ""))
_AFFORD = re.compile(r"can only afford (\d+)")  # OpenRouter: "You requested up to 599400 tokens, but can only afford 538612"


def affordable(e: BackendError) -> int | None:
    """The output tokens a provider says its account can pay for, when it refuses a request for asking more (HTTP 402)."""
    m = _AFFORD.search(e.message or "") if e.status == 402 else None
    return int(m.group(1)) if m and int(m.group(1)) > 0 else None
_TAG_PAIR = re.compile(r"^\s*([A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,64})\s*=\s*([^,]{0,200}?)\s*$")


class GatewayError(Exception):

def error_body(fmt: str, status: int, message: str, kind: str) -> dict:
    if fmt == "anthropic":
        return {"type": "error", "error": {"type": kind, "message": message}}
    return {"error": {"message": message, "type": kind, "code": status}}


def error_response(fmt: str, status: int, message: str, kind: str = "api_error") -> JSONResponse:
    return JSONResponse(error_body(fmt, status, message, kind), status_code=status)


EFFORT_ORDER = ("minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")


def fit_effort(effort: str | None, accepted: list[str]) -> str | None:
    """The client's effort if the model accepts it, else the highest accepted level below it (or the lowest)."""
    if not effort or not accepted or effort not in EFFORT_ORDER:
        return None
    if effort in accepted:
        return effort
    rank = EFFORT_ORDER.index(effort)
    known = sorted((e for e in accepted if e in EFFORT_ORDER), key=EFFORT_ORDER.index)
    below = [e for e in known if EFFORT_ORDER.index(e) <= rank]
    return (below[-1] if below else known[0]) if known else None
