# Merit Order configuration.
#
# Strings support ${ENV_VAR} and ${ENV_VAR:-default}. Secrets come from the
# environment (see .env.example), never from this file.
#
# Backends whose credentials or URLs are missing are switched off automatically,
# so this file works with whatever provider keys you have. Run `meritorder check`
# to see what is usable.
#
# PRICES are live: the worker refreshes them every prices_refresh_minutes (15) from OpenRouter's catalog
# (OpenRouter routes) and the price list LiteLLM maintains (direct provider APIs: Anthropic, OpenAI,
# Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, Foundry), long-prompt tiers included, and alerts when one changes or the two
# lists disagree. prices.json is the last refresh. Set `price:` on a route only to override the list,
# e.g. for a negotiated discount; `price_key:` names the model when a route's id isn't its name (an
# Azure deployment). QUALITY scores (1-5) come from published benchmarks too (the `quality:` section below).
# The ones written on each model apply only with `source: config` or until live scores are first fetched; a
# model the source doesn't cover isn't picked by `auto` unless it has a `quality_override`.

# "What you'd use without Merit Order": the counterfactual for savings reports.
baseline_model: claude-sonnet

# Open-weight models, direct vendor APIs, and OpenRouter's free tier.
include:
  - models-open.yaml
  - models-embeddings.yaml

default_max_tokens: 16000

# Where `auto` gets each model's 1-5 quality scores, refreshed daily by the worker (docs/11-evals.md).
quality:
  source: epoch               # epoch (Epoch AI's benchmark data, no key) | artificial_analysis (ARTIFICIAL_ANALYSIS_API_KEY) | config
  scale: best                 # best: the best model is 5, others in proportion | range: the weakest is 1, the best 5
  reference: {coding: FrontierSWE, general: FrontierSWE}   # Epoch: scores are each model's chance on a task this hard
  evidence: {coding: [FrontierSWE, FrontierCode]}         # Epoch: results that show a model's coding strength, beyond its general ability
  fallback: {coding: [Terminal Bench, GSO-Bench, MirrorCode]}   # Epoch: older coding results, only for a model with neither of those nor an index

routing:
  auto_model: auto              # clients send model="auto" to let the router choose
  switch_margin_pct: 10         # only move a session if it's this much cheaper (after cache rebuild)
  est_output_tokens: 600
  # Among routes that cost about the same, the faster one wins. cost: only ties (2%); balanced: a faster
  # route may cost 20% more; speed: up to 100% more. Teams (priority:) and X-MeritOrder-Priority override it.
  priority: cost

backends:
  # Keys come from the environment (value_env). In Kubernetes you can also add
  # value_file: /run/secrets/meritorder/<NAME> so a rotated key works without a restart
  # (docs/07-deployment.md#secrets). Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure can run keyless on workload identity.
  # --- always available: in-process mocks for trying things out and for tests
  mock-anthropic:
    kind: mock
    format: anthropic
    mock_min_cache_tokens: 1024   # like Anthropic: shorter prompts aren't cached
  mock-openai:
    kind: mock
    format: openai

  # --- Anthropic Messages API family
  anthropic:
    format: anthropic
    base_url: https://api.anthropic.com
    auth: {type: api_key, header: x-api-key, value_env: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}

  bedrock:                      # Claude in Amazon Bedrock (Messages API, SigV4 or bearer token)
    enabled: ${MERITORDER_BEDROCK:-true}   # false until the account can use the models (quotas, model access)
    format: anthropic
    base_url: https://bedrock-mantle.${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}.api.aws/anthropic
    anthropic_version: "2026-10-21"
    forward_anthropic_beta: false
    auth: {type: aws_sigv4, service: bedrock-mantle, region: "${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}", profile: "${AWS_PROFILE:-}"}

  foundry-claude:               # Claude in Microsoft Foundry
    enabled: ${MERITORDER_FOUNDRY_CLAUDE:-true}   # false until the Claude deployments exist
    format: anthropic
    base_url: ${AZURE_FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT}/anthropic
    forward_anthropic_beta: false
    auth: {type: api_key, header: x-api-key, value_env: AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY}

  vertex:                       # Claude on Vertex AI (needs: uv sync --extra gcp; the Docker image has it)
    enabled: ${MERITORDER_VERTEX:-true}   # switched off automatically without Google credentials
    format: anthropic
    flavor: vertex
    project: ${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}
    region: global
    auth: {type: google}

  vertex-gemini:                # Gemini on Vertex AI, through its OpenAI-compatible endpoint: Google's own prices and quotas
    enabled: ${MERITORDER_VERTEX:-true}
    format: openai
    base_url: https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT}/locations/global/endpoints/openapi
    auth: {type: google}
    effort_format: openai
    price_prefix: "vertex_ai/"

  # --- OpenAI-compatible family
  azure-openai:
    format: openai
    base_url: ${AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT}/openai/v1
    auth: {type: api_key, header: api-key, value_env: AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY}
    max_tokens_field: max_completion_tokens

  openai:
    format: openai
    base_url: https://api.openai.com/v1
    auth: {type: api_key, value_env: OPENAI_API_KEY}
    supports_prompt_cache_key: true
    max_tokens_field: max_completion_tokens
    api: responses                # GPT-5.6 and later take function tools with reasoning only on the Responses API

  xai:                          # xAI's own API (Grok); off until XAI_API_KEY is set
    format: openai
    base_url: https://api.x.ai/v1
    auth: {type: api_key, value_env: XAI_API_KEY}
  openrouter:                   # one key for open-weight and Chinese models (and most others)
    format: openai
    base_url: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
    auth: {type: api_key, value_env: OPENROUTER_API_KEY}

  local-vllm:                   # a vLLM/SGLang server you already run (always used while it's up)
    enabled: ${MERITORDER_LOCAL_VLLM:-false}
    kind: self_hosted
    format: openai
    gpu_cost_per_hour: 8.0          # per replica; used for chargeback and break-even
    capacity_tokens_per_second: 2500
    max_concurrency: 64             # vLLM --max-num-seqs (or what the KV cache fits): saturation seen within seconds
    cache_ttl_seconds: 600
    serve:
      provisioner: static
      model: qwen3-coder-next
      static_url: ${LOCAL_VLLM_URL:-http://localhost:8000/v1}
      min_replicas: 1

  gpu-qwen-coder:               # SkyPilot starts this on cloud GPUs when demand pays for it
    enabled: ${MERITORDER_SKYPILOT:-false}
    kind: self_hosted
    format: openai
    gpu_cost_per_hour: 16.0         # fallback only: with SkyPilot installed, prices come from its catalog per cloud/region/instance
    capacity_tokens_per_second: 4000
    max_concurrency: 64             # per replica; at full, requests spill to APIs or wait (max_waiting, default 32)
    cache_ttl_seconds: 600
    serve:
      provisioner: skypilot
      model: qwen3-coder-next
      accelerators: "H100:4"
      use_spot: true
      clouds: [aws, gcp, lambda]
      image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.11.0
      vllm_args: "--max-model-len 262144"
      max_replicas: 4
      scale_up_after_minutes: 10
      hold_minutes: 30

models:
  # --- frontier
  claude-fable:                  # Anthropic's most capable tier; priced above Opus, so `auto` only picks it when it scores higher
    effort_levels: [low, medium, high, xhigh, max]
    aliases: ["claude-fable-*", "anthropic/claude-fable*", "fable"]
    quality: {coding: 5, general: 5}
    routes:

"""Server-side tool fees (Anthropic web search) count toward cost, budgets, and the baseline."""

from meritorder.config import Price
from meritorder.formats.translate import UsageTracker, usage_from_anthropic
from meritorder.formats.sse import SSEEvent
from meritorder.pricing import Usage, attribute, cost


def test_web_searches_are_charged_per_search():
    u = usage_from_anthropic({"input_tokens": 1000, "output_tokens": 100, "server_tool_use": {"web_search_requests": 3}})
    assert u.web_search_requests == 3
    p = Price(input=3, output=15)
    assert abs(cost(p, u) - (1000 * 3 + 100 * 15) / 1e6 - 0.03) < 1e-12
    c = attribute(u, p, Price(input=3, output=15), proxy_cache=False)
    assert abs(c.actual - cost(p, u)) < 1e-12 and abs(c.savings_routing) < 1e-12  # same searches in the baseline
    assert cost(p, Usage(input_tokens=10)) == 30 / 1e6


def test_web_searches_read_from_the_stream():
    t = UsageTracker("anthropic")
    t.feed(SSEEvent(event="message_start", data='{"type":"message_start","message":{"usage":{"input_tokens":50,"output_tokens":1}}}'))
    t.feed(SSEEvent(event="message_delta",
                    data='{"type":"message_delta","usage":{"output_tokens":40,"server_tool_use":{"web_search_requests":2}}}'))
    assert t.usage.web_search_requests == 2 and t.usage.input_tokens == 50 and t.usage.output_tokens == 40


def test_anthropic_beta_allowlist():
    from meritorder.backends.http import AnthropicBackend
    from meritorder.backends.auth import BackendAuthProvider
    from meritorder.config import BackendConfig

    sent = "interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14, context-1m-2025-08-07,fine-grained-tool-streaming-2025-05-14"
    open_ = AnthropicBackend(BackendConfig(name="a", format="anthropic", base_url="https://x"), BackendAuthProvider())
    assert open_._headers({"anthropic-beta": sent})["anthropic-beta"] == sent
    cfg = BackendConfig(name="a", format="anthropic", base_url="https://x", anthropic_betas=["interleaved-thinking", "fine-grained"])
    b = AnthropicBackend(cfg, BackendAuthProvider())
    assert b._headers({"anthropic-beta": sent})["anthropic-beta"] == "interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14,fine-grained-tool-streaming-2025-05-14"
    cfg.anthropic_betas = []
    assert "anthropic-beta" not in b._headers({"anthropic-beta": sent})

# 07 — Deployment Goal: **clone, add one API key, `docker compose up`, point pi at it.** Everything else is an opt-in layer. ## Two supported ways to run it The same container images run under **Docker Compose** or **Kubernetes (Helm chart)**. Each organization picks one. | | Docker Compose | Kubernetes (Helm) | |---|---|---| | **For** | Trying it out, small teams, a single VM | Production at organizations with real spend | | **Setup** | `docker compose up`, minutes | Needs a cluster and Helm | | **High availability** | One machine | Multiple gateways, restarts, rolling upgrades | | **Scaling** | Manual | Gateway autoscales | | **Postgres / Redis** | Containers in the compose file | Usually managed cloud services | | **Secrets** | `.env` | A Secret synced from your cloud's store by External Secrets ([Secrets](#secrets)) | What keeps supporting both cheap: - **No Kubernetes-specific code in the app.** Config is env vars plus one YAML file, health checks are plain HTTP (`/healthz`, `/readyz`), logs go to stdout. - **One active controller, enforced by a Postgres advisory lock.** Works the same under both. - **Migrations are a command** (`meritorder migrate`): a one-off service in Compose, a pre-install / pre-upgrade hook in Helm. - **CI checks both** on every change: a Compose smoke test (build, start, send requests) and a Helm lint plus schema validation of the rendered manifests (kubeconform). - Nomad, ECS, Docker Swarm, etc. can be community recipes; they aren't officially supported. Where GPUs run is a separate choice. SkyPilot can start GPU VMs on clouds and neoclouds, or target an existing Kubernetes cluster with GPUs, from either deployment style. ## Containers One image, `ghcr.io/therick/meritorder`, runs every Merit Order process; the command picks which. | Service | Image and command | Required? | |---|---|---| | gateway | `meritorder serve`: APIs, console at `/ui/`, reports, admin, SCIM | Yes | | worker | `meritorder worker`: rollups, partitions, alerts, digests | Yes, for reports and alerts | | migrate | `meritorder migrate`, once per upgrade | Yes | | controller | `meritorder controller` on the **`-gpu` image variant**, which adds SkyPilot in its own environment (`--build-arg SKYPILOT=`) | Only for the GPU tier | | postgres | People, keys, config versions, ledger, GPU cost | Yes | | redis | Sessions, counters, GPU state, live feed | Yes | | caddy (profile: tls) | HTTPS for single-machine installs | No | The SkyPilot controller needs cloud credentials and keeps state in `~/.sky`: mount them into the controller (commented example in `compose.yaml`) or point it at a SkyPilot API server. For local testing without a cloud, `scripts/fake_vllm.py` stands in for a GPU server (`provisioner: static`). ## Topology: laptop / single VM ```mermaid flowchart LR pi["pi / Claude Code"] --> gw subgraph compose["docker compose"] gw["gateway"] pg[("postgres")] rd[("redis")] wk["worker"] ctl["controller
(profile: gpu, -gpu image)"] gw --> pg gw --> rd wk --> pg ctl --> pg ctl --> rd end gw --> own["Your own vLLM server
(provisioner: static)"] gw --> apis["API backends
Bedrock / Vertex / Foundry / OpenRouter"] ctl --> sky["SkyPilot → cloud GPUs"] gw --> sky ``` ## Quickstart ```bash git clone https://github.com/therick/meritorder && cd meritorder cp .env.example .env # set MERITORDER_DEV_KEY and at least one provider key docker compose up -d # gateway + worker + Postgres + Redis on :8080, UI at /ui/ docker compose exec gateway meritorder keys create --user you@example.com --role admin ``` Turning on more: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.aws.yaml up -d # use your ~/.aws profile (incl. SSO) for Bedrock docker compose --profile gpu up -d # adds the GPU capacity controller docker compose --profile tls up -d # adds Caddy for HTTPS on one machine ``` Entra: set `MERITORDER_OIDC_ISSUER` and `MERITORDER_OIDC_CLIENT_ID` in `.env`. ## Topology: production (Kubernetes) ```mermaid flowchart LR users["Harnesses / apps"] --> ing["Ingress / LB"] subgraph k8s["Kubernetes (Helm chart)"] ing --> gw1["gateway"] ing --> gw2["gateway"] ing --> gw3["gateway"] ctl["controller, -gpu image
(1 active: Postgres lock)"] end gw1 & gw2 & gw3 --> rd[("Managed Redis")] gw1 & gw2 & gw3 --> pg[("Managed Postgres")] ctl --> pg ctl --> skyapi["SkyPilot API server"] skyapi --> gpus["GPU clusters
any cloud / neocloud"] gw1 & gw2 & gw3 --> gpus gw1 & gw2 & gw3 --> apis["API backends"] gw1 & gw2 & gw3 -.-> otel["OpenTelemetry →
Grafana / Datadog / ..."] ``` - Gateways are stateless; scale with HPA on CPU. - One controller is active at a time, enforced by a Postgres advisory lock; a standby is fine. - Same images as Compose. ## Performance and scaling Measured against zero-latency mock backends with real Postgres and Redis (one laptop, Apple M4 Max), so the numbers are Merit Order's own work. The benchmark is in `scripts/bench_gateway.py`. **Added latency per call** (before the request goes upstream; the same for time to first token on streams): | Request | Merit Order's own time | |---|---| | Chat with a short or 2k-token prompt | ~0.6 ms | | Agent turn: 30k tokens of history + tools | ~2 ms | | Agent turn: 120k tokens of history + tools | ~6.5 ms (mostly parsing and hashing a ~500 KB body) | Add the network hop to the gateway, and **two Redis round trips** (one pipeline for budgets, rate limits, session, and GPU load and in-flight counts; one to save the session). With a managed Redis in the same zone, that's about 0.5–2 ms. Ledger writes, spend counters, and telemetry happen after the response, in one more pipeline. For comparison, models take 0.3–2 s to first token, and many seconds to prefill 120k tokens. **Throughput:** about **1,100 requests/s per process** (one CPU core); it scales nearly linearly with processes (7,100 requests/s with 8 on one machine that was also running Redis, Postgres, and the load generator). Gateways share nothing but Redis and Postgres, so add pods or `--workers` (`MERITORDER_WORKERS`) to scale. Long streams are cheap to hold open: what limits a process is CPU per request, not open connections. A rough sizing for 10,000 requests/s: 10–16 gateway cores, one Redis node (~20 commands per request in three pipelines), and Postgres taking 10,000 ledger inserts/s, the first part that would need work (batched inserts) at that scale. For perspective, an organization spending $300k a month on LLMs makes about 5–50 requests/s. Connection pools, all per process: | Pool | Default | Setting | |---|---|---| | Upstream, per backend (each stream holds one connection) | 500 | `MERITORDER_UPSTREAM_MAX_CONNECTIONS`, `MERITORDER_UPSTREAM_KEEPALIVE` (100) | | Redis (waits for a free connection rather than failing) | 200 | `MERITORDER_REDIS_MAX_CONNECTIONS` | | Postgres | 10 | `MERITORDER_DB_POOL_SIZE`; with many processes, put PgBouncer in front | ## Ingress and TLS Merit Order is a plain HTTP service. It runs behind whatever the organization already uses: a cloud load balancer, an existing ingress controller, NGINX, Envoy. We don't ship or require a proxy in front of it. Single-machine installs that want HTTPS can enable the Caddy profile. ## Configuration `config/meritorder.yaml` (plus `include:`d files and environment variables for secrets) describes everything. The image ships the default config; override files with a volume (Compose) or `--set-file configFiles.=...` (Helm). ```yaml baseline_model: claude-sonnet # counterfactual for savings reports include: [models-open.yaml] # open-weight catalog, direct vendor APIs backends: bedrock: format: anthropic base_url: https://bedrock-mantle.${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}.api.aws/anthropic auth: {type: aws_sigv4, service: bedrock-mantle, region: "${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}"} models: claude-sonnet: aliases: ["claude-sonnet-*"] quality: {coding: 5, general: 4} routes: - {backend: anthropic, model: claude-sonnet-5-5, price: {input: 2, output: 10, cache_read: 0.20, cache_write: 2.5}} - {backend: bedrock, model: anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5, price: {input: 2, output: 10, cache_read: 0.20, cache_write: 2.5}} teams: platform: budget_usd_month: 20000 user_budget_usd_month: 500 allowed_models: ["*"] allowed_backends: ["*", "!openrouter-free"] compression: {enabled: true} ``` Useful commands: | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `meritorder check` | Which backends and models are usable with the current credentials | | `meritorder prices refresh` | Update `prices.json` and context windows from OpenRouter's catalog | | `meritorder models discover` | List the model IDs each enabled backend serves | | `meritorder keys create / list / revoke` | Manage API keys | | `meritorder login`, `meritorder setup pi` / `claude-code` | Sign in with Entra and point a harness at the gateway | | `meritorder usage` | Your own spend | | `meritorder eval --models a,b [--apply]` | Measure quality scores with graded tasks (asks before spending) | | `meritorder export --out file.csv` or `s3://…` | Export the ledger | | `meritorder worker --backfill` | Rebuild hourly report rollups from the raw ledger | | `meritorder controller [--once] [--interval 60]` | Run the GPU capacity controller | Once the first configuration is saved from the console, the stored version (in Postgres) is what gateways, the worker, and the controller use; the YAML file is the starting point and the format for import and export. ## Secrets Merit Order never stores provider keys. It reads them from the environment (`value_env`) or from a file (`value_file`), and a configuration saved from the console is refused if it contains a literal key, so keys never reach Postgres or the config history. What it does store: | Secret | Where | How | |---|---|---| | Provider keys | Environment or a mounted file | Supplied by the platform from your secret store | | `MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL`, `MERITORDER_REDIS_URL` | Environment | Same Secret as the provider keys | | Merit Order keys (`mo-…`) for people and harnesses | Postgres | Shown once; stored only as a SHA-256 hash (random 256-bit tokens, so a slow hash isn't needed) | | Entra / OIDC tokens | Not stored | Verified against the issuer's signing keys, then exchanged for a short-lived `mo-` key | **The best key is no key.** For each cloud's own models, use the workload's identity instead: | Models | Config | Identity | |---|---|---| | Claude in Bedrock | `auth: {type: aws_sigv4, service: bedrock-mantle, region: …}` | IRSA or EKS Pod Identity: a role allowed to invoke the Bedrock models you route to | | Claude on Vertex | `auth: {type: google}` | GKE Workload Identity: a Google service account with `roles/aiplatform.user` | | Azure OpenAI, Foundry | `auth: {type: azure_ad}` | AKS Workload Identity: a managed identity with *Cognitive Services OpenAI User* (or the Foundry equivalent) on the resource | The image includes the Google and Azure identity libraries. In Helm, put the identity on the service account (`serviceAccount.annotations`; AKS also needs the pod label `podLabels: {azure.workload.identity/use: "true"}`). Third-party providers (Anthropic direct, OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, Mistral) always need a key. ### Kubernetes: three ways to provide the Secret Every component reads its environment from one Secret. Set exactly one of these (the chart refuses more than one): | Value | What it does | Use for | |---|---|---| | `externalSecret.enabled` | The chart creates an `ExternalSecret`; [External Secrets Operator](https://external-secrets.io) syncs it from AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, Vault, … | Production (recommended) | | `existingSecret` | Use a Secret you create and manage some other way (Sealed Secrets, SOPS, CSI sync, by hand) | Production | | `secretEnv` | The chart creates the Secret from Helm values | Trying it out only: the values end up in Helm's release history (one Secret per revision) and in whatever values file you passed | The `ExternalSecret` is a pre-install/pre-upgrade hook, because the migration hook needs `MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL` before anything else starts. Its synced Secret is kept across upgrades; delete it by hand after `helm uninstall`. ### Rotating keys | Approach | Values | What happens when a key changes | |---|---|---| | **Rolling restart** (default) | `secrets.reloadOnChange: true` and [Stakater Reloader](https://github.com/stakater/Reloader) installed in the cluster | Reloader rolls the gateways, worker, and controller; pods start with the new environment. Works for every secret, including the database and Redis URLs | | **No restart** | `secrets.mountAsFiles: true`, and `value_file:` on each backend's `auth` | The Secret is also mounted as files under `/run/secrets/meritorder/`; Kubernetes refreshes them about a minute after the Secret changes, and the next request uses the new key. Provider keys only | With External Secrets, a rotation in the cloud store reaches the Secret within `externalSecret.refreshInterval` (default 1 h; lower it, or annotate the ExternalSecret with `force-sync` to pull at once). For zero-restart rotation of provider keys: ```yaml # values.yaml secrets: {mountAsFiles: true, reloadOnChange: false} ``` ```yaml # meritorder.yaml: the file when it's there, the environment otherwise (so the same config works locally) backends: openrouter: auth: {type: api_key, value_file: /run/secrets/meritorder/OPENROUTER_API_KEY, value_env: OPENROUTER_API_KEY} ``` Keep the old key valid until the new one is everywhere (most providers allow two keys at once), then revoke it. ### AWS: Secrets Manager One JSON secret holding every variable: ```bash aws secretsmanager create-secret --name meritorder/prod --secret-string '{ "MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL": "postgresql://…", "MERITORDER_REDIS_URL": "rediss://…", "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY": "…", "OPENROUTER_API_KEY": "…"}' ``` ```yaml # Once per cluster. # 07 — Deployment Goal: **clone, add one API key, `docker compose up`, point pi at it.** Everything else is an opt-in layer. ## Two supported ways to run it The same container images run under **Docker Compose** or **Kubernetes (Helm chart)**. Each organization picks one. | | Docker Compose | Kubernetes (Helm) | |---|---|---| | **For** | Trying it out, small teams, a single VM | Production at organizations with real spend | | **Setup** | `docker compose up`, minutes | Needs a cluster and Helm | | **High availability** | One machine | Multiple gateways, restarts, rolling upgrades | | **Scaling** | Manual | Gateway autoscales | | **Postgres / Redis** | Containers in the compose file | Usually managed cloud services | | **Secrets** | `.env` | A Secret synced from your cloud's store by External Secrets ([Secrets](#secrets)) | What keeps supporting both cheap: - **No Kubernetes-specific code in the app.** Config is env vars plus one YAML file, health checks are plain HTTP (`/healthz`, `/readyz`), logs go to stdout. - **One active controller, enforced by a Postgres advisory lock.** Works the same under both. - **Migrations are a command** (`meritorder migrate`): a one-off service in Compose, a pre-install / pre-upgrade hook in Helm. - **CI checks both** on every change: a Compose smoke test (build, start, send requests) and a Helm lint plus schema validation of the rendered manifests (kubeconform). - Nomad, ECS, Docker Swarm, etc. can be community recipes; they aren't officially supported. Where GPUs run is a separate choice. SkyPilot can start GPU VMs on clouds and neoclouds, or target an existing Kubernetes cluster with GPUs, from either deployment style. ## Containers One image runs every Merit Order process; the command picks which. Docker Compose builds it from the repo (`meritorder:dev`, and `meritorder:gpu` for the controller). The release workflow publishes it as `ghcr.io/therick/meritorder` when a `v*` tag is pushed; no release is tagged yet (2026-11-11). | Service | Image and command | Required? | |---|---|---| | gateway | `meritorder serve`: APIs, console at `/ui/`, reports, admin, SCIM | Yes | | worker | `meritorder worker`: rollups, partitions, alerts, digests, live prices (every 15 minutes), quality scores (daily), eval runs started on the console | Yes, for reports, alerts, and live prices | | migrate | `meritorder migrate`, once per upgrade | Yes | | controller | `meritorder controller` on the **`-gpu` image variant**, which adds SkyPilot in its own environment (`--build-arg SKYPILOT=`) | Only for the GPU tier | | postgres | People, keys, config versions, prices and quality scores, ledger, GPU cost, eval runs | Yes | | redis | Sessions, counters, GPU state, live feed | Yes | | caddy (profile: tls) | HTTPS for single-machine installs | No | In the compose stack every service is built with SkyPilot in its own environment (`SKYPILOT_VERSION`, default 0.14.2; empty leaves it out), so the gateway prices GPUs for the console's break-even itself; price lookups use no credentials. The benchmark is in `scripts/bench_gateway.py`. **Added latency per call** (before the request goes upstream; the same for time to first token on streams): | Request | Merit Order's own time | |---|---| | Chat with a short or 2k-token prompt | ~0.6 ms | | Agent turn: 30k tokens of history + tools | ~2 ms | | Agent turn: 120k tokens of history + tools | ~6.5 ms (mostly parsing and hashing a ~500 KB body) | Add the network hop to the gateway, and **two Redis round trips** (one pipeline for budgets, rate limits, session, and GPU load and in-flight counts; one to save the session). With a managed Redis in the same zone, that's about 0.5–2 ms. Ledger writes, spend counters, and telemetry happen after the response, in one more pipeline. For comparison, models take 0.3–2 s to first token, and many seconds to prefill 120k tokens. **Throughput:** about **1,100 requests/s per process** (one CPU core); it scales nearly linearly with processes (7,100 requests/s with 8 on one machine that was also running Redis, Postgres, and the load generator). Gateways share nothing but Redis and Postgres, so add pods or `--workers` (`MERITORDER_WORKERS`) to scale. Long streams are cheap to hold open: what limits a process is CPU per request, not open connections. A rough sizing for 10,000 requests/s: 10–16 gateway cores, one Redis node (~20 commands per request in three pipelines), and Postgres taking 10,000 ledger inserts/s, the first part that would need work (batched inserts) at that scale. For perspective, an organization spending $300k a month on LLMs makes about 5–50 requests/s. Connection pools, all per process: | Pool | Default | Setting | |---|---|---| | Upstream, per backend (each stream holds one connection) | 500 | `MERITORDER_UPSTREAM_MAX_CONNECTIONS`, `MERITORDER_UPSTREAM_KEEPALIVE` (100) | | Redis (waits for a free connection rather than failing) | 200 | `MERITORDER_REDIS_MAX_CONNECTIONS` | | Postgres | 10 | `MERITORDER_DB_POOL_SIZE`; with many processes, put PgBouncer in front | Request bodies are capped at 32 MB (`MERITORDER_MAX_BODY_MB`; Anthropic's own limit), 64 KB for sign-in, and 1 MB for SCIM; larger ones get a 413 before anything reads them. ## Ingress and TLS Merit Order is a plain HTTP service. It runs behind whatever the organization already uses: a cloud load balancer, an existing ingress controller, NGINX, Envoy. Nothing requires a proxy in front of it. Single-machine installs that want HTTPS can enable the Caddy profile (`MERITORDER_DOMAIN` is the hostname it gets a certificate for); the Helm chart can create an Ingress (`ingress.enabled`). What's exposed: Docker Compose publishes the gateway on `127.0.0.1` (set `MERITORDER_BIND=0.0.0.0` to open it to your network). Behind a public ingress, `/metrics` is reachable too; it shows spend and traffic totals, not prompts or users, but set `MERITORDER_METRICS_TOKEN` (and Helm `metrics.tokenKey`) to require a token. The image ships the default config. Compose mounts the repo's `config/` over it (read-only); in Helm, override files with `--set-file configFiles.=...`. API prices are not typed in. """Reports API: who sees what (user / team lead / finance / admin), every grouping, CSV and JSONL export, GPU reports."""

import csv
import io
import json
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

import pytest
from conftest import ADMIN_KEY, LEAD_KEY, TEST_KEY, auth, ledger_row

from meritorder.config import BackendConfig, ModelConfig, Route, ServeConfig

NOW = datetime.now(UTC)


async def seed(gateway):
    """alice and bob in team default, carol in ops; one tagged request; one error."""
    rows = [
        ledger_row(user_id="alice", team="default", served_model="small", backend="mock-openai", actual_cost=0.10,
                   baseline_cost=0.50, savings_routing=0.40, tags={"project": "apollo"}),
        ledger_row(user_id="alice", team="default", served_model="big", backend="mock-anthropic", actual_cost=1.00,
                   baseline_cost=1.00),
        ledger_row(user_id="bob", team="default", served_model="big", backend="mock-anthropic", actual_cost=2.00,
                   baseline_cost=2.00, status=500, error="upstream failed"),
        ledger_row(user_id="carol", team="ops", served_model="small", backend="mock-openai", actual_cost=4.00,
                   baseline_cost=8.00, savings_caching=4.00, upgraded=True),
    ]
    for r in rows:
        await gateway.store.record(r)
    await gateway.store.rollup()  # Postgres reads month-long ranges from the hourly rollup (the worker keeps it fresh)


async def finance_key(gateway) -> str:
    return (await gateway.store.create_key("fin", "ops", "finance", name="finance"))[1]


async def summary(client, key, **params):
    r = await client.get("/v1/reports/summary", params=params, headers=auth(key))
    assert r.status_code == 200, r.text
    return r.json()


async def test_role_scoping_on_summary(client, gateway):
    await seed(gateway)
    fin = await finance_key(gateway)

    # A user sees only themselves, whatever they ask for.
    for params in ({}, {"user": "bob"}, {"team": "ops"}):
        d = await summary(client, TEST_KEY, group_by="user", **params)
        assert [r["key"] for r in d["rows"]] == ["alice"] and d["user"] == "alice" and d["team"] is None

    # A team lead sees their team; asking for another team is clamped to their own.
    d = await summary(client, LEAD_KEY, group_by="user")
    assert {r["key"] for r in d["rows"]} == {"alice", "bob"} and d["team"] == "default"
    assert (await summary(client, LEAD_KEY, group_by="user", team="ops"))["team"] == "default"
    assert (await summary(client, LEAD_KEY, group_by="user", user="carol"))["rows"] == []  # carol isn't on their team
    assert [r["key"] for r in (await summary(client, LEAD_KEY, group_by="user", user="bob"))["rows"]] == ["bob"]

    # Finance and admins see everyone, and can filter.
    for key in (fin, ADMIN_KEY):
        d = await summary(client, key, group_by="team")
        assert {r["key"]: r["actual_cost"] for r in d["rows"]} == {"default": 3.1, "ops": 4.0}
        assert d["totals"]["requests"] == 4 and d["totals"]["errors"] == 1 and d["totals"]["upgraded"] == 1
        assert d["totals"]["actual_cost"] == pytest.approx(7.1) and d["totals"]["savings_total"] == pytest.approx(4.4)
        assert [r["key"] for r in (await summary(client, key, group_by="user", team="ops"))["rows"]] == ["carol"]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("group_by, expected", [
    ("model", {"small": 2, "big": 2}),
    ("backend", {"mock-openai": 2, "mock-anthropic": 2}),
    ("none", {"total": 4}),
    ("tag:project", {"apollo": 1, "(untagged)": 3}),
])
async def test_every_grouping(client, gateway, group_by, expected):
    await seed(gateway)
    d = await summary(client, ADMIN_KEY, group_by=group_by)
    assert {str(r["key"]): r["requests"] for r in d["rows"]} == expected


@pytest.mark.parametrize("group_by", ["day", "hour", "month"])
async def test_time_groupings(client, gateway, group_by):
    await seed(gateway)
    d = await summary(client, ADMIN_KEY, group_by=group_by)
    assert sum(r["requests"] for r in d["rows"]) == 4 and len(d["rows"]) >= 1


async def test_date_range_and_bad_input(client, gateway):
    await seed(gateway)
    today = NOW.date()
    d = await summary(client, ADMIN_KEY, group_by="none", start=str(today), end=str(today + timedelta(days=1)))
    assert d["rows"][0]["requests"] == 4 and d["start"].startswith(str(today))
    past = await summary(client, ADMIN_KEY, group_by="none", start="2020-01-01", end="2020-02-01")
    assert past["rows"] == [] and past["totals"]["requests"] == 0
    for params in ({"start": "yesterday"}, {"end": "2026-13-40"}):
        r = await client.get("/v1/reports/summary", params=params, headers=auth(ADMIN_KEY))
        assert r.status_code == 400 and "YYYY-MM-DD" in r.text
    for bad in ("nonsense", "tag:", "tag:bad name", "user; DROP TABLE requests"):
        r = await client.get("/v1/reports/summary", params={"group_by": bad}, headers=auth(ADMIN_KEY))
        assert r.status_code == 400, bad
    assert (await client.get("/v1/reports/summary")).status_code == 401
    assert (await client.get("/v1/reports/summary", headers=auth("mo-not-a-key"))).status_code == 401


async def test_summary_csv(client, gateway):
    await seed(gateway)
    r = await client.get("/v1/reports/summary.csv", params={"group_by": "tag:project"}, headers=auth(ADMIN_KEY))
    assert r.status_code == 200 and r.headers["content-type"].startswith("text/csv")
    assert 'filename="meritorder-tag-project.csv"' in r.headers["content-disposition"]
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(r.text)))

    assert {"key", "requests", "actual_cost", "savings_total"} <= set(rows[0])

    assert [row["key"] for row in mine] == ["alice"]
    assert (await client.get("/v1/reports/summary.csv?group_by=bogus", headers=auth(ADMIN_KEY))).status_code == 400

async def test_export_jsonl_scoping(client, gateway):
    await seed(gateway)
    assert (await client.get("/v1/reports/export.jsonl", headers=auth(TEST_KEY))).status_code == 403

    def users(r):
        assert r.status_code == 200 and r.headers["content-type"].startswith("application/x-ndjson")
        rows = [json.loads(line) for line in r.text.splitlines() if line]
        assert all("messages" not in row and "prompt" not in row for row in rows)  # metadata only
        return sorted(row["user_id"] for row in rows)

    assert users(await client.get("/v1/reports/export.jsonl", headers=auth(LEAD_KEY))) == ["alice", "alice", "bob"]
    r = await client.get("/v1/reports/export.jsonl", headers=auth(await finance_key(gateway)))
    assert r.status_code == 403 and "summary.csv" in r.text  # finance sees aggregates only
    r = await client.get("/v1/reports/export.jsonl", headers=auth(ADMIN_KEY))
    assert users(r) == ["alice", "alice", "bob", "carol"] and ".jsonl" in r.headers["content-disposition"]
    old = await client.get("/v1/reports/export.jsonl", params={"start": "2020-01-01", "end": "2020-01-02"}, headers=auth(ADMIN_KEY))
    assert users(old) == []


async def test_requests_detail_scoping(client, gateway):
    await seed(gateway)
    rows = lambda r: sorted(x["user_id"] for x in r.json()["rows"])  # noqa: E731
    assert rows(await client.get("/v1/reports/requests?user=carol", headers=auth(TEST_KEY))) == ["alice", "alice"]

Anthropic format"] --> same same -- "yes (common case)" --> pass["Pass through untouched

# Merit Order

An open-source LLM gateway that cuts LLM spend for day-to-day use, without changing how
people work.

Power grids dispatch generators in **merit order**: cheapest marginal cost first, with expensive
peaker plants switched on only when demand requires them. Merit Order does the same with tokens:

- **Routes** every session to the cheapest model and backend that meets the task's quality bar,
  counting what it would cost to rebuild the prompt cache somewhere else.
- **Runs open-weight models on your own GPUs** (via SkyPilot) when steady load makes that cheaper
  than paying per token, and turns them off when it doesn't. APIs (Bedrock, Foundry, Vertex,
  Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Mistral, ...) are always there for overflow.
- **Saves tokens**: automatic prompt caching, sticky sessions, cache-safe compression of huge tool
  outputs, and an optional response cache.
- **Shows the money**: every request is recorded with what it cost and what it would have cost
  without Merit Order, broken down by cause, per user, team, project, and day.

Point Claude Code, pi, OpenAI or Anthropic SDKs, or anything that speaks either API at it.

## Quickstart (no keys needed)

```bash
uv sync
cp .env.example .env            # set MERITORDER_DEV_KEY (and any provider keys you have)
uv run meritorder serve         # http://localhost:8080, reports UI at /ui/
```

```bash
curl localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $MERITORDER_DEV_KEY" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "auto", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]}'
```

With no provider keys, requests go to built-in mock backends. `uv run meritorder check` shows
which backends and models are live with the keys you've set. Without `MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL`,
storage is in memory; use Docker Compose for the real thing.

## Run the full stack with Docker

```bash
cp .env.example .env            # add at least one provider key
docker compose up -d            # gateway + worker + Postgres + Redis on :8080
docker compose exec gateway meritorder keys create --user you@example.com --role admin
```

Bedrock with your AWS profile (including SSO): `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.aws.yaml up -d`.
Kubernetes: `helm install mo charts/meritorder` (see [docs/07-deployment.md](docs/07-deployment.md)).

## Point your harness at it

```bash
meritorder login --gateway https://llm.example.com   # Entra sign-in; or: meritorder use-key <key>
meritorder setup pi                                    # adds a "meritorder" provider to pi
meritorder setup claude-code                           # sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL + apiKeyHelper
```

Write a Python module that parses a small INI-like configuration language into nested dicts. It must define:

```python
class ConfigError(Exception): ...   # must have an int attribute `line`: the 1-based line number of the error

def parse_config(text: str) -> dict: ...
```

`parse_config` raises `ConfigError` for every error described below. Parsing goes line by line from the top and stops at the first invalid line, so `line` is the number of the first line that breaks a rule.

## Lines

Split `text` on `"\n"`; if a line then ends with `"\r"`, that one `"\r"` is removed. Lines are numbered from 1. In this spec, *whitespace* means spaces and tabs. Each line, with surrounding whitespace removed, is one of:

- **empty**: ignored.
- a **comment**: it starts with `#` or `;`. Ignored.
- a **section header**: it starts with `[`.
- otherwise a **key/value pair**.

## Section headers

`[NAME]`, where `NAME` may have whitespace around it inside the brackets and is one or more *parts* joined by single dots. Each part is one or more of the characters `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -` (ASCII only), with no whitespace. After the closing `]` the line may contain only whitespace, optionally followed by a comment that starts with `#`. Anything else (`[]`, `[a..b]`, `[a b]`, `[a. b]`, `[a`, `[a]]`, `[a] x`) is an error.

A header `[a.b.c]` makes `result["a"]["b"]["c"]` the current table, creating any missing dicts along the way. Key/value pairs before the first header go into the top-level dict. The same dotted name may appear in a header only once (a second `[a.b]` is an error). A table created implicitly by a longer header may be declared later exactly once: `[a.b]` followed by `[a]` is fine.

## Key/value pairs

`KEY = VALUE`, split at the first `=`. No `=` on the line is an error. `KEY`, with surrounding whitespace removed, must be one or more of `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -` (ASCII only, so no dots and no spaces). Within one table a name may be used only once: a key repeated in the same table, a header naming a table whose name is already used by a key (or whose path runs through a key's value), and a key whose name is already used by a table are all errors, reported on the line that causes the clash. Section names and keys are case-sensitive.

The value is the text after the `=`, with leading whitespace skipped. Its first character decides its type:

1. `"`: a **basic string**, ending at the next `"` that isn't escaped. Escapes: `\\`, `\"`, `\n` (newline), `\t` (tab), and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hex digits (either case) giving that code point, which must not be a surrogate (`D800`-`DFFF`). Any other backslash sequence, a bad `\u`, or no closing quote on the line is an error.
2. `'`: a **literal string**, ending at the next `'`. No escapes: backslashes are kept. No closing quote on the line is an error.
3. `[`: a **list** on one line. Elements are separated by commas, with optional whitespace around each element and comma. An element must be a basic string, a literal string, a number, `true` or `false` (no bare strings, no nested lists). A comma after the last element is allowed. `[]` and `[ ]` are empty lists. Commas and brackets inside quoted elements are ordinary characters. A missing `]`, an empty element (`[,]`, `[1,,2]`), or an invalid element is an error.
4. After a basic string, literal string or list, the rest of the line may contain only whitespace, optionally followed by a comment that starts with `#`; anything else is an error.
5. Anything else is **unquoted**. The unquoted text runs to the end of the line, except that a `#` starts a comment (ending the text) when it is the first character of the value or the character just before it is a space or tab. Trailing whitespace is then removed. The text is:
   - empty: the value is `""`;
   - exactly `true` or `false`: the `bool`;
   - if it starts with a digit, `+`, `-` or `.`: it must be a number (below), otherwise it's an error;
   - otherwise a **bare string**, kept exactly (inner spaces, quotes, `=`, `;`, backslashes and all).

## Numbers

Let *digits* mean one or more ASCII digits where single underscores may appear between two digits (`1_000`, not `1__0`, `_1` or `1_`).

- An **integer** is an optional `+` or `-`, then *digits* that are either exactly `0` or don't start with `0` (so no leading zeros: `012`, `00`, `0_1` and `-01` are invalid; `7`, `0`, `10` and `1_0` are fine). Its value is a Python `int`; `-0` is `0`.
- A **float** is an integer as above (same sign and leading-zero rules), followed by a fraction `.` *digits*, an exponent `e` or `E` with an optional `+` or `-` and then *digits*, or both (fraction first). Its value is the Python `float` of the text without underscores. So `1e3` is `1000.0`, while `.5`, `1.`, `1.e5`, `1e` and `01.5` are invalid.

## Example

```python
parse_config('''
# service settings
name = demo server   # trailing comment
port = 8_080
[db.primary]
hosts = ["a:1", 'b:2',]
ratio = 2.5e-1
url = postgres://u@h/db?x=1#frag
''') == {"name": "demo server", "port": 8080,
         "db": {"primary": {"hosts": ["a:1", "b:2"], "ratio": 0.25, "url": "postgres://u@h/db?x=1#frag"}}}
```

# 11 — Evals: measuring model quality

`auto` routing sends each request to the cheapest model good enough for it. "Good enough" comes from
each model's **quality scores**: 1–5 per task type (coding, general). The classifier gives every
request a floor (coding:3 for ordinary coding, coding:4 for agent work with many tools, +1 for hard
tasks or large contexts), and only models scoring at least that are considered. Scores that are too
high send hard work to models that can't do it; scores that are too low waste money. Evals measure
them.

## Running one

**From the console:** Models → **Evals** → *Run an eval…*. Pick models and suites, see the
estimated cost, and start it. The worker runs it in the background, against the gateway like any
client. Progress, cost, and every task's result show on the page. When it finishes, *Apply
scores…* writes the measured scores into the configuration as a new version, which you can roll
back from Config → History. *Run again…* repeats a run with the same settings.

**From the command line** (on a machine with Docker, so code tasks run too):

```bash
uv run meritorder eval --models claude-sonnet,claude-opus,claude-fable          # estimates cost, asks first
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --only 'c5-*,a5-*' --repeat 3               # just the hardest coding work, 3 times each
uv run meritorder eval --models ... --apply                                      # also write the scores into the config
```

CLI runs are recorded too, so they appear on the Evals page, and cancelling one there stops it.

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `--suite` | `starter,frontier` | Built-in suites, task directories or YAML files, comma-separated |
| `--only` | all tasks | Task id patterns, e.g. `c5-*,g4-*` |
| `--repeat` | 1 | Runs per task. More runs mean less luck in the scores, at proportional cost |
| `--judges` | `claude-opus,gpt-sol,gemini-carbon` | Models that grade open-ended tasks (those with a live route); each answer gets the two from other families |
| `--sandbox` | `docker` | `none` skips tasks that run model-written code |
| `--threshold` | 0.75 | Pass rate a model needs at a level to earn it |

Eval traffic goes through the gateway with its usual budgets, rate limits and per-request cap, and is
tagged `eval=<suite>-<time>` in the ledger. Its spend counts like any other (for the person who ran it,
their team, the models, and the organization), and Reports → Breakdown → **Tag** → `eval` shows each
run's cost on its own line. It isn't counted as savings: a run on Haiku isn't money saved and one on
Fable isn't money lost, because you'd have run those models anyway, so its baseline is the model it
ran. Runs from the console use
a temporary key for the person who started them, revoked when the run ends.

## How each model is run

A comparison is only fair if nothing but the model differs, so a run fixes everything else and records it:

- **No output limit.** Requests set no `max_tokens`, so each model may write as much as it can
  (`max_output_tokens`: 128,000 for current Claude and GPT models), thinking included. A reply that
  fills the model's own maximum fails and is marked *cut off*. The per-request cost limit on Controls
  still applies: if it stops a reply first, the result is *not graded* (left out of the scores) and
  says how many tokens it allowed, so you can raise the limit and run it again. At $40 per million
  output tokens, Fable's full 128,000 costs $5.12.
- **The same effort.** Each task runs at the reasoning effort `auto` uses for its level
  (`routing.effort_by_floor`: low for 1–2, medium for 3, high for 4–5), not at each model's own
  default, which differs (Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 default to medium, Fable and Sonnet to high).
  A model that doesn't take that effort runs at its default. A task can set its own (`effort: max`).
- **One route per model.** Each model runs on its first live route, which in the shipped config is
  its own provider's API, rather than whichever reseller the router finds cheapest or fastest that
  minute. Judges too.
- **Each model in its own API.** Agent tasks talk to Claude over Anthropic's Messages API, the way
  Claude Code does, sending each reply back unchanged so Claude's thinking carries from one tool call
  to the next (Chat Completions has nowhere to put it, so it would be lost). Other models use Chat
  Completions; Gemini's reasoning details go back with each turn's tool results.
- **Answers are kept.** Each result keeps what the model wrote (the first 60,000 characters), an
  agent's tool calls in order, and each judge's verdict and reason on every rubric point. Click a
  result on the Evals page to read them, for instance to see which judge was right when they
  disagree.

Long replies take a while: 100,000 tokens is 15–20 minutes on the largest models. The gateway streams
from the provider meanwhile, so nothing times out.

## The suites

| Suite | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `starter` | 24 short tasks, levels 1–5: facts, arithmetic, one tool call, small code questions. Cheap; strong models max it out |
| `frontier` | 32 hard tasks at levels 3–5, built so strong models separate from the very top: 12 code tasks with 14–48 hidden tests each (an interpreter with tail calls, a regex engine matching Python's, unified diffs, recurrence rules, cron, a streaming JSON tokenizer…), 6 multi-step tool tasks (fixing bugs in small repositories, a purchase with traps, revenue from a messy database, an incident's root cause), and 14 general tasks (multi-hop questions over documents of 6k–45k words, logic grids, exact combinatorics, writing under constraints, and 3 judged pieces of open-ended work) |

Levels mean what the classifier means by them: 3 is ordinary coding, analysis or long context;
4 is agent work with many tools, or hard reasoning; 5 is the hardest of both.

## Seeing the tasks

Models → Evals → **Tasks** lists every task in the built-in suites: what it tests and how it's graded.
Open one to read everything about it: the full prompt and the tools the model gets, then what only the
grader sees (the checks, the hidden tests with a reference solution and a plausible wrong one, an agent
task's repository and the grader's data, a judged task's rubric and reference answer), and how each
model did on it in its latest run.

## Four kinds of task

| Kind | The model gets | Graded by |
|---|---|---|
| `answer` | One prompt | Mechanical checks: an exact final answer (`Final answer: …`), a number, JSON fields, a tool call, or writing constraints (word count, bullets, required phrases) |
| `code` | A precise spec for a Python module | Hidden unit tests, run against its code in a sandbox. Every test must pass |
| `agent` | A goal and tools | A scripted environment answers the tools (a small repository, a booking API, a database, logs), then checks the end state: the right fix with stricter hidden tests, the right booking made once, the exact figure |
| `judged` | Open-ended work (a summary, a critique, a recommendation) | Two judge models from different families, against a rubric of concrete statements and a reference answer. Both must agree every point is met |

**The judges.** A model tends to rate answers like its own higher, and a weaker model misses what a
stronger one gets right or wrong. So there are three judges, one from each family at the same tier:
Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. Each answer is graded by the two whose family isn't
its model's: a Claude answer by Sol and Carbon, a GPT answer by Opus and Carbon, a Gemini answer by
Opus and Sol. The judges don't know which model wrote the answer, they work at high effort, every
criterion is a checkable statement ("states the outage lasted 47 minutes"), and the answer passes
only if both say every criterion is met. Each judge's verdict and reason on every point is kept with
the result. Everything else is graded mechanically, which is cheaper and repeatable.

**The sandbox.** Model-written code runs in a throwaway Docker container (`python:3.12-slim`):
no network, a read-only filesystem apart from a small `/tmp`, an unprivileged user, no
capabilities, and limits on memory, CPU, processes and time. Each hidden test also has its own
CPU-time limit (10 s), so one runaway loop fails that test, not the whole task. A task can forbid
imports (the regex task forbids `re`); that's checked in the code's syntax tree, which keeps honest
solutions honest but wouldn't stop code written to get around it. Without Docker, those tasks are skipped
and the results say so. The worker in the Docker Compose stack has no Docker access by default, so
console runs skip code tasks there: run those with `meritorder eval` on a machine with Docker, and
their results land on the same page. (Giving a container the Docker socket gives it control of the
host, so it isn't on by default.)

## From results to scores

For each model and task type:

- **Score** (what routing uses): the highest level L where the model passes at least 75% of tasks at
  L **and every level below**. A model that aces level 5 but fails level 3 scores 2.
- **Ability** (0–5, shown next to it): the sum of its pass rates by level. Two models with the same
  score can differ a lot here; it's the finer view. A level the suite doesn't cover counts as the
  level below it did.
- **?**: at some level, there were too few task runs to be sure which side of 75% the model is on
  (its 90% confidence interval straddles 75%). Run again with `--repeat` to firm it up.

Beside the scores, each model shows what its tasks took, because two models that pass the same tasks
can still differ a lot in time and money:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Median time** (and 90th percentile) | The model's own time to complete a task: every request it answered, without grading, judges or the environment's tools |
| **Turns / tools** | Average requests and tool calls per task. An agent that needs 20 turns where another needs 6 is slower and costs more even at the same price per token |
| **Output** | Average output tokens per task, thinking included |
| **Per solve** | Cost divided by tasks passed: what a solved task costs on this model, which is what matters when choosing one |
| **Cut off** | Replies that hit an output limit |

Runs that say nothing about quality are skipped and don't count: no sandbox, no judges, a judge that
failed to give a verdict, a provider's rate limit or outage (HTTP 429 or 5xx), or a reply the
per-request cost limit stopped. Run again to fill them in. Other errors (a reply that fills the
model's maximum output or its context window, a request the model rejects) count as fails.

## Writing your own tasks

The best suite is made from your own work: a model that's good at public puzzles may still be wrong
for your codebase. A suite is a directory of task directories (or a YAML file of `answer` tasks).

```yaml
# my-suite/c4-invoice-rounding/task.yaml
id: c4-invoice-rounding
task: coding          # or general
level: 4
kind: code            # answer | code | agent | judged
prompt_file: prompt.md
code: {tests: tests.py, timeout: 30}   # hidden tests: top-level test_* functions; forbid: [re] bans imports
reference: reference.py                                    # a correct solution, never sent to models
```

- `answer`: `prompt` and `checks` (see `src/meritorder/evals/runner.py` → `grade`). Ask for
  `Final answer: …` on the last line and check it with `final`, `final_number` or `final_one_of`.
- `agent`: `env: module:Class`, `env_args`, `max_turns`. Environments subclass
  `meritorder.evals.envs.Env`: tools, `call`, and `grade`.
- `judged`: `rubric` (concrete statements) and `reference_answer`.
- Generated prompts (long documents built from a seed): `generate: module:function` with
  `generate_args`.
- Optional on any task: `effort` (instead of the level's) and `max_tokens` (only if you want the
  task to have a limit; built-in tasks don't).

Run it with `meritorder eval --suite ./my-suite`, or alongside the built-in ones:
`--suite starter,frontier,./my-suite`. Check every task offline before trusting it: the repository's
`tests/evals/` shows how (reference solutions pass the hidden tests, deliberately wrong ones fail).

**Public tasks leak.** Anything in a public repository can end up in a model's training data, which
makes it easier than it looks. Keep a private suite for the decisions that matter, and refresh it.

## Cost

The estimate before a run counts each task's prompt and a typical reply for every model, and
judging. Reasoning models often write several times more than that, and with no output limit a hard
task can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so treat it as a rough guide.
Long-document and agent tasks dominate: a level-5 document task sends about 60k tokens, and an agent
task resends its growing conversation every turn. Organization and personal budgets and the
per-request cap (Controls) apply to eval traffic like any other.

Connection pools, all per process: | Pool | Default | Setting | |---|---|---| | Upstream, per backend (each stream holds one connection) | 500 | `MERITORDER_UPSTREAM_MAX_CONNECTIONS`, `MERITORDER_UPSTREAM_KEEPALIVE` (100) | | Redis (waits for a free connection rather than failing) | 200 | `MERITORDER_REDIS_MAX_CONNECTIONS` | | Postgres | 10 | `MERITORDER_DB_POOL_SIZE`; with many processes, put PgBouncer in front | Request bodies are capped at 32 MB (`MERITORDER_MAX_BODY_MB`; Anthropic's own limit), 64 KB for sign-in, and 1 MB for SCIM; larger ones get a 413 before anything reads them. ## Ingress and TLS Merit Order is a plain HTTP service. It runs behind whatever the organization already uses: a cloud load balancer, an existing ingress controller, NGINX, Envoy. We don't ship or require a proxy in front of it. Single-machine installs that want HTTPS can enable the Caddy profile. What's exposed: Docker Compose publishes the gateway on `127.0.0.1` (set `MERITORDER_BIND=0.0.0.0` to open it to your network). Behind a public ingress, `/metrics` is reachable too; it shows spend and traffic totals, not prompts or users, but set `MERITORDER_METRICS_TOKEN` (and Helm `metrics.tokenKey`) to require a token. The console is served with a strict Content-Security-Policy and refuses to be framed. ## Configuration `config/meritorder.yaml` (plus `include:`d files and environment variables for secrets) describes everything. The image ships the default config; override files with a volume (Compose) or `--set-file configFiles.=...` (Helm). ```yaml baseline_model: claude-sonnet # counterfactual for savings reports include: [models-open.yaml] # open-weight catalog, direct vendor APIs backends: bedrock: format: anthropic base_url: https://bedrock-mantle.${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}.api.aws/anthropic auth: {type: aws_sigv4, service: bedrock-mantle, region: "${AWS_REGION:-us-east-1}"} models: claude-sonnet: aliases: ["claude-sonnet-*"] quality: {coding: 5, general: 4} routes: - {backend: anthropic, model: claude-sonnet-5-5, price: {input: 2, output: 10, cache_read: 0.10, cache_write: 2.5}} - {backend: bedrock, model: anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5, price: {input: 2, output: 10, cache_read: 0.10, cache_write: 2.5}} teams: platform: budget_usd_month: 20000 user_budget_usd_month: 500 allowed_models: ["*"] allowed_backends: ["*", "!openrouter-free"] compression: {enabled: true} ``` Useful commands: | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `meritorder check` | Which backends and models are usable with the current credentials | | `meritorder prices refresh` | Update `prices.json` and context windows from OpenRouter's catalog | | `meritorder models discover` | List the model IDs each enabled backend serves | | `meritorder keys create / list / revoke` | Manage API keys | | `meritorder login`, `meritorder setup pi` / `claude-code` | Sign in with Entra and point a harness at the gateway | | `meritorder usage` | Your own spend | | `meritorder eval --models a,b [--apply]` | Measure quality scores with graded tasks (asks before spending) | | `meritorder export --out file.csv` or `s3://…` | Export the ledger | | `meritorder worker --backfill` | Rebuild hourly report rollups from the raw ledger | | `meritorder controller [--once] [--interval 60]` | Run the GPU capacity controller | Once the first configuration is saved from the console, the stored version (in Postgres) is what gateways, the worker, and the controller use; the YAML file is the starting point and the format for import and export. ## Secrets Merit Order never stores provider keys. It reads them from the environment (`value_env`) or from a file (`value_file`), and a configuration saved from the console is refused if it contains a literal key, so keys never reach Postgres or the config history. What it does store: | Secret | Where | How | |---|---|---| | Provider keys | Environment or a mounted file | Supplied by the platform from your secret store | | `MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL`, `MERITORDER_REDIS_URL` | Environment | Same Secret as the provider keys | | Merit Order keys (`mo-…`) for people and harnesses | Postgres | Shown once; stored only as a SHA-256 hash (random 256-bit tokens, so a slow hash isn't needed) | | Entra / OIDC tokens | Not stored | Verified against the issuer's signing keys, then exchanged for a short-lived `mo-` key | **The best key is no key.** For each cloud's own models, use the workload's identity instead: | Models | Config | Identity | |---|---|---| | Claude in Bedrock | `auth: {type: aws_sigv4, service: bedrock-mantle, region: …}` | IRSA or EKS Pod Identity: a role allowed to invoke the Bedrock models you route to | | Claude on Vertex | `auth: {type: google}` | GKE Workload Identity: a Google service account with `roles/aiplatform.user` | | Azure OpenAI, Foundry | `auth: {type: azure_ad}` | AKS Workload Identity: a managed identity with *Cognitive Services OpenAI User* (or the Foundry equivalent) on the resource | The image includes the Google and Azure identity libraries. In Helm, put the identity on the service account (`serviceAccount.annotations`; AKS also needs the pod label `podLabels: {azure.workload.identity/use: "true"}`). """Capacity controller (docs/05-gpu-autoscaling.md).

Every interval, for each self-hosted backend with a ``serve:`` section:

1. Measure addressable demand: what traffic this model could serve costs per hour
   at API prices, and its token throughput. Free upgrades are excluded, so idle
   capacity can't keep GPUs alive by attracting traffic.
2. Size replicas: enough for throughput, but each replica must pay for itself.
3. Advance the state machine (gpu.decide) and act through the provisioner.
4. Publish state, endpoint, and vLLM utilization to Redis for the gateways.

Only one controller is active at a time (Postgres advisory lock).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging
import os
import time
from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

from .alerts import notify
from .config import Config
from .gpu import API_ONLY, Deployment, Demand, Status, addressable, decide, desired_replicas, fetch_utilization, make_provisioner
from .state import make_state
from .store import make_store

log = logging.getLogger("meritorder.controller")
LOCK_ID = 0x4D45524954  # "MERIT"


def deployments(cfg: Config) -> list[Deployment]:
    out = []
    for b in cfg.backends:
        if b.kind != "self_hosted" or b.serve is None or not b.enabled:
            continue
        model = cfg.model(b.serve.model)
        if model is None:
            log.warning("backend %s serves unknown model %r; skipping", b.name, b.serve.model)
            continue
        out.append(Deployment(backend=b, model=model, provisioner=make_provisioner(b, cfg)))
    return out


async def tick(cfg: Config, store, state, deps: list[Deployment], now: float | None = None) -> list[dict]:
    now = now or time.time()
    wall = datetime.fromtimestamp(now, UTC)
    rows_1h = await store.demand_rows(wall - timedelta(hours=1))
    rows_15m = await store.demand_rows(wall - timedelta(minutes=15))
    published = []
    for dep in deps:
        b, serve = dep.backend, dep.backend.serve
        cost_1h, tok_1h = addressable(dep.model, rows_1h, cfg)
        cost_15, tok_15 = addressable(dep.model, rows_15m, cfg)
        demand = Demand(usd_per_hour=max(cost_1h, cost_15 * 4), tokens_per_second=max(tok_1h / 3600, tok_15 / 900))
        desired = desired_replicas(serve, b.gpu_cost_per_hour, b.capacity_tokens_per_second, demand)

        key = f"deploy:{b.name}"
        rec = await state.get_json(key) or {}
        if rec.get("state", API_ONLY) == API_ONLY and serve.provisioner != "static":
            status = Status()  # don't poll the cloud for something that isn't running
        else:
            status = await dep.provisioner.status()
        new, action = decide(rec, serve, desired, status, now)
        if action is not None:
            try:
                if action.kind == "up":
                    await dep.provisioner.up(action.replicas)
                elif action.kind == "scale":
                    await dep.provisioner.scale(action.replicas)
                elif action.kind == "down":
                    await dep.provisioner.down()
            except Exception as e:
                log.error("%s: %s failed: %s", b.name, action.kind, e)
                new.update(state=API_ONLY, since=now, endpoint=None, replicas=0, cooldown_until=now + 1800, reason=f"{action.kind} failed: {e}"[:300])
            else:
                if action.kind == "up":
                    # A server that is already running (static) or comes up fast goes warm this cycle.
                    status = await dep.provisioner.status()
                    if status.ready:
                        new, _ = decide(new, serve, desired, status, now)
        if new.get("endpoint"):
            util = await fetch_utilization(new["endpoint"])
            if util is not None:
                await state.set_utilization(b.name, util)
                new["utilization"] = round(util, 3)
        new.update(
            backend=b.name,
            model=dep.model.name,
            desired=desired,
            demand_usd_per_hour=round(demand.usd_per_hour, 4),
            demand_tokens_per_second=round(demand.tokens_per_second, 1),
            gpu_usd_per_hour=b.gpu_cost_per_hour,
            updated=wall.isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        )
        if new.get("state") != rec.get("state", API_ONLY):
            await notify(f"GPU tier: {b.name} ({dep.model.name}) {rec.get('state', API_ONLY)} -> {new['state']}: {new.get('reason', '')}. "
                         f"Demand ${demand.usd_per_hour:,.2f}/h at API prices vs ${b.gpu_cost_per_hour:,.2f}/h per replica.")
        await state.set_json(key, new)
        published.append(new)
        log.info("%s (%s): %s, demand $%.2f/h at API prices, %.0f tok/s, desired %d replica(s) at $%.2f/h each",
                 b.name, dep.model.name, new["state"], demand.usd_per_hour, demand.tokens_per_second, desired, b.gpu_cost_per_hour)
    return published


async def run_controller(cfg: Config, once: bool = False, interval: int = 60) -> None:
    store = make_store(os.environ.get("MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL"))
    state = make_state(os.environ.get("MERITORDER_REDIS_URL"))
    if store.kind != "postgres":
        raise SystemExit("the controller needs Postgres: set MERITORDER_DATABASE_URL")
    deps = deployments(cfg)
    if not deps:
        log.warning("no self-hosted backends with a `serve:` section are enabled; nothing to control")
    await store.init()
    lock_conn = await store.pool.acquire()
    try:
        while not await lock_conn.fetchval("SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1)", LOCK_ID):
            log.info("another controller is active; standing by")
            if once:
                return
            await asyncio.sleep(interval)
        log.info("controller is active for: %s", ", ".join(d.backend.name for d in deps) or "(none)")
        while True:
            try:
                await tick(cfg, store, state, deps)
            except Exception:
                log.exception("controller cycle failed")
            if once:
                return
            await asyncio.sleep(interval)
    finally:
        await store.pool.release(lock_conn)
        await store.close()
        await state.close()

# Task: apply a unified diff

Write a Python module that applies a single-file unified diff to a text, the way `patch` does when the file has
drifted a little since the diff was made. Follow the rules below exactly; where they differ from what you know of
GNU or BSD `patch`, these rules win.

## Interface

```python
class PatchError(Exception):
    """Raised for a malformed diff or a hunk that can't be applied."""
    hunk: int   # the 1-based number of the hunk the error is about; 0 if the diff has no hunks at all

def apply_patch(original: str, diff: str, *, reverse: bool = False) -> tuple[str, list[int]]:
    """Returns (patched_text, offsets): offsets[k-1] is the offset at which hunk k was applied."""
```

`PatchError` must be an `Exception` subclass whose instances have an integer `hunk` attribute (construct it however
you like, e.g. `PatchError(message, hunk)`). Every error described below is a `PatchError`; nothing else is raised
for any `str` inputs.

## 1. Lines

A text is a sequence of lines. Only `"\n"` ends a line (`"\r"` is an ordinary character). Every line keeps its
terminating `"\n"`, except that the last line of a text may have none. The empty string has zero lines; `"a\n"` has
one line `"a\n"`; `"a\nb"` has two lines, `"a\n"` and `"b"`. Joining a text's lines gives the text back. Lines are
compared exactly, terminator included, so `"b"` and `"b\n"` are different lines.

The diff is split into lines the same way, and then each diff line's own terminating `"\n"` is dropped. (So a diff
that ends with `"\n"` has no extra empty last line, and one that doesn't end with `"\n"` is read the same way.)

## 2. Diff syntax

**Preamble.** Every line before the first diff line that starts with `@@` is ignored, whatever it contains
(`diff --git ...`, `index ...`, `--- a/file`, `+++ b/file`, notes, anything).

**Hunk header.** A line starting with `@@` begins a hunk. It must have exactly this form: `@@ -` then *A*, optionally
`,` followed by *B*, then ` +` then *C*, optionally `,` followed by *D*, then ` @@`, then the end of the line or any
further text at all (often a space and a function name). *A*, *B*, *C* and *D* are each one or more ASCII digits
`0`-`9`, read as decimal numbers. An omitted count (*B* or *D*) means 1. Single spaces exactly where shown; no other
spaces are allowed. *A*,*B* is the old range (*B* lines starting at line *A* of the old file, 1-based) and *C*,*D*
the new range. A non-empty range can't start at line 0: if *B* > 0 and *A* = 0, or *D* > 0 and *C* = 0, that's an
error. Any line starting with `@@` that doesn't have this form is an error for the hunk it would have started.

**Hunk body.** The lines after a header are the hunk's body, read one at a time until the hunk has exactly *B*
old-side lines and *D* new-side lines (immediately, if *B* = *D* = 0). Each body line is one of:

- `" "` + *text*: a context line, on both sides;
- `"-"` + *text*: a line on the old side only;
- `"+"` + *text*: a line on the new side only;
- an empty diff line (`""`): treated exactly like `" "` with empty text (editors often strip that trailing space).

The body line stands for the file line *text* + `"\n"` (but see the marker below). The prefix alone decides the kind
of line, so a body line `--- x` is an old-side line with text `-- x`, and `+++ y` a new-side line with text `++ y`.

While the hunk still needs lines, it is an error if: the diff ends; the next line is anything other than the four
forms above or a marker (for example a line starting with `@@` or with a letter); or a body line would give the old
side more than *B* lines or the new side more than *D* lines.

**No-newline marker.** A diff line that starts with a backslash (`\`, usually `\ No newline at end of file`, but any
text may follow it) says that the body line immediately before it has no `"\n"`: on both sides for a context line, on
the old side for a `-` line, on the new side for a `+` line. It doesn't count as a body line. A marker is allowed only
directly after a body line of the current hunk — including the body line that completes the hunk, so the marker may
be the line right after the body. A marker directly after a hunk header, or directly after another marker, is an
error. (Markers in the preamble are just ignored preamble lines.)

**After a hunk.** Once a hunk's body is complete (and after its marker, if one follows), the next diff line must start
a new hunk header, or the diff must end. Exception: if every remaining diff line is empty, they are ignored. Any other
line is an error for the hunk just completed.

Hunks are numbered 1, 2, 3, … in diff order. If the diff contains no line starting with `@@`, raise `PatchError` with
`hunk == 0`.

## 3. Direction

Normally (`reverse=False`) the **source** side of each hunk is its old side (context and `-` lines, range *A*,*B*)
and the **target** side is its new side (context and `+` lines, range *C*,*D*): the patch turns old into new. With
`reverse=True` the roles swap — the source is the new side (context and `+` lines, range *C*,*D*) and the target is
the old side (context and `-` lines) — so the patch is undone. Parsing and every check in section 2 are the same in
both directions. Below, *S*,*N* means the source range ((*A*,*B*) or (*C*,*D*)), and a hunk's source lines and target
lines are its lines of that side, in body order, each ending in `"\n"` unless a marker removed it.

## 4. Nominal positions and order

A hunk's **nominal position** is a 0-based index into the original text's lines: *S* - 1 if *N* > 0, and *S* if
*N* = 0 (an empty range at *S* means "just after line *S*"; *S* = 0 means "before the first line").

Hunks must be in order and must not overlap: for every hunk *k* ≥ 2, nominal(*k*) must be ≥ nominal(*k*-1) +
*N*(*k*-1); otherwise it's an error for hunk *k*.

The **entire diff is parsed and checked first** (sections 2 and 4, hunk by hunk in diff order, so the first problem
in diff order is the one reported), and only then are hunks located and applied. A malformed hunk 3 is therefore
reported even if hunk 1 wouldn't apply.

## 5. Locating each hunk

Let `lines` be the original text's lines and `L = len(lines)`. Hunks are located in order, each in the *original*
line numbering. For hunk *k*, with *N* source lines:

- `lo` = 0 for the first hunk; otherwise the position where hunk *k*-1 was applied plus *N*(*k*-1) (a hunk can never
  start inside, or before, the part of the original that the previous hunk consumed).
- `hi` = `L - N` (the last position at which *N* lines fit).
- `expected` = nominal(*k*) + the offset of hunk *k*-1 (0 for the first hunk). The previous hunk's offset is carried
  forward because a file that drifted usually drifted for every later hunk too.
- Try candidate positions in this order: `expected`, `expected+1`, `expected-1`, `expected+2`, `expected-2`, …
  (at equal distance, the later position first). Skip candidates outside `lo..hi`; keep going until every position
  in `lo..hi` has been tried. The first candidate `p` with `lines[p:p+N]` equal to the hunk's source lines (exact
  comparison, terminators included) is where the hunk applies. A hunk with *N* = 0 matches at any candidate.
- If no position in `lo..hi` matches (including when `lo > hi`), it's an error for hunk *k*.
- The hunk's **offset** is `p - nominal(k)`.

There is no fuzz (every source line must match exactly) and no special anchoring of hunks to the start or end of the
file: the search above is the only rule.

## 6. Result

The patched text is the original with, for each hunk, the `N` lines at its position replaced by its target lines;
everything else is kept. Return the patched text (lines joined with nothing in between) and the list of offsets, one
per hunk in order. A hunk's context lines come out the same either way, since they matched exactly.

def reply(text="", calls=()):
    msg = {"role": "assistant", "content": text}
    if calls:
        msg["tool_calls"] = [{"id": f"c{i}", "type": "function", "function": {"name": n, "arguments": a}} for i, (n, a) in enumerate(calls)]
    return {"choices": [{"index": 0, "message": msg, "finish_reason": "stop"}]}


def gateway_of(answer):
    """A fake gateway: ``answer(body)`` returns a reply dict (or an httpx.Response)."""
    seen = []

    def handler(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
        body = json.loads(request.content)
        seen.append(body)
        out = answer(body)
        if isinstance(out, httpx.Response):
            return out
        return httpx.Response(200, json=out, headers={"x-meritorder-cost-usd": "0.001"})
    return httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.MockTransport(handler)), seen

class CountEnv(Env):
    """Count to a target with an `add` tool, then report the total."""

    tools = [tool("add", "Add n to the counter", {"n": {"type": "integer"}})]

    def __init__(self, sandbox=None, target=3, **args):
        super().__init__(sandbox, **args)
        self.total, self.target = 0, target

    def call(self, name, arguments):
        if not isinstance(arguments.get("n"), int):
            return json.dumps({"error": "n must be an integer"})
        self.total += arguments["n"]
        return json.dumps({"total": self.total, "padding": "x" * 30_000})

    def grade(self, final_answer):
        ok = self.total == self.target and str(self.target) in final_answer
        return ok, [] if ok else [f"total {self.total}, wanted {self.target}"]
